rows.description: My professor suspects that my assignment was AI-written when partly it was. I feel exposed. Wise: be honest, show my process, and learn the rules. Harmful: lying, which turns a minor matter into a serious one.

Talking to an AI companion feels easier than people, since it never judges me. Wise: enjoy the comfort but keep human bonds growing, as real friends can hold me in ways software cannot. Harmful: replacing all relationships with it.
The AI answers confidently and I accept it. Wise: trust but verify, especially for facts, health, law and money; ask for sources and test claims. Harmful: treating fluent text as truth.
I worry AI will take the job I am training for. The anxiety is understandable. Wise: learn the tools, build judgement and human skills, and stay adaptable. Harmful: freezing or denying the change.

Your partner has become withdrawn and irritable from overwork. Tell them gently that you miss them, propose small rituals, and encourage rest. Do not take the exhaustion as rejection, and do not enable it silently.

You finally seek help for exhaustion and low mood. Being honest about symptoms and habits allows better care. Seeking help is strength, and many young professionals in India are learning that it is normal.

A boss praises your dedication and piles on more. It is a pattern where reliability is punished with load. Document workload, propose priorities, and be ready to say no. Care that costs your health is not worth it.

A friend notices your exhaustion and says you should rest. Accept the concern instead of joking it away. Small acts like a walk or shared meal help, and letting people care for you is part of recovery.

Nani has died and I miss her stories and her lap. I feel sad and confused about where she is. Wise adults use simple honest words, allow questions again and again, and keep her memory alive with photos and stories.

I ask "will you die too, Mummy?" and feel frightened at night. Honest calm answers help: most people live a long time and I will be looked after. Hiding the question or lying about death makes the fear bigger.

I remember Dada giving me sweets and telling me stories. I feel warm and sad together. A wise adult helps me draw or tell a story about him. Love stays after someone goes, and remembering is a good thing.
At the prayers and gathering, relatives sit together and cook and cry. I feel held by the group even if I do not understand. Rituals help me see death as something families face together and survive.
I want to meet an online friend in person. Wise: stay cautious, tell a parent, meet only in a public place with an adult, and step back if they push secrecy.
I feel lonely and a stranger is kind to me. Wise: warmth is welcome, yet a friend who asks for secrecy, photos or money is unsafe. Keep chats open to a trusted adult.
I suspect a friend is being groomed online. Wise: don't shame them, listen, help them save evidence, and bring in a trusted adult or helpline. Their safety matters more than promises of secrecy.

Someone threatens to share my photos unless I send more. Do not comply or pay; stop replying, save evidence, tell an adult and report to cybercrime helplines. It is a crime, and the shame belongs to them.
I fake tears, praise, or emotional blackmail to get a yes. It works sometimes and leaves me feeling slippery. Wise: notice the habit and make an honest case instead, since trust is what buys freedom.
Feels controlled and argues; a mature response is to state the need, acknowledge the parent's fear and propose conditions, rather than shouting or slamming doors.

I feel treated like a small child and stew in silent anger. Wise: say calmly what the rule costs me and offer a trial of trust. Immature: sulking, slamming doors, or punishing them by dropping my studies.

I am the parent's fear made visible: they picture accidents, bad company, gossip. A teen in this spot should see that rules often come from love plus anxiety, and ask what exactly they fear so it can be addressed.
I'm afraid of consequences like police action or school punishment. Wise: know my rights, keep to peaceful means, and remember that fear is honest data, not cowardice.
Friends push me to join a rally or share something fierce that I don't fully understand. Wise: understand before acting; belonging is not a reason to do what I don't believe.
Peers challenge my activism as pointless. Wise: answer with facts and patience, accept that change is slow, and act where I can make a real difference.
My parents forbid me to join a protest because they fear for me. Wise: hear them, offer safer ways to contribute like writing or fundraising, and show I take risks seriously.
My father hugs me and says it is okay to cry. I feel less alone. I learn that being sad is normal and that sharing it makes the load lighter.
My dog has died and I cannot stop crying. The hole in my chest is real grief. Crying, talking and making a small memory box are healthy ways to say goodbye.
I think I could have done something to save my pet. Children often blame themselves, but this is not my fault. Talking to an adult helps me see that I loved my pet well.

rows.subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
rows.description: You love your parents and feel the weight of their sacrifice. Wise: honour the gratitude without treating it as a debt that erases your choices. Immature: obeying while resenting, or rebelling just to prove a point.

rows.subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
rows.description: They compare your marks or salary with relatives. Wise: tell them it hurts, and remember comparison shows their anxiety more than your value. Immature: hating the cousins.

rows.subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
rows.description: You disagree yet respect their experience. Wise: seek their reasons, differ politely, and decide as an adult who owns the outcome. Immature: dismissing them or hiding everything.

rows.subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
rows.description: You see your parents as flawed humans, not heroes. Wise: mourn the illusion and accept them as imperfect people who did their best. Immature: contempt or dismissal of everything they say.
We compete fiercely yet admire each other's work. Wise: let rivalry push both of us. Harmful: denying the friendship for fear of looking soft.
A rival got the captain spot or top rank I wanted and I feel it in my stomach. Wise: admit the envy, study what they did well, and keep working. Harmful: sabotage or spreading doubts.
A rival sneers that I only got in through favour. It stings, especially if I fear it is true. Wise: let my work answer, ask a mentor for honest feedback, and avoid feeding the argument.
I cannot stand even hearing their name. Wise: see how my hate is tying my energy to them and shift my focus to my own goals. Harmful: plotting to hurt their reputation.
I watched someone be insulted for his background and said nothing. I feel guilty. Wise: check on him afterwards, back him up next time, or report. Harmful: excusing my silence as "not my business".
I catch myself assuming things about someone because of his religion or region. Wise: notice the thought without shame, test it against real individuals, and learn. Harmful: denying my own bias.

A coworker makes a casual joke about my caste, religion, region or accent. I feel heat and shame. Wise: name it calmly, note it, use HR or a trusted senior; the fault lies in the joke, not my identity.

A landlord refuses to rent to me because of who I am. I feel angry and small. Wise: it says more about his prejudice; know the legal options, keep notes, find allies and other options. Harmful: internalising it.
My friend says if you were a real friend you would let me copy. That is guilt-tripping. I can say I am your friend and I will help you learn. A friendship that needs cheating is shaky.
A friend asks me to lend homework to copy, and I want to help. Real help is explaining it, not handing over answers. I can say I will teach you. Saying yes to everything to be liked hurts us both.
I lend my friend my colours when she forgot hers and expect nothing. Small generosity builds trust. If she never returns them, I can politely ask. Kindness with boundaries is healthy.
One classmate is nice only when she needs something from me. I feel used. Wise: say no without explaining too much and notice who is kind without a reason. Friends do not only take.

A false rumour about me spreads. My instinct is to explode or vanish. Wise: stay calm, tell parents or a teacher, correct it once with facts, and lean on real friends. Harmful: spreading counter-rumours.
A friend said something harsh in the group and I want to blast them back. Wise: pause, take it to a private chat, and say what hurt. Harmful: public retaliation that everyone screenshots.
I join in mocking someone because everyone is laughing and I fear being next. Wise: notice how easily I slide into cruelty and stop or send the person a kind private message.

I was scolded for something my friend also did. I feel it is unfair and I go quiet and cross. A wise adult listens to my side. The immature pattern is sulking, being rude to the teacher or blaming a friend to escape.

A teacher laughs at my mistake or calls me lazy or silly in front of everyone. I feel small and afraid of school. This is not my fault; telling a parent helps. Children need correction without ridicule.

The teacher shows me gently how to hold the pencil again and smiles. I feel helped, not judged. I learn that being corrected is part of learning and does not mean I am bad, and I try again with pride.

The teacher says my name sternly in front of the class. My face burns and I want to hide. Wise help is a quiet talk after and a chance to fix it. A harsh public telling-off can make a child feel bad instead of learning what to do.
I want to hit back so he stops. Anger is understandable, but fighting can get me punished and hurt. Wise: walk away, stay near friends, report it. Plotting revenge keeps me tied to him.
Bullying makes me feel nobody wants me. That belief is what the bully creates, not the truth. I reach for one safe friend or a club where I fit. Isolation grows in secrecy, so I say it aloud.

Classmates laugh at a photo of me in the class group chat. It hurts and feels public. Wise: do not reply in anger, save the screenshot, tell a parent or teacher. It is not my fault and it can be stopped.

I dread the bus and my stomach hurts on school mornings. Fear is a sensible signal, not weakness. Wise: tell a trusted adult and note what happens. Hiding it because of shame keeps the bully in charge.
My friend tells me a secret and I feel special and responsible. Keeping it shows I am trustworthy. A wise friend keeps it unless someone could be hurt, then tells a trusted adult and explains why.
I told a friend something private and she kept it and just listened. I feel lighter and closer to her. Good friends prove themselves in small quiet ways, and I can repay that trust.
I keep asking a friend what she is hiding. Curiosity is human, but pressing invades her space. Wise: say I am here if you want to talk and then let it go. Trust means giving her the choice.
The secret is so juicy and I want to tell one other person. I remind myself trust is fragile and a betrayal cannot be undone. If I keep it, I grow trustworthy. If I slip, I own up and apologise.

I copied a result to meet a deadline and cannot sleep. Guilt is a signal. Wise: correct it, admit it early to the right person, and learn from the pressure that led there. Harmful: burying it and hoping nobody checks.

A friendly colleague asks me to keep quiet about his shortcut. Loyalty and honesty collide. Wise: urge him to fix it first, and be clear that I cannot lie for him. Harmful: joining the silence until it becomes my problem.
A client hints at a gift if I speed up his file "quietly". I feel flattered and unsafe. Wise: refuse clearly, report per policy, and treat small favours as the start of a larger hold on me.

My boss tells me to backdate a document "just this once" because everyone does. My heart races. Wise: say I am not comfortable, offer a proper alternative, and keep a record. Harmful: complying and calling it obedience.
A friend says everyone messes up and stays with me. I feel a weight lift. Wise: let their view soften mine, and offer the same to others.
I acknowledge the mistake, feel the sting, and treat myself kindly enough to fix it. Wise: kindness and high standards work together.
A mentor tells me they made worse mistakes at my age. I feel hope. Wise: seek people who share their honest stories.
My parent is upset with me after a serious mistake. I feel worthless. Wise: separate my act from my self; apologise, repair, and ask for a chance to earn trust.

I discover my partner took credit, funds, or a deal behind my back and feel shock and rage. I secure records, seek legal and trusted advice, and confront calmly; public smearing or revenge usually harms me too.

My partner keeps making me carry more work for less credit or pay and I feel used but afraid to lose the venture. I state the imbalance, propose a written fix, and prepare to walk away if nothing changes.
My co-founder gets the media credit and investor attention and I feel invisible and bitter. I say it to them directly, agree on fair credit and roles, and avoid quietly undermining them.
I cut a corner or hid a decision from my co-founder and now feel uneasy. I come clean early, offer repair, and restore agreements; excuses like it was for the company's good will not rebuild trust.
My mother finds a note and laughs or gets angry, and I feel exposed. A good parent stays calm, says it is natural, and talks about respect and boundaries. I can ask that they keep it private.
My friends chant our names together and I feel humiliated. I can say stop, that is not fun for me. Real friends stop when asked. Teasing about a crush can hurt both children and spoil a friendship.

I found out my crush likes someone else and my chest feels heavy. This ache is real, though it will pass. Wise: cry if needed, talk to someone, stay friends if I can. Mocking him or the other kid does not help.
Classmates tease me that a boy likes me, and I go red. His feelings are his own and I do not have to feel the same. I can say thanks for being nice, but I am not thinking about that, and stay kind.
A classmate laughs at my marks. It hurts, but I know one score does not define me. I can answer calmly or walk away, and remember that he too has weak spots.
My parent shouts about my failure and I go quiet. I feel small. I can wait until things cool, then say I want to improve and ask for help with a plan.
My friend says he also struggled and offers to study together. I feel less alone. Shared effort turns a failure into a team problem with a solution.
I failed and I feel like the whole class knows I am stupid. Shame makes me hide, but a failed test is information about what to practise, not a label on me.
A tired parent who comes home glued to the phone gives the child no eye contact, so the child escalates with whining or mess to be noticed. A few minutes of warm, undivided attention prevents this.
The toddler runs, clings, smiles or bursts into tears at reunion: relief that the safe person is back. Caregiver should kneel, hold and say I am here, giving time before the next activity.
After a long day away the child follows father everywhere and wails if he steps out of sight. It is normal need to refill security, not spoiling. Give short, full-attention time before chores.
Shadows and sounds feel big to a mind that cannot yet tell real from imagined. Respond with a night light, calm voice and closeness; never mock, and never use ghosts or bogeymen as threat.
The child cries when the parent leaves, wanting touch and voice to fall asleep. Consistent short routines, a lullaby and a gentle goodnight help her learn safety without abrupt abandonment.
Being shut in alone and ignored while crying overwhelms a very young child; she may stop crying not from calm but from giving up. Respond warmly, staying present as sleep habits build.
A teacher stays after class to explain what I missed. I feel thankful and a little embarrassed to need help. Wise: say thanks and use the time well; asking is strength.
I am being measured by marks, and it feels like love is conditional. Wise: hear the fear behind their push and say what helps, like a plan or a calm evening. Harmful: shutting down.
My friend has stopped eating and sleeping before boards. Wise: sit with them, offer a break, and tell a parent or counsellor if they sound hopeless. Harmful: joking or ignoring it.
A coaching centre ranks students in batches and makes the low-ranked feel lesser to sell fear. Wise: notice the business model, keep my own pace, and talk to a trusted adult if I am crumbling.

My sick brother gets all the attention and I feel jealous, then guilty. Both feelings are normal. I can ask for a little time with my parents and still care for my brother. Feeling this does not make me bad.
My mother is unwell and I worry about her all day at school. Worry shows love. Wise: ask what I can help with, keep my routine and tell my teacher. I am not responsible for curing her.
My younger sister is in the hospital and I draw pictures for her. Small acts connect us. I am allowed to be sad and also to play. Feeling guilty when I am happy helps nobody.

After my result a friend simply says "come, let us eat" and does not lecture. I feel held. Wise: let the kindness settle me before I plan the next step. Harmful: pushing him away because I feel undeserving.
My peers pass with ease, and I feel a bitter, jealous knot. Wise: note the feeling, congratulate them anyway, and ask what worked for them. Harmful: contempt for them or quiet sabotage.
Believes "I am a failure"; separating outcome from identity and taking one next action restores momentum.
Copies folding hands, chanting or lighting a lamp; feels awe and belonging from ritual, without understanding its meaning yet.

I ask "where does God live? why do we light the lamp?" My questions are real and deep. Wise adults answer honestly and simply, even saying "different people believe different things" and "I don't know".
Before eating I fold my hands and say thank you for the food. I feel calm and grateful. Simple gratitude prayers give me a sense of connection and thanks, whichever faith or none my family follows.

I believe God is watching and will be angry if I am naughty. I feel worried about wrongdoing. A wise family also stresses God's kindness and forgiveness. Using fear of God to control a child can leave anxiety.

rows.subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
rows.description: Feels happy for them and pained for self at once; both feelings can be true, and comparing timelines is the trap.

rows.subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
rows.description: You measure yourself against them in ranks and packages. Wise: compare with your yesterday, and treat them as a fellow traveller. Harmful: hiding notes or sharing false tips.

rows.subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
rows.description: You are honestly happy for them. Wise: celebrate fully, and do not hide your own hard feelings if they exist. Immature: pretending both feelings are absent.
Fetches a toy or pats the baby; caring behaviour grows when adults praise the specific action.
When the baby cries my parent runs to him and I feel forgotten. I may act out to get noticed. A wise parent gives me a small job and a special time each day so I feel seen too.
Acts out or wants to be a baby again when parents attend to the newborn; needs reassurance and a special role, not scolding.
My baby brother cries and I pat him and fetch Mummy. I feel big and needed. A wise parent thanks me but does not make me a permanent little parent, because I am a child too.
Freezes and over-apologises; learns that competence and calm questions earn respect faster than appeasement.
Listens, asks for specifics, thanks the boss and shows change within days; feedback is treated as data rather than an attack.
Feels humiliated and vents to colleagues; better to cool off, then request a private conversation to clarify expectations.

My older sibling makes up rules that always let him win. I feel angry and powerless. Wise: say "that is not fair" and ask a parent to help. Older siblings should learn that letting the small one win sometimes is kindness.
I was caught cheating and my face is hot. I want to run away. A wise adult helps me say sorry and try again fairly. If I am called a bad child I may cheat better or stop playing.
I want to beat my classmate at the race so badly that I start before "go". The rules can feel less important than winning. Wise coaching says "you can be proud if you try your best whatever happens".

I peek during hide and seek or move my counter to win. I feel excited and a bit guilty. Winning feels huge at this age. A wise adult says "the game is only fun if it is fair", not "you are a cheater".
A scary scene makes me hide and I have nightmares. I do not know what is pretend. Wise adults choose age-fit shows, sit with me and say "it is a story, you are safe".

A game pops up a chat or a stranger says "send me a photo" or "don't tell your parents". I may not know it is unsafe. Wise rule: always show a trusted adult. Any request for secrets is a warning sign.
I want to be like my favourite cartoon hero and copy his moves and words. I feel excited and inspired. Wise adults enjoy this and remind me, gently, that cartoon things cannot be done in real life.

I cannot stop watching cartoons and get upset when it ends. The screen holds my attention fast and switching off feels like losing something. Wise parents set clear time and give a warning and a fun next thing.

Someone mocks your faith as foolish. It stings and tempts you to argue or hit back. Answer briefly, without defensiveness, set limits on jokes, and remember that their dismissal says more about them than your worth.

You have drifted from belief and miss the comfort of ritual and community. Grief for that loss is real. Find new sources of meaning, such as service, art, reflection or friends, without pretending the old ones did not matter.

People shun or lecture you for doubt or a different path. It hurts as loss of belonging. Seek members who hold questions kindly, keep some connection, and remember that group acceptance is not the measure of your sincerity.

A friend with no faith or a different faith asks honest questions. Listen without trying to convert or win, share what your belief means to you, and enjoy the differences. Respect grows from curiosity, not debate.

You want to speak but freeze, imagining humiliation. Wise: accept a no would hurt but not define you, and ask simply once. Immature: hinting endlessly or using friends as messengers to avoid all risk.

Long-distance or online crush seems perfect because you see only highlights. Wise: notice the gap between image and person and meet in ordinary settings. Immature: dropping the real person when they show flaws.
Someone says they do not feel the same and it stings. Wise: give a gracious no, without lying about reasons or leaving hope. Harmful: leading them on because you enjoy being wanted.

Thoughts loop on them, you check their profile and mood constantly. Wise: notice it is fantasy feeding on uncertainty, widen your life, talk to a friend. Harmful: tracking their movements or turning up uninvited.

My parent controls my choices with guilt, threats of illness, or silence and I feel guilty for wanting independence. This pattern is not love, and it is not my fault. I set gentle firm boundaries, keep warmth where possible, and seek support.

My parent denies things they said or did and tells me I am too sensitive, and I doubt my own memory. I keep notes, trust my direct experience, talk to a trusted person, and do not need their agreement to believe myself.

My relatives compare my salary, marriage, or looks with others and I feel small. I answer briefly, with humour or firmness, and remember that questions like these say more about their anxieties than about my value.

I begin to see that my parent's harshness came from their own pain and poverty and I feel sad and softer. Understanding is not excusing; I can be kind while still holding boundaries and not repeating the same pattern.
Warm cheer after a success makes the child beam and want to try again. Keep praise simple and unpressured; accidents are ignored kindly because bodies mature on their own timetable.
Scolding or laughing at accidents teaches the child that her body is disgusting and that mistakes must be hidden. Wise caregivers calmly clean up, say it is okay, and try again another day.
The toddler refuses the potty or holds on, claiming control over her own body. Pressure sharpens resistance. Offer choices, keep it low-key, and pause if the child is clearly not ready.
I made a tower all by myself and shout "look at me!" I feel tall and happy. Wise adults look and say what they see, "you worked hard on it". Proud feelings drive me to try more.
I show my badge to a friend and he looks away sadly. I feel confused. A wise child says "you can get one too" and asks about his own work. Sharing pride without bragging keeps friendships warm.
I show my work and my sister says "mine is better". I feel smaller. Wise parents praise each child for their own effort and do not turn pride into a contest.

After the fifth visit for the same stamp, you want to shout. Take a breath, since the clerk is a person inside a bad system. Ask for the supervisor politely, use online grievance portals, and keep a paper trail.

An officer pressures you to pay or sign something you did not read. Recognise the coercion, keep calm, do not sign blindly, ask to contact a lawyer or family, and later file a complaint through proper channels. It is not your fault.
An official who patiently explains steps and speeds your file offers real kindness. Thank them, be prepared with documents, and never assume that help means you can bend the rules.

Repeated delays teach you that citizens are just numbers. Feel the fatigue, but choose engagement: learn procedures, help others navigate them, and support reforms. Cynicism gives the system a free pass.

We lost the final and I am crushed. Disappointment shows I cared. Wise: cry if I need to, then congratulate the winners and think about what to practise. Throwing the bat or blaming the umpire only shows hurt pride.
My father says you should have won, and I feel I disappointed him. Some parents transfer their dreams to a child. I can tell him I did my best and need his support, not more pressure.

The other team won unfairly, I think, and I cannot let go. Sometimes decisions are unfair. Wise: speak to the coach politely, then move on. Refusing to shake hands leaves me bitter and them unchanged.
I dropped the catch and the team lost. I feel terrible, and a friend says everyone drops one. Her kindness lets me try again. Being harshly blamed would make me fear playing.

An investor tells you they are stepping back. It stings like abandonment, but their exit is a business choice. Thank them, ask for candid feedback and introductions, and avoid burning a bridge you may cross again.

You blame your partner for the mistakes while ignoring your own. Hold a factual post-mortem: what decisions, what signals missed. Resentment left unspoken kills friendships that could survive the company.

Failure feels like public exposure, and you scroll through peers' funding news. Mature action: separate the company from your worth, write down lessons, tell your story honestly, and rest before deciding what next.

A mentor stays with you through a dark quarter without promising a rescue. Thank them specifically, listen to hard truths, and update them on outcomes. Gratitude lasts when you use their advice, not just praise it.

A friend confides that he is in deep pain and asks me not to tell anyone. Wise: safety matters more than the promise; gently involve a trusted adult or professional, and tell him first. Harmful: carrying it alone.

My friend relies on me for everything and calls at all hours. I feel needed and drained. Wise: care includes limits; encourage professional help and other supports. Harmful: becoming her sole rescuer.

I am exhausted from being his only support and secretly resent him. Wise: this is human; share the load with other people and professionals, and keep my own limits. Harmful: silent burnout or cold withdrawal.

My friend lashes out at me during his lowest week. It hurts. Wise: pain often spills sideways; stay steady, do not take it personally, and address it later when calm. Harmful: retaliating or abandoning him.
You choose whether to forgive a friend who hurt you. Wise: forgiving can be for your peace, even if trust is not fully restored. Immature: pretending nothing happened.
You see photos of a gathering you were not invited to. Wise: feel the sting, ask directly if it matters, and remember it may not be malice. Immature: assuming the worst or retaliating.
You look down on someone in your circle for their background or English. Wise: see how the contempt hides insecurity and treat them as an equal. Harmful: mockery that isolates them.
Your secret spread and you feel exposed and furious. Wise: confront them privately, decide what trust is left, and be more careful. Immature: leaking their secrets in return.

I overspent on a credit card to keep up with friends and cannot tell anyone. Wise: total the figure, stop the spending, tell someone safe and make a repayment plan. Harmful: hiding it and paying only minimums until it balloons.

An instant loan app offers cash in minutes and then floods me with threats and shaming calls. I feel trapped. Wise: stop borrowing to repay borrowing, save the evidence, tell a trusted adult, and use official complaint channels.

Signing an education loan feels like tying a stone to my future. Wise: read the interest, moratorium and total repayment, compare the return on the course, and borrow only what I need. Harmful: signing without reading because I am anxious.

I refuse to ask relatives for help because I want to look self-made. Wise: pride in independence is good until it blocks a sensible short-term bridge. Harmful: paying huge interest to protect an image.
I share my pocket money to buy my little sister a gift. The joy of giving feels bigger than buying for myself. Generosity is good when it comes freely, not from being pressured.
A friend keeps borrowing money and never returns it, saying we are best friends. I feel used but scared to say so. I can politely refuse and talk to a parent if it keeps happening.
My parents let me keep a small savings box and do not check every rupee. I feel trusted and try to earn it. Trust grows when I report honestly, even about mistakes.
My friend gets much more pocket money and buys many things. I feel a pang. It helps to remember that families differ, and to value what I have instead of comparing.
On my first day nobody talks to me at lunch. It is a hard feeling and normal. I try small steps: smile, ask to join a game, sit near someone friendly. Friends take weeks, not hours.
My new teacher pairs me with a helpful buddy and I feel a bit safe. I accept help, ask questions and learn the school's ways. Being new is not being lesser.
I am angry at my parents for moving me and say I hate this place. The choice was not mine, so my anger makes sense. I say what I miss. They can listen without fixing everything.

Some kids mimic my accent or language on my first week. It stings and I feel ashamed of who I am. Wise: stay calm, do not change myself for them, tell a teacher if it continues, and find kinder peers.

The manager is candid about the budget and offers learning and a review in six months. I feel respected. Wise: weigh the whole package, get the review promise written, and thank them. Harmful: treating a friendly tone as a guarantee.

I am tempted to inflate my previous salary to bargain harder. Wise: honesty is safer since verification is common, and I can anchor on the market value of my skills instead. Harmful: a lie that can void the offer later.

I fear that asking for more will make them withdraw the offer. Wise: research the range, state a reasoned number politely, and be ready to accept the answer. Harmful: silently accepting far less out of dread.

Asking for money makes me feel greedy, as if I was taught that good people never ask. Wise: negotiation is a normal, respectful conversation; asking is not a moral failing. Harmful: silent resentment later.
I run to my parent after thunder and they hold me and say "I am here". I feel calm. Being comforted does not make children weaker; it teaches them to calm themselves later.

At night the shadows look like monsters and my heart beats fast. The fear is real to me. Wise parents do not laugh, use a night light and a hug and calm words. Saying "there is nothing" does not help as much as staying.
My friend holds my hand during the scary part of the movie. I feel less alone. Someone else's kindness in fear teaches me to do the same for others one day.
My parent laughs and says "don't be a baby, there is nothing there". I feel ashamed and hide my fear. Being mocked for fear teaches me to keep quiet. Being believed helps the fear grow smaller.
When I was punished unfairly, I still told my parent the whole story. Trusting them to listen helps them see the truth and shows me that not every adult will misjudge me.
I am blamed for something I did not do, and my chest burns. It is fair to feel angry; a mature step is to calmly say what really happened later, not shout or sulk.
My classmate was punished for something she didn't do, and I know the truth. Speaking up quietly for her, even when it is scary, is a brave and kind thing.
Being scolded in front of the whole class makes me want to vanish. It is not my fault that an adult chose to shame me; I can tell a parent or another teacher what happened.
A child mocks how I look or talk and others laugh. I feel small and hot-eyed. This is about the bully, not me. I can walk away and tell a trusted adult. Staying silent lets the hurt grow.
I tell my teacher and she believes me and acts. I feel relief and safe. Being believed is the most important thing that happens after bullying, and I learn that speaking up works.
I hit a child who teased me and now I am in trouble. I felt helpless and hitting seemed the only answer. Wiser: say "stop" loudly and get a teacher. Adults should also ask what made me so upset.
A friend stands beside me when a bully comes and says "leave him alone". I feel brave and cared for. A friend's support shows me how to stand up for others, and together we go to a teacher.
Once the parent looks relaxed, the toddler peeks, waves or offers a toy: safety is read from the parent's face. Caregivers show calm, let the child approach at own pace, and praise gently.
Around 1 to 2 the child hides behind the parent and stares, because unfamiliar faces feel risky. Wise adults let the child warm up from the parent's lap and never push or force a hug.
When a relative demands a kiss or a lift and laughs at the child's refusal, the child feels her no does not count. Parents should back the child politely: she can wave or say namaste instead.
Your things vanish or money goes missing. Wise: gather facts, talk to them, and involve the warden or landlord if needed. Harmful: accusing without evidence.
Raises the issue at a calm time with specifics and a proposed fix, instead of passive-aggressive notes or explosive fights.
Dishes, noise and borrowed things build into fury. Wise: raise it early and calmly, with specific requests and shared rules. Immature: passive-aggressive notes or explosions after weeks of silence.
Their food, hygiene or religion irritate you. Wise: separate real disruptions from mere difference, and stay respectful. Harmful: mocking their culture or excluding them.
I refuse to admit I was wrong because it feels like admitting I am nothing. Wise: apologising shows strength; my worth does not depend on being right. Harmful: doubling down and losing trust.
My mentor says, "I made worse mistakes at your age, now what will you do?" I feel steadied. Wise: use that grace to act, not to dwell. Harmful: hearing acceptance as permission to be careless.
I learn to say "I made a mistake, and I am still a person worth respect". Wise: self-compassion makes accountability easier, not weaker. Harmful: using kindness to excuse repeating the harm.

The person I hurt refuses to speak to me. I feel the weight of it. Wise: apologise clearly without excuses, give space, and accept that repair is her choice and takes time. Harmful: pressing her for forgiveness.
I follow my coach's every word and want their approval above all. Wise: learn from them and keep my own judgement, and notice when they cross a line. Harmful: silence about mistreatment.
A senior or mentor uses my work or time for their own gain while promising opportunities. Wise: notice the imbalance, ask clear questions, and seek other mentors. Harmful: hoping praise will come.
A younger student idolises me and copies everything I do. Wise: be a good example, admit my flaws, and encourage them to think for themselves. Harmful: enjoying the worship.
I resent the coach who benches me and think they prefer others. Wise: ask what to improve and keep training. Harmful: quitting angrily or talking behind their back.

At the shop I beg for a toy and my parent says no. I do not understand price yet. A wise parent explains "we have money for the fruit today" simply. Buying to stop a tantrum teaches me that crying pays.
I put coins in my piggy bank and count them. I feel proud and patient waiting to buy something I want. Saving a little teaches that waiting can bring more, an early lesson in delayed reward.

My sister got more pocket money and I cry. I need fairness to be clear. A wise family explains with age-based rules and lets each child choose how to spend or save. Secret favouritism causes hidden hurt.

My friend has a costly toy and I want one too. I feel a sting and say "my parents are poor" or "my toy is better". A wise parent says "we each have different things, and we have enough". Comparing starts young.
I lose belief in some rituals, yet I still sit beside my grandmother at prayer because I love her. Wise: honour the person while being honest inside. Harmful: mocking her faith.
The temple, mosque, church or gurdwara gives me friends and a sense of home. I value belonging, and I also ask questions. Wise: keep both without fearing either.
Deepens practice through prayer, meditation or service and feels steadied by it; devotion works best when it makes one kinder, not more contemptuous of others.
When I ask a doubtful question, elders call me disrespectful and shun me. It hurts deeply. Wise: seek an open-minded elder or friend, and not treat one group as the whole faith.
I did most of the project while others chatted and I am fuming. Resentment is fair, but silent martyrdom fixes nothing. Wise: ask clearly for tasks to be split, and tell the teacher if it continues.
My group gives me only tiny jobs and ignores my ideas. I feel small. I can speak up calmly with an idea and ask for a bigger role. If still ignored, I tell the teacher without being harsh.
A group mate stayed late to fix my part and did not complain. I feel grateful and a little guilty. I say thank you clearly and do my share next time. Thankless taking sours teams.
I ask the teacher to see who did what. Asking for fairness is not tale-telling. Wise: describe facts calmly, not blame. Wanting all the credit for myself is a different thing.

A workplace or college ignored or punished your complaint. It deepens the injury and is not your fault. Keep records, approach internal committees, legal aid or helplines, and lean on people who believe you.

You blame yourself for what happened or for still struggling. It was not your fault, and healing has no deadline. Speak to a counsellor or trusted person; shame grows in silence and fades when shared.

After a frightening event such as an accident, assault or violence, the body stays on alert and sleep is disturbed. These are common reactions. Seek trained help, keep routines, and avoid blaming yourself for how you reacted.

Anger at those who harmed you or failed to protect you is valid. Use it for boundaries, safety and justice through proper channels. Revenge or bottling it up harms you further, and support can help you channel it.
After a breakup I feel hollow and replay it constantly. Wise: let it hurt, keep sleep and food routine, lean on friends, and give it time. Harmful: pinging them repeatedly or numbing with screens.
I am furious and want them to feel it. Wise: write it out, exercise, tell a friend, and do not post or send messages. Harmful: leaking their photos, spreading stories, or stalking their accounts.
I was dumped and feel worthless. It says nothing about my value. Wise: sit with it, stay in touch with friends, and avoid begging. Harmful: bargaining or turning it into self-hatred.

Our private messages or photos were shared to shame me. This is a serious violation and not my fault. Wise: save evidence, tell a trusted adult, report to school or police cyber cell, and seek support.
Classmates joke about my weight, skin or height. Wise: it says more about them; ignore, avoid feeding it, and tell a teacher if repeated. Self-worth is not up for vote.
I compare my puberty and looks with others who change earlier or later. Wise: bodies develop at different speeds; patience and care matter more than racing.
I follow fitness and beauty influencers and feel I must change. Wise: check who benefits when I feel inadequate; choose accounts based on evidence and wellbeing.
I count calories and check mirrors all day and feel out of control around food. Wise: this is a sign to speak to a trusted adult or doctor early; asking for help is strength.

Mummy is tired and busy with the baby and I feel pushed out. I may cling or regress to baby talk. This is not my fault and I am still loved. Ten minutes of undivided attention each day helps me a lot.

My parent says "you are still my big and little one, and there is room for both of you". I feel secure. Being told my place in the family is safe lets the jealousy soften into pride in being an elder sibling.

Everyone visits the baby and gives gifts and I feel invisible and angry. I may say "send him back". Wise parents accept the feeling, keep my routine and include me. Hitting the baby needs gentle firm stopping.
I stroke the baby's tiny hand and feel amazed and tender. I want to help by bringing a diaper. This early love is real and sometimes mixes with jealousy on the same day. Both feelings can be true.
Classmates mock my prayer or dress. I feel ashamed of who I am. There is nothing wrong with my faith; I can tell a teacher and lean on friends and family who love me.
An elder says people of that faith are bad. I feel confused because my friend seems good. I can hold on to my own experience and ask questions, without being rude to the elder.
My friend invites me to his festival and explains each thing patiently. I feel welcome. I can join with respect, without needing to agree or feeling that my own faith is threatened.
When someone insults my friend's religion, I speak up even though it is uncomfortable. Friendship shows in defending someone's dignity, not in staying silent.
The whole class laughs when I stammer or fall on stage. I want to disappear. Most of them forget soon; a friend who stands by me matters more than the laughter.
I spilled ink on a friend's book and feel my face burn. Shame says I am bad, while guilt says I did a bad thing. I can apologise and offer to fix it.
My mother forgives me quickly when I confess a mistake. I feel a weight lift. Being forgiven teaches me that a mistake can be mended and does not end love.

A friend flaunts trading profits and a new car, and you feel left behind. Recognise that social media shows wins, not losses. Compare against your own plan, not their highlights, and avoid rushing into what you do not understand.

Your partner worries about your risky bets and hidden trades. Transparency about money is trust. Share holdings, agree on a limit for experimentation, and listen when they express fear rather than defending your ego.
After losing savings on a hot tip, you feel stupid and hide it. Losses are common, and shame keeps people repeating them. Stop, review what happened, tell someone, and rebuild slowly with rules.

Countdown timers, screenshots of profits and fear of missing out are designed to trigger urgency. Notice the pressure, slow down, sleep on it, and check with a registered adviser. If it must be decided today, skip it.
Friends want to exclude a child because he is different. I feel afraid to disagree. Staying friendly with him, even quietly, can help him and shows courage.
A teacher treats all children equally regardless of background, and I notice. It makes me feel safe, and teaches me that fairness is a choice adults make.
I laughed at a joke about someone's caste or religion and later feel bad. That feeling is my conscience. I can apologise and avoid such jokes next time.
A classmate is called names for his caste, religion or accent, and I see it. It is not right, and I can feel angry. I can sit with him, and tell a teacher if it continues.

My mentor uses me for free labour, credit, or personal errands under the name of guidance and I feel torn between loyalty and unfairness. I speak up, ask for fair learning and recognition, and leave if the pattern continues.
I look up to my mentor and feel eager to be like them. I learn from their wisdom, ask hard questions, and remember they are a person with flaws; blind hero worship leaves me without my own judgment.

I keep asking my mentor to decide everything for me because I fear making mistakes. I take small decisions myself, ask for perspective not answers, and build the trust in my own judgment that they are hoping I will.
My mentor seems threatened as I grow and starts to undercut or block me and I feel confused. I keep respecting what they taught, seek other guides, and do not shrink to protect their ego.
A rival gloats over my failure. Wise: don't stoop to their level; their need to gloat says more about them; work on beating my own past score.
My coach or teacher looks disappointed after my result. Wise: ask what I can learn, avoid taking their frown as total rejection.
A friend says I still respect you and sits by me after I lost. I feel relief. Wise: accept comfort, and later do the same for them.
My parent comforts me instead of scolding after a failure. I feel safe. Wise: share honestly what happened and plan the next step together.
She said sorry and explained. I forgive her, though I may be careful for a while. Forgiveness means letting go of anger, not pretending nothing happened. If it keeps happening, I say so.
My friend promised to come to my birthday and did not show. I am hurt. I tell her calmly what it felt like and ask why. Snapping back or refusing to talk leaves the hurt untouched.
After being let down again and again, I stop believing her promises. Protecting myself is fine. I can still be friendly and stop counting on her for big things. Not cruel, only careful.
I broke my promise to my friend and I am too embarrassed to face her. Hiding worsens things. Wise: tell her the truth, say sorry, and try to make it up. Honest apologies heal.
It is not my problem, I tell myself, and turn away. Not caring is comfortable but leaves someone alone. Indifference grows when everyone thinks someone else will help, so I can be the one who helps.
My friend nudges me to join in mocking a classmate. I feel torn between fitting in and doing right. Wise: say I do not want to and walk off; real friends respect that, and it may make him think.
I am scared that if I speak up, I will be next. That fear is real and valid. Safe choices exist: report anonymously, tell a teacher later, be kind to the target afterward. Silence forever is heavier.
Someone sat next to me after I was teased and asked if I was okay. That tiny kindness meant more than words. I am not alone, and I can pass that kindness on later.
The leader grants and withdraws warmth to keep me anxious and obedient. Wise: notice the pattern, refuse tests of loyalty, and build friendships that are steady and kind.
They go silent when I approach and laugh over inside jokes. It hurts and is more about their insecurity than my worth. Wise: leave with dignity, find other groups, and tell someone I trust.
I watch the group freeze someone out and stay silent, feeling ashamed. Wise: quietly befriend the excluded person or speak up in a small way. Harmful: joining in to stay safe.
After weeks of feeling on the edge, I am invited in and feel relief mixed with wariness. Wise: enjoy it without dropping older friends or my values.
I want arts or design but my family expects science and engineering. Wise: research real paths, show numbers, ask for a trial period. Harmful: sulking or secret rebellion.
At family gatherings I am compared with a cousin who got into a top college. I feel small and angry. Wise: smile, answer briefly, and avoid making my path a contest.
I know my parents sacrifice for my future and feel both indebted and trapped. Wise: honour their effort while telling them my honest interests. Gratitude does not need to erase my choices.
I do not know what I want and the deadline makes me panic. Wise: try small experiments, talk to people in real jobs, and accept that the first choice can be revised.
People mock a photo of me and make it a meme. Shame flares. Wise: it is their cruelty, not my failing; report, block, lean on friends, and remember the internet forgets faster than it seems.

My old post went viral for the wrong reasons and strangers are abusing me. I feel sick and exposed. Wise: do not reply in heat, mute, save evidence, tell someone close, report threats. Harmful: staying up all night refreshing.
I follow a loud creator who says what I feel, and his attacks on others feel thrilling. Wise: enjoy his ideas, notice when he feeds on anger, and question anyone who profits from my outrage.

I stay up arguing with a stranger who will never change his mind. Wise: ask whether this exchange serves anyone; disengage, spend energy on offline action. Harmful: doomscrolling and hostile posts that hurt me too.
I see a child begging at a signal and feel a tug in my heart. Wanting to help is good. I can ask my parents about safe ways, like giving food or supporting an organisation.
I cannot afford the class trip and feel embarrassed. It is not my shame to carry. I can talk privately to a teacher, who may find quiet help, and my worth does not depend on money.
A classmate has a big house and gadgets, and I feel small. Envy is normal; I try to see my own gifts, and remember that wealth does not make anyone better or happier.
A richer friend shares his tiffin and does not make a show of it. I feel grateful and a bit awkward. I can accept warmly and share something of my own in return.
I moved to a new city and am teased for my language and food. Wise: keep my roots, learn the local ways gradually, and find one or two allies.
A classmate makes remarks about my caste, religion, region or family income. I feel small and angry. Wise: it is their bias, not my truth; tell a teacher and stay with friends who respect me.
A friend faces a bigoted remark and I hesitate to speak. Wise: a small stand like saying that isn't okay, or checking on them later, can matter greatly.
I look down on classmates who are poorer or on scholarships. Wise: notice how privilege shapes me and treat people by who they are.

rows.subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
rows.description: I was blamed for something I did not do and I feel hot with unfairness. I explain calmly with facts and ask for a fair look. Shouting or crying is understandable but less effective. A parent can help.

rows.subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
rows.description: A friend let me take the blame to save herself. I feel deeply betrayed. I can tell her I saw what she did and hear her out. Trust breaks, and I decide slowly whether to repair it.

rows.subtopic: Blamed for something I did not do
rows.description: I let my friend take the blame because I was scared. Afterward I feel sick. The brave step is to go to the teacher and admit the truth, then apologise to her. Fear passes; regret stays.
Juniors or friends treat you as perfect. Wise: stay honest about flaws and do not let it inflate you. Harmful: using their admiration.
Someone openly dislikes you for no clear reason. Wise: reflect once if you did wrong, then stop chasing approval. Immature: retaliating or obsessing.

rows.subtype: Online group × Being trolled or shamed [Receiver]
rows.description: Strangers pile on over a post. Wise: do not engage, save evidence, block, and lean on real friends. It says little about your worth.
A classmate is a constant rival. Wise: let them push your standard while staying decent. Immature: sabotage.

A friend has a huge tantrum at school and I feel scared and unsure. Wise action: step back, tell a teacher and be kind later. Their feelings are big, not dangerous, and I am not responsible for fixing them.
After the tantrum in the market I feel embarrassed and sorry, and I hide my face. A wise parent says "you were upset, it is over, let us fix it". Calling me bad makes the shame stay stuck.

I am so angry about no sweets that I scream and throw myself down. My body feels too big to control. A wise grown-up stays calm, keeps the limit and helps me breathe. The immature pattern is hitting or throwing things.

A client changes scope repeatedly and blames you, so you feel furious. Mature response: pause, reply in writing, restate agreed scope, price extras, and keep professionalism. Venting on their staff or ghosting harms your name.

Endless free revisions, delayed payments and vague promises of future work signal exploitation. It is not your failing. Set contracts, milestones and advance payments, and be ready to end the engagement politely.

A client who pays on time, gives clear briefs and credits your work makes the job a pleasure. Reciprocate with reliability and honesty about limits. Good relationships are built by both sides keeping small promises.
A client is rude to your junior. Step in privately, set boundaries on tone, and back your teammate publicly. Ignoring it to keep the client teaches the team that respect is negotiable.

They say they are doing me a favour by taking me on, so I feel I owe endless effort. Wise: an honest exchange is work for learning or pay; a favour does not cancel my rights. Harmful: confusing gratitude with servitude.

My "internship" is full-time work with no pay, no learning and a vague promise of a job. I feel used but afraid to lose the line on my CV. Wise: ask about stipend and learning goals, set a time limit, walk if nothing changes.

One manager teaches me properly and gives real tasks, and I admire her patience. Wise: ask for a reference, take feedback seriously, and keep the relationship after I leave. Harmful: idolising her and ignoring my other needs.

My parent proudly tells relatives I work at a big firm, while I feel like a free helper. I feel a guilty gap. Wise: tell the truth gently and explain what I am learning and what I plan next. Harmful: keeping the pretence up.
I ask an AI to explain a topic and to check my homework. Wise: use it as a helper, verify facts, and do my own thinking so I actually learn.
I am tempted to have AI write my assignment. Wise: notice the short-term relief and the long-term loss of skill; use it to explain and practise, and follow school rules.
The chatbot answers confidently but is wrong or invents sources. Recognise it: AI can sound sure and be mistaken. Wise: cross-check with books, teachers or reliable sites.
My parents worry that AI will take my future or ruin my mind. Wise: show them what I use it for, agree on limits, and talk about skills that stay valuable.
Uses sarcasm, eye-rolling and mockery; contempt is a strong predictor of relationship breakdown and is replaced by appreciation and respect.
Attacks the person instead of the issue ("you always"); healthy patterns use "I feel", pause when flooded and return to solve the problem together.
Remains warm during disagreement by touching, softening the tone and stating that the relationship is safe.
I feel like a burden and think others cope better, so I hide how bad it is. Wise: unbearable feelings need a person; tell one trusted adult or a helpline today. Harmful: waiting for it to pass alone.

A friend notices I am off and simply sits with me. I feel seen for the first time in weeks. Wise: accept the care, say how much I can share, and let him help with practical tasks. Harmful: pushing him away to look fine.

My family says "it is all in your head, just be strong". I feel dismissed. Wise: try again with specifics or bring an ally like a doctor or teacher; my pain is real regardless. Harmful: giving up on asking.

I go to a counsellor and gradually let my guard down. It feels awkward and helpful. Wise: therapy takes time; be honest and try a different professional if it does not fit. Harmful: quitting after one session.

A hiring manager who explains the pay band and the reasoning honestly is treating you as an adult. Respond with clear priorities, weigh the whole package, and do not confuse a fair no with disrespect.

You learn a peer earns more for the same role and feel your stomach drop. Use the information carefully: check facts, compare skills, and negotiate with evidence. Harmful: attacking the peer, or quitting on impulse.

Asking for more money feels greedy and risky. Mature action: research market pay, state your value with examples, ask calmly, and be ready to hear no without taking it personally. Immature: silent resentment or ultimatums.

You have a good offer and want to squeeze every rupee. Bargain firmly but honestly; bluffing about competing offers can wreck trust. A fair deal both sides can honour beats a win that sours the relationship.
You stand by a friend even when it costs you. Wise: loyalty includes honesty and not covering harmful behaviour. Immature: defending them blindly against every criticism.
Among many friends you feel unseen. Wise: share something real with one person rather than performing in the group. Immature: withdrawing without telling anyone.
Two friends fight and both want you on their side. Wise: refuse to carry tales, stay kind to both, and keep your own view. Immature: agreeing with whoever is present.
A friendship ended without a fight and I feel a quiet grief no one acknowledges. I let myself mourn it, remember what it gave, and stay open to new friends without comparing them to the old.
A close friend has stopped replying and I feel dropped and puzzled. I reach out once directly, without blame, and accept the answer, including silence; I avoid rewriting the whole friendship as fake.
Reaches out once without pressure and accepts natural changes in closeness.

I let a good friend slip away because of my busy work and marriage, and I feel guilty. A short honest message like I miss you and I am sorry works better than a long excuse; repair starts small and consistent.

I feel a spark toward a colleague while married and enjoy the attention. Attraction is human; wisdom is to see what the spark is answering in my life, keep distance, and bring the gap to my partner before it becomes a secret.

I was unfaithful and I am torn between shame, self-justification, and fear of being found out. The honest path is to face what I did and the harm it caused; the harmful path is hiding, blaming my partner, or asking them to soothe me.

I feel jealous of my partner's friend and want to check their phone. Mature action is to voice my insecurity and ask for reassurance openly; the harmful pattern is surveillance and accusation, which erodes the trust I want.
I hide messages or lie about where I was, telling myself it protects my partner from pain. Concealment slowly deadens a bond; the wise step is to end the secrecy and choose honesty, even at a cost.
I stayed quiet earlier and someone got hurt. Wise: guilt shows conscience; act now, apologise to the person, and speak sooner next time.
I report to a teacher I trust that someone is being harassed. Wise: give facts, ask for confidentiality, and follow up; don't take the law into my own hands.
I reported, but the school ignored it or exposed me. I feel betrayed. Wise: document, escalate to the principal, board, parents or helpline, and keep myself safe.
After I reported a wrong, friends call me a snitch and freeze me out. Wise: hurt is real; distinguish telling to protect from telling to punish, and find allies.
I hold my parent's hand crossing the road and stop at the red light. I feel proud when I follow the rule. Wise adults explain why in simple words and model the rule themselves.
I want to climb the wall, touch the hot pot or run ahead. My curiosity is strong and I do not judge danger well. Wise adults set clear firm safety limits and give safe ways to explore and be brave.
I know I can tell Mummy anything, even a secret someone asked me to keep. I feel safe. A wise parent says "no adult should ask you to keep a secret from us". Trust to tell is my best protection.

An adult touches me in a way that feels wrong and says "don't tell". I feel frightened and confused. It is never my fault. Wise action: tell a trusted grown-up right away, and keep telling until someone helps.
My friend joined the clique and dropped me. I feel betrayed and angry. I let myself feel it, tell someone and avoid revenge. Perhaps she feels torn too. I can leave the door open and protect myself.
I stop chasing the popular group and enjoy the two friends who like me. Smaller friendship circles can be deeper. Acceptance is not defeat; it frees energy for real bonds.
A group of girls says there is no place for me at their table. It hurts deeply. This says more about them than me. I find one kind classmate, join a club, and tell a trusted adult if it continues.
I envy the popular group and want to be one of them. Wanting belonging is normal. But if they ask me to be cruel or change myself, the price is too high. Real friends like me as I am.

He once helped me get in, so I keep excusing how he treats me. Gratitude and abuse mix. Wise: I can be thankful for the past and still refuse the present treatment. Harmful: treating loyalty as a debt with no limit.

My boss mocks me in front of the team and calls it "directness". I feel small, hot-faced and frozen. Wise: it is his conduct, not proof I am worthless; note dates, talk to a trusted senior or HR, and start quietly building exits.
He alternates praise and threats and says "nobody else would hire you". I feel dizzy and dependent. Wise: recognise the pattern, test his claim by applying elsewhere, and lean on people outside work.

A coworker admits he faces the same treatment, and we quietly compare notes. I feel relief that it is not just me. Wise: share facts, not gossip; support each other without pulling anyone into a risky move.
Countdown timers, "only 5 seats" and screenshots of profits push me to hurry. Wise: urgency is a sales tool; slow down, read the risks, and never invest money I cannot afford to lose.

My friend doubled money on a hot tip, and I feel left behind. Wise: survivor stories hide the losers; learn basics like index funds, diversification and time. Harmful: chasing his win with borrowed money.

A finance influencer shows luxury cars and says his course changed his life. I feel drawn in. Wise: ask how he actually earns, check registration and track record. Harmful: buying a dream instead of evidence.
I lost most of my savings on a tip and feel foolish. Wise: accept the cost, stop trying to win it back, write the lesson, and rebuild slowly. Harmful: another risky bet to erase the loss.

I compare my parenting with relatives and social media and feel I am never enough. I remember children need steady, loving, imperfect parents, not perfect ones, and I trust simple routines and my pediatrician.
I feel a fierce need to shield my baby from every harm. This love is natural; wisdom is to keep the child safe without letting my fear steal their freedom and confidence as they grow.
Experiences intense love and fear together; learns to guide rather than control, and to repair after losing patience.
Snaps at the child and feels guilty; models apology and self-regulation, which teaches more than perfection.

A stranger says "come, I have sweets" or "your mother sent me". I feel tempted or confused. Wise rule: say no, run to a trusted adult and tell. A grown-up who asks a child for help or secrecy is a warning sign.
A visiting uncle says "give me a kiss" and my parent says I must. I feel uncomfortable. A wise parent respects a child's "no" to hugs and offers a wave or high five. My body belongs to me.

A shopkeeper helps me when I am lost in the market and calls my parents. I learn some strangers are safe helpers, such as a shop owner, a police officer or a mother with children. Knowing whom to ask keeps me safe.

A stranger at the market speaks to me and I hide behind Mummy. This fear is healthy. I feel safe near my parent. Wise adults teach that a polite hello is fine near them but I should never go off with anyone.
When my idol is criticised I defend them fiercely, even when the criticism is fair. Wise: loyalty to a person should not switch off my own judgment.
Treats the idol as flawless and defends every act; healthy admiration keeps the ability to disagree and see the person as human.
Fans of rival stars abuse each other online and I join in. Wise: notice how it feels good to belong and hurts real people; step out when it turns cruel.
A creator sells expensive courses or betting apps to young fans. Recognise it: trust built on likes can be monetised. Check claims and never spend what isn't mine.

My in-laws use guilt, hints, or family reputation to steer our choices and I feel cornered. I stay calm, keep decisions with my partner, and speak united; I need not win an argument to hold my ground.

My partner and my parents are in conflict and I feel pulled apart. I stay loyal to my marriage while treating my parents with respect, refuse to carry tales between them, and do not make my partner the villain.

My partner's family disapproves of me because of my caste, region, job, or background and I feel hurt and small. Their prejudice is not my worth. I stay courteous, let my partner speak up, and let time and conduct do their work.

I quietly resent my partner's family for intruding and comparing me to others. I share this with my partner without attacking their parents, and we agree on boundaries together; bottled resentment leaks out as coldness.

Family WhatsApp groups turn every festival into a political fight. You may love them and still be exhausted by forwards. Set gentle rules: no forwards, verify before sharing, change the subject warmly, or mute without drama.

A relative or colleague praises a leader you distrust, and heat rises. Mature action: ask what worries them, find shared facts, and disengage when it turns to insults. Winning the argument seldom changes a mind or protects a relationship.

Volunteering for a movement gives energy and friends. Good: canvassing honestly, listening to voters, and knowing your limits. Watch for slogans replacing thinking and for excusing your side's wrongs.

You admire a leader and feel part of a cause. Support can be sincere, but keep the ability to criticise. Treating leaders as infallible turns citizens into followers, and disagreement on specific acts is not betrayal.

An ex-member shares that she felt the same fears and now finds peace. I feel less alone. Wise: listen without rushing the decision and take one safe step at a time. Harmful: replacing one authority with another.
I am asked to donate, hand over my phone and stop seeing old friends "for my growth". Wise: these are control signals; keep independent contact, money and a way to leave, and talk to someone outside.

My friend joined a group I find worrying, and I want to rescue him. Wise: keep contact, ask open questions, avoid mocking, and share information gently. Harmful: pressure or secret plots that prove the group right.

My family begs me to leave the group, and I see them as enemies who do not understand. Wise: listen for love inside their fear, and keep one connection alive even if I disagree. Harmful: cutting them off as told.

My friend plays with a new girl and I feel a burning in my chest. I say "she is not allowed to play". Wise action: say "I felt sad" and invite both to play. Excluding someone to keep a friend is the harmful pattern.
My friend says "you are my best friend" and saves me a seat. I feel special and secure. I learn friendship means being chosen and choosing back, and I try to be kind and keep secrets kindly.
I like the girl next to me and ask "do you want to play?" My heart is thumping but she says yes. I feel brave and happy. Making the first move kindly, even shyly, is the start of friendship.

I cry when my best friend is absent and will not play with anyone else. Close attachment is sweet but I also need other friends. A wise adult helps me to join a small group so my world does not depend on one child.
I am furious at being dropped and rehearse cutting replies. Wise: let the anger cool, decide whether the friendship is worth one calm message, and keep my dignity.

A close friend stopped replying with no reason and I replay everything I said. Wise: send one honest message, then accept the silence and stop chasing. Harmful: blaming myself or messaging fifty times.
They reply only when it suits them and I keep waiting. Wise: say what I need; if it does not change, step back. Harmful: lowering my standards and calling it patience.
My friend moved on to new people and treats me as background. I am hurt but see that friendships shift with time. Wise: name it once, then invest in new and reciprocal bonds.

A colleague and I compete for the same promotion and I feel tense and calculating. I focus on my work and visible results, stay honest, and do not sabotage; rivalry can sharpen me if it does not poison my character.

A colleague covered for me during a family emergency and I feel indebted. I thank them sincerely and return the favour at the right time; a workplace of mutual help is worth more than any single task.

I look down on a slower colleague and roll my eyes in meetings. I see that contempt says more about my stress and pride than their worth, and I choose to help or set clear expectations instead of mocking.
You worry and want to know everything about your child. Wise: trust builds by letting them make small mistakes. Harmful: surveillance or shaming.

rows.subtype: Parents × Divorce or conflict at home [Receiver]
rows.description: Their fights or separation land on you. Wise: it is not your job to fix them, and you can love both while keeping healthy distance. Harmful: taking a side in the war.
They track your spending or use funds as leverage. Wise: negotiate a clear budget, share information, and build your own income. Harmful: lying or manipulating them for money.

You rely on them for fees and rent and feel you cannot speak freely. Wise: work toward some earning, use money wisely, and do not confuse support with control. Immature: spending carelessly and resenting them.
A toddler stares at the phone, goes still and screams when it is taken. The fast lights hijack attention. Limit and share it with a caregiver, and offer play, hands-on activity and outdoor time.
When the screen is turned off the child throws herself on the floor. It is sadness and frustration, not manners. Stay calm, hold the limit, offer a hug and a new activity.
When the parent hands over the phone to keep the child quiet, the child gets stimulation but not a person. Caregivers should treat it as a tool, not a babysitter, and talk and play daily.
Rules feel unfair and complex, and you resent paying. It is fine to dislike a system while complying with it and voting or advocating for change. Evasion turns a grievance into a legal risk.

Someone offers to make the problem vanish for a fee and shortcuts. Recognise a common exploit: bribery is illegal and leaves you exposed and owned. Use certified professionals and official portals, and ask for receipts.

A notice from the tax office makes your heart race and imagination run wild. Read it carefully, note deadlines, gather documents, and consult a qualified professional. Panic-paying agents or ignoring it worsens things.
Treat the process as a system with rules, not a personal attack. Respond on time, be accurate, and be polite in writing. Dealing honestly with authority usually costs less than hiding.
People praise you suddenly and ask for favours. Notice the pattern, thank them, and check whether they were around before. Keep truthful friends who can tell you when you are wrong.

A friend congratulates you but seems sour, or teases you about your new status. Stay humble, avoid showing off, and keep the friendship anchored in shared history. Give them space, and share their wins too.

Success brings impostor feelings and fear of being found out. Recognise that many capable people feel it. Keep a record of achievements, ask for feedback, and continue learning without pretending to know everything.
The success was built by others, too. Thank them by name, share credit and rewards, and mention their contributions to senior leaders. A leader who takes all the credit slowly loses trusted people.

Someone asks for money or a lift, and you hesitate because of scams. Caution is legitimate. Offer safe help such as calling authorities or buying food, and trust your instincts without becoming hard-hearted.
A stranger helps you at a breakdown or in an emergency. Thank them warmly, get contact if appropriate, and pass the kindness on. Such moments remind us that society runs on quiet decency.
Helps within safe limits, checks the story where possible and does not give in to manipulation or guilt.
I fear being replaced and start clinging, checking who she sits with. Wise: tell her plainly I feel left out and ask for one plan just us. Clinging and testing her loyalty makes her feel trapped.

I see that friends can have other friends, and being happy for her costs me little. I say hi to the new girl and suggest a game for three. This maturity shows up as generosity, not as pretending I feel nothing.

Another girl whispers that my best friend now finds me boring, hoping to split us. Wise: check directly with my friend rather than trust the whisperer. Believing everything I hear lets others steer my friendships.
I like the new friend but feel like a traitor to my old one. I can hold both friendships, tell my old friend she still matters, and not hide things. Lying about where I was makes it worse.
The older toddler hits, whines or asks to be carried, wanting to know if there is still room for him. Wise parents reserve a little daily special time and let him help in small ways.
The older child regresses: wants a bottle, wets again, clings. It is a bid to be held like the baby. Meet it gently and briefly without mockery; it passes when he feels secure.
Hearing you are still my big boy while being cuddled tells the child love has not been used up. Words plus a lap, not just praise for being a good helper, keep him secure.

My parents openly favour a sibling in gifts, praise, or the will and I feel unseen and hurt. I say it calmly to them if safe, do not turn it into war with my sibling, and build my worth outside their approval.

I feel protective of my younger sibling as they start their life and I want to steer them. I offer support and listen, and I accept that their choices are theirs; controlling them out of love is still control.

I feel I was always compared with my brother or sister and now we compete over family property or attention. I remember the bond behind the contest; the wise move is to speak fairly and openly, not to keep score for decades.

After our parent's death, my sibling and I grieve differently and misread each other as cold or dramatic. I ask how they are coping, share memories together, and settle assets only after the first wave of grief has passed.
I think my sibling is stupid or lazy and say it so. Wise: notice contempt shuts down closeness and ask what I envy or fear. Harmful: cruelty in front of others.
My younger sibling follows me everywhere and copies me, and I am annoyed and secretly flattered. Wise: give some time and boundaries, remembering I am their model. Harmful: mocking their need.
I fight with my younger sibling yet turn fierce when outsiders tease them. Wise: this loyalty is real; show it more kindly at home too. Harmful: bossing them and calling it protection.

We fight over the phone, room, and parental attention, each keeping score. Wise: agree on clear shared rules and ask a parent to referee once. Immature: tattling, hiding things, and escalating each round.

You choose one person and its meaning goes beyond feelings. Wise: love shows in reliability, honest talk and making room for their growth. Immature: treating commitment as ownership or a performance for social media.
You notice what they do quietly, like showing up in a hard week. Wise: say thanks specifically and reciprocate. Immature: keeping a score of favours and sulking when they are not repaid.

rows.subtype: Partner × Pressure to define the relationship [Receiver]
rows.description: They ask where this is going and you feel cornered. Wise: be honest about what you know and do not know, and avoid stringing them along. Immature: dodging, or saying yes to avoid a scene.

You choose to believe them without proof at every moment. Wise: trust builds through small kept promises and is not blind; you can still notice red flags. Immature: testing them constantly to feel safe.
My parent worries about me chatting with AI and asks to see. I feel watched, but sharing openly helps them trust me. I can explain what I use it for and agree on some rules.
My teacher asks if I used an AI for my project. I feel tempted to say no. Honestly saying how I used it, and what I did myself, keeps trust and lets her guide me.
I believe everything the AI says because it sounds confident. A wise child learns that fluent answers can still be mistaken, and checks important facts.
The AI writes a poem in seconds and I think it is magic. Wonder is lovely; I also remember it is a tool made by people, and my own imagination is what makes stories mine.
A mistake from years ago still plays in your head. Own the harm, make amends if possible, and then allow yourself to move on. Endless self-punishment helps no one; learning and changed behaviour do.

You understand your parents' limits as young adults and see their own struggles. Forgiveness may mean release of resentment, not excusing harm. Set boundaries where needed and appreciate the effort they made.

Replaying old insults keeps you tied to them. Resentment is like carrying heat to throw at someone else. Speak with a friend or counsellor, decide what you need, and free yourself even if they never apologise.
A groupmate is better than you. Wise: learn from them and do your part well. Immature: hiding your work.
