You disagree strongly on the approach. Wise: listen, test the ideas with data, and accept the group's decision. Immature: overriding others or sulking.
You hand over a part and hope they do it well. Wise: agree on checkpoints and give feedback kindly. Immature: micromanaging.
A groupmate stayed late to help you. Wise: thank them and offer help in return. Immature: taking it for granted.

My partner threatens to leave or shames me to get their way in private matters and I feel afraid and confused. This is not love and not my fault. I keep my boundary, confide in a trusted person, and seek help early.

I want closeness with my partner but they are tired or unsure. Real intimacy means asking, listening to a no without sulking, and understanding that willingness must be free; pressure or guilt-tripping is not love.

I love my partner deeply but forget to say or show it amid daily routine. Wise love is small and regular: attention, thanks, touch that they welcome, and noticing them, not waiting for grand gestures.
I want to share a deep fear or past shame with my partner but dread judgment. Trust grows in small disclosures met with kindness; I share at a pace I choose and notice whether they hold it with care.

A child repeatedly left crying with no comfort learns that need brings nothing, and may go quiet or flat, which looks like being good. Caregivers should respond warmly and consistently; the child is never at fault.
On her return the toddler may hit or turn away: the fear turned into fury. Mature response is calm welcome and naming it: you were upset when I went. Punishing the anger teaches hiding need.
The child has learned she always comes back, so protest is brief and play resumes. Caregivers build this by short, predictable goodbyes with a clear return word, never sneaking out.
Stays close to the caregiver and watches the stranger before engaging; warms up slowly if the caregiver acts relaxed (social referencing).
I look down on friends who follow rules and call them babies. Wise: see the same insecurity in myself and respect different choices. Harmful: forcing others to join my risks.
I go along because I fear being laughed at or left out. Wise: admit to myself the fear is real, find one ally who will say no with me, and practise a short reply.
I cover for a friend's rule-breaking because loyalty matters. Wise: be loyal to their wellbeing, not to the risky act; tell an adult if they could be hurt.
I refuse pressure and someone follows me. Wise: stay friendly and never preach. Harmful: sneering at those who cave.

rows.subtype: Partner × Being tempted but staying faithful [Actor]
rows.description: Attraction to someone else arises even though you are committed. Wise: attraction is human; you choose limits and do not feed it. Immature: guilt spirals or acting because you are bored.

You are eaten by guilt and want to confess just to feel lighter. Wise: consider what confession actually serves and be ready for the fallout. Immature: turning your guilt into their burden to comfort you.

Discovering a partner was unfaithful brings shock, shame, rage and doubt about yourself. Wise: take time before decisions, lean on friends, and remember their choice was theirs. Harmful: revenge or blaming yourself.
Their behaviour changes and you doubt yourself. Wise: trust your observation, ask directly, and avoid spying. Harmful: excusing every sign because you cannot bear the answer.
A raised voice and hard face make the child freeze or cry, and she cannot yet understand why. Best is a short, calm no with the reason in a few words, and a hug when she settles.
Being called bad or naughty makes the child feel she is wrong, not that the act was wrong. Wise adults name the behaviour, not the child: we do not hit, you are still loved.
The toddler screams back, throws or hits after a scolding: overwhelmed, not disrespectful. Adults keep their tone steady, hold the limit, and help the child calm before teaching.
I barely know the people next door and prefer to stay private. Privacy is fine, but a small greeting and shared contact numbers build safety and belonging when something goes wrong.

My neighbour's noise, parking, or garbage keeps annoying me and my irritation has built up. I speak to them calmly before it explodes, propose a specific fix, and use society rules only if talking fails.

I join festivals and residents' meetings and feel part of something larger than my own flat. I contribute my time and skills, and respect differences of faith and background; belonging is built by showing up.
My neighbours are curious or judgmental about my visitors, job, or marriage and I feel watched. I stay courteous, keep boundaries without hostility, and do not let gossip decide how I live.
My parent believes me when I say I did not do it, even though I once lied. I feel respected and want to earn that trust. Being believed makes honesty feel like a gift rather than a risk.

I tell the teacher "my mummy said I need not do it" to avoid homework. I feel smart and scared at once. Wise teachers stay calm and check gently. Learning that small lies are found out builds honesty.
I lie because I am afraid of being scolded or hit. The fear is bigger than the wish to be honest. Homes where truth is safe get more truth; harsh punishment teaches children to hide better.
I broke the vase and said the dog did it. My tummy feels heavy. At this age lying is often wishing it undone. A wise parent says "tell me the truth, I will not shout", and thanks me for honesty.
I told a small lie and nobody knows, yet I feel uneasy. Small lies grow bigger if I keep them. Fixing it by telling the truth helps my conscience and my relationships.
The teacher leaves the room and the answer key lies open. My heart beats fast. Deciding beforehand not to look, and walking away, helps more than fighting the urge in the moment.
Nobody is watching and I could take an extra sweet or skip my chore. Doing right anyway builds a self I can trust, and that inner steadiness is worth more than getting away with it.
My parents leave me at home alone and trust me to follow their rules. I feel grown up. Keeping their trust when unobserved makes them give me more freedom.

I say "then I will not eat" or cry loudly in front of visitors so they say yes. It sometimes works, so I keep doing it. Wise parents stay kind and steady. Rewarding pressure teaches that shouting wins.
I ask for one more show and hear no. I grumble but I believe my parent has a good reason. Trust grows when the no is kind and consistent, and I begin to accept rules without a fight.

My parent said no to the toy and I am furious, I feel like they do not love me right now. A wise child asks "can I have it on my birthday?" The immature pattern is crying and screaming until the parent gives in.
I say "you are mean, I hate you" and feel both angry and afraid to have said it. Wise reply from a parent: "you are angry, I still love you". Children need to learn hard words do not end love.

I blame one parent and cannot sit in the same room with them. Wise: recognise that anger covers sadness and that adult relationships are more complicated than I see. Harmful: cutting one parent off entirely.
I mourn the family I thought I had and feel it as my loss too. Wise: let myself cry, keep routines, and talk to a friend or counsellor. Harmful: pretending I am fine to protect everyone.
After time I see both parents as flawed humans who do better apart, and I take care of my own life. Wise: stay open to visits and honest with them. Risk: forcing calm before I have grieved.
I secretly wonder if my fights or grades caused the split. Wise: hear from the parents plainly that it was not my fault and keep loving both. Harmful: trying to fix them by behaving perfectly.
My classmates return to normal life while I feel frozen, and it hurts that nobody asks. Wise: tell one or two people what I need; grief is invisible unless named. Harmful: assuming nobody cares.

I keep replaying what I should have said before my friend died. Wise: guilt is love with nowhere to go; write him a letter, share memories, talk to someone. Harmful: punishing myself for what I could not have known.

After my father's death, my mother leans on me as if I were the adult. I feel pride and heaviness. Wise: support her while also grieving myself and involving relatives. Harmful: taking on all the roles alone.
Why did God take him? I am angry and a bit ashamed of it. Wise: anger and faith can coexist; allow the questions, seek people with wisdom and patience. Harmful: forced acceptance that hides the pain.

After you reported an issue, you get sidelined and labeled troublemaker. Retaliation is real and not your fault. Keep records, contact a lawyer or regulator, lean on friends, and remember integrity has a cost but keeps you whole.
You went along once and now feel sick about it. Guilt is useful if it leads to repair: come clean where possible, correct the record, and refuse a second time. Wallowing or hiding deepens the harm.

Fear of losing the job, visa or reference makes compliance feel practical. Wise action: write down facts, consult a lawyer or ethics line, and avoid being the only signature. Immature: going along and telling yourself you had no choice.

Boss says fudge the numbers or delay disclosure, hinting at your job. Recognise it as pressure, not a favour. Note the instruction in writing, refuse politely, and know your escalation channel. It is not your fault they asked.
My friend gives me a drawing and I say "thank you, I love it" and hug it. I feel loved and want to give back. Saying thanks kindly teaches me how gifts make friendships warm.
I give Papa a card I made and he puts it on the fridge. I feel proud. A parent who treasures a child's small gift teaches that giving is valued, and that my own effort matters.
I draw a card for my friend's birthday and give it with a big smile. I feel excited that they will like it. Giving something I made myself teaches that love is in the effort, not the price.
The teacher mocked me in front of the class and I wanted to vanish. That was wrong of her. I tell my parents so they can raise it with the school. Adults should correct, not shame.
I am scared of my strict teacher and my hands shake. Fear of getting it wrong blocks learning. I can ask a question after class and see her softer side. Many strict teachers care.
My favourite teacher was unfair to me once, and I am shocked. Adults can make mistakes. I can politely tell her how I felt. Cutting her off forever or mocking her is not needed.
The teacher seems to like some kids more, and I feel invisible. It may be real or not. I do my best, ask for help, and speak to her or a parent if unfair. Sulking helps nobody.
I see friends' holidays, looks and parties and feel left out. Wise: remember they post highlights; limit scrolling time, and message a friend instead.
A post of mine goes viral and I feel a rush. Wise: enjoy it lightly, and do not tie my worth to numbers that will drop.
A friend keeps flashing new things and grades. I sense they compare to feel better than me. Wise: stay warm, avoid competing, and stay grounded in my own values.
I keep posting for likes and feel low when they are few. Wise: notice the loop, post for reasons that are mine, and mute accounts that make me feel less.
Every place reminds you of them and you cry without warning. Wise: this is real grief, so sleep, eat, move and talk. Immature: numbing with distractions or rushing into a rebound.

rows.subtype: Ex-partner × Sharing private images or messages [Receiver]
rows.description: Fear that an ex will leak private material. Wise: it is a crime and not your shame, so keep evidence and report to the cyber cell or a trusted adult. Harmful: bearing it alone.
Months later you can think of them without hurt. Wise: take lessons about your patterns and needs, without rewriting the past as all bad or all good. Immature: swearing off love.
You replay how they wronged you and feel bitter. Wise: allow anger as information, then let it go for your own peace. Harmful: spreading their private matters or turning friends against them.
Balances career, spouse and care duties, splits tasks with siblings and keeps the parent's dignity.

My ageing parent refuses help, skips medicines, or resents advice and I feel frustrated and worried. I respect their dignity, offer choices, not orders, and involve their doctor or a trusted relative rather than fighting every day.
Carries childhood hurt while caring for them; can provide care and hold boundaries while processing the past, possibly with support.

I live far from my parents for work and feel guilty for not being there. I stay in regular contact, arrange practical support, and make honest visits; guilt is useful when it moves action and harmful when it just torments.
I saw it and did nothing and now feel ashamed. Wise: check on the target privately, report to a teacher, and refuse to laugh. Small acts matter.
After the bully apologises I feel mixed: relief, doubt, anger. Wise: accept the apology without forgetting, keep boundaries, and take time. Forgiving is not the same as trusting again.
I look down on someone weaker and see them as fair game. Wise: challenge that story; it is a fear of being weak myself. Harmful: turning contempt into a public habit.

I hate the person who torments me and picture hurting them. Wise: feel that anger as a sign of harm done, share it with someone safe, and seek adult intervention. Harmful: retaliating, which can put me at risk.
I go to the station to report a theft and hope that they will help. Wise: bring documents, stay respectful, get a copy of the complaint. Harmful: expecting everything to go wrong and not trying.

After an unfair fine or harassment I feel furious and helpless. Wise: record calmly, pursue complaint channels, and channel anger into action rather than confrontation. Harmful: heated words that turn a bad situation into worse.
My friend asks me to lie to the police about where he was. Wise: loyalty does not mean false statements; help him find a lawyer instead. Harmful: perjury that pulls me in with him.

An officer asks me for money or presses me to sign a paper I have not read. Wise: do not sign what I do not understand, ask for a lawyer or a family member, and note names and numbers. Harmful: panicking and complying.
They say if you loved them you would. Wise: you decide your pace; someone who respects you accepts a no. Harmful: giving in out of fear of losing them. Talk to a trusted friend if pressure continues.
You are asked for private photos. Wise: once sent, control is gone; you can refuse without guilt. Harmful: sending under pressure or threats. If threatened, tell an adult and report.
You are told no or not yet and feel hurt. Wise: say thank you for the honesty, step back, and do not sulk or bargain. Harmful: punishing them with coldness or threats.
You want closeness and must ask and listen, not assume. Wise: consent is clear, freely given and can change; a hesitation or silence is not a yes. Harmful: pressure, guilt or persistence.
On my first day I cry as Mummy leaves, then the teacher takes my hand and shows me the toys. I feel scared then a little safe. A warm, steady teacher makes school feel like a friendly place.
I look at the other children and wonder who will be my friend. I feel shy and curious. A wise teacher pairs children for an activity so friendships can begin easily.
I hold on to Mummy's dress and cry at the school gate. Separation is truly hard. Wise parents say a short kind goodbye, tell when they will return and do not sneak away. Lingering makes it harder.
My friend fell and I help him up and ask "are you okay?" I feel a warm ache for him. Wise adults notice and say "that was kind". A child who cares about others is learning to read feelings.
My parent notices I helped set the table and says "thank you, that was a big help". I feel important. Small chores with real thanks build a sense of being useful, without turning help into payment.
My friend helped me find my lost shoe and I feel relieved and happy. I say "thank you". Being helped by a peer teaches that friends look out for each other, and I plan to help back.
I beg my parents for something I saw in an ad and they refuse. I feel angry and it seems unfair. Understanding their limits and offering to save for it myself shows growing maturity.
My parent buys me something after I waited patiently. It feels extra special. Learning to wait makes me value things and understand the effort behind them.
I love watching a YouTuber who seems to have a perfect life. Admiration can inspire me, but I remember that videos are edited and nobody's real life is only fun.
All my friends have the new branded shoes and I feel left out. Wanting to fit in is human. I can ask myself whether friendship depends on shoes, and talk to my parents honestly.
My friends tell scary stories about police and I get nervous. I can ask parents what police really do, and learn that a good officer helps children.
I see a policeman in uniform and feel respect and slight fear. Police exist to keep people safe; I can learn that I may ask them for help if I am lost or in trouble.
I learn to stop at red lights and cross at zebra crossings. Rules keep everyone safe, and I remind adults politely if they break them.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior seems to dislike me and speaks against me in the team. I feel stung. I ask myself what they may have felt from my behaviour, speak with them openly, and hold my standards without needing everyone to like me.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior treats every word of mine as gospel and I feel flattered and slightly uncomfortable. I share my mistakes, encourage them to think for themselves, and avoid using their admiration to gain control.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior who once admired me sees my mistake and turns cold. I feel exposed. I own the error without fuss, let them adjust their picture of me, and value being trusted as real over being admired as perfect.

rows.subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
rows.description: A junior keeps running to me for every decision and I feel needed and drained. I ask them what they think, gently step back, and show that my job is to grow their judgment, not their reliance.
Riders at the tea stall share safe routes, warn about bad customers and help with a broken bike. I feel belonging. Wise: nurture this network and use it to ask for better terms together.

The app cuts my per-trip rate and blocks my ID with no human to speak to. I feel powerless against an algorithm. Wise: keep screenshots, join a workers' group, track real earnings after fuel, and build other income.

A customer offers water and says "take care on the road". A tiny kindness makes my day. Wise: accept it warmly and pass it on. Harmful: none; but do not let strangers' moods decide my self-worth either way.

I hide from relatives that I deliver food because they see it as low status. I feel a private sting. Wise: honest work is nothing to be ashamed of; explain my plan and timeline. Harmful: lying and drifting into stagnation.
A friend gave me an expensive gift and I feel I must give back. Gifts should not be a debt. I thank her, and give something within my means when I can. Feeling pressured is a sign to talk openly.
An older person gives me presents and asks me to keep it secret. Gifts with secrets are a warning. I tell my parents right away and stay away. It is never my fault and telling is always right.
I got a nice gift and my friend looks unhappy. I understand she may feel left out. I share or include her, but I do not need to hide my joy. Bragging is the part to avoid.
A friend gives me a small handmade card and I feel warm. I say thank you and mean it. The thought counts more than the price. Comparing it with fancier gifts spoils the joy.
Learns to say thank you even when the gift is not wanted, understanding the giver's intention; honesty can wait for private moments.

I say "I don't like this" out loud in front of the giver. I am not being rude on purpose, I say what I feel. A wise parent shows a kind way: "thank you, it was kind of you", and later hears my real feeling.
I open the box and it is socks, not a toy. My face drops. Wise: say thank you first and cry later at home if needed. Parents can teach that the gift is someone's love even if it is not what I wanted.

The child made a face at my gift and I feel sad. As the giver I understand small children do not hide feelings. A wise adult does not scold; they may say it lightly and remind the child gratefulness matters.
When I admit a mistake, the teacher stays calm and talks about what to do next. I feel relieved, and I learn that being honest earns trust even when I have done wrong.
I feel superior because I never break rules, and I look down on those who do. Following rules matters, but scorn makes me lonely; kindness and firmness can sit together.
My friend broke the rule and I want to cover for him. Real loyalty means urging him to own up and standing beside him, not lying so nobody gets in trouble.
I keep replaying what I did, and it feels heavy. Guilt is useful when it leads me to say sorry and fix things, and unhelpful when it makes me sit alone with it for days.
After beating my rival, I show off and rub it in. It feels sweet for a moment but costs respect. The mature response is to be gracious, because next time I may lose.
I scored the winning point and a teammate goes quiet and sulks. I understand he wanted that chance. I credit his pass and include him. Downplaying myself completely is not needed either.
I won and feel wonderful. Pride in effort is healthy. Wise: thank the team, be kind to the losers, and remember they feel bad. Gloating and mocking makes winning small.

A caller posing as a bank or a job recruiter sounds friendly and urgent. Scams exploit trust and fear. Never share OTPs or pay upfront fees, verify through official numbers, and remember that anyone can be fooled.

Rage at the fraudster is natural. Use it to file a proper complaint, gather screenshots and transaction IDs, and warn friends. Trying to hunt them yourself or scam them back is risky and rarely helps.

After losing money, you feel too embarrassed to tell anyone. Shame is what scammers rely on. Report immediately to bank and cyber portal, since speed can recover funds, and share the story to protect others.
A friend or an elderly relative has just been scammed. Do not blame or say I told you so. Help them stop further payment, report the incident, and rebuild confidence with clear safety habits.
A mentor changed your direction. Wise: say thanks, pass on what you learn, and later pay it forward. Immature: forgetting them once you succeed.
A student looks up to you and hangs on your words. Wise: guide without creating dependence and be honest about your limits. Harmful: using their admiration for favours.
A senior or guide uses your work, credit or time without fairness. Wise: name the unfairness politely, set limits and involve someone neutral if needed. It is not ungrateful to protect your work.
Grades or projects go to a favourite. Wise: gather facts, raise it through proper channels, and keep your own standards. Harmful: bitterness that damages your work.

Papa compares me with the neighbour's child and I feel hurt and stubborn. I may stop trying. A wise child says "I feel sad when you say that". A wise parent apologises and encourages me on my own progress.
My parent says "why can't you be like your sister?" I feel less loved and angry at her. It is not my fault or hers. Wise parents avoid comparison and value each child's own strengths and pace.
I see another child run fast and think "I want to run like her". I feel inspired and a little jealous. Wise adults help me ask "can you teach me?" and say each child is good at different things.

I compare my colouring with the girl beside me and feel bad because hers is neater. I want to hide mine. A wise teacher says "look how far you have come", turning comparison into pride in my own growth.

I count who got the bigger piece and cry "not fair!" Fairness matters hugely to me. A wise family lets one child cut and the other choose. I learn that equal is not always the same as fair, but that takes years.

A friend says "I will not share with you, you are not my friend". It stings. I can say "that makes me sad" and go play elsewhere. I should not be blamed for wanting a share, and a teacher can help us take turns.

I see a classmate's shiny box and want it so much my tummy hurts. Envy is normal at this age. Wise action: name the feeling, ask for a turn, or say "I wish I had that". The harmful pattern is hiding it or telling lies about it.

My parent says "give it to him right now" before I am ready. I feel angry and confused because it is my favourite thing. Better help is "you may keep it special, but pick another to share". Forced sharing can make a child hold tighter.
My parent says I am beautiful just as I am, though I do not believe it. Even so, it plants a seed. Being loved unconditionally helps me build a steady view of myself.
Films and ads show only fair, slim, perfect people. I begin to feel I am not good enough. I remember that images are edited and that real people come in every shape and shade.
A classmate teases me about my weight, height or skin colour. It cuts deeply. Their words reflect their unkindness, not my worth; I can tell a trusted adult and seek kind friends.
I feel strong and happy after winning a race. Feeling proud of my body for what it can do is healthy, and I can respect other bodies that are different from mine.
I find a hundred-rupee note in the corridor, and my heart races with ideas of what I could buy. Wanting is natural; a wise choice is handing it to a teacher or asking whose it is.
The shopkeeper gives me extra change by mistake. Nobody will know, but I would. Returning it feels awkward for a moment and then makes me feel light and trusted.
My parent hears that I returned a wallet and hugs me. I feel proud, but I should do the right thing even when nobody praises me, because honesty is for me first.
Friends say, finders keepers, let's buy chips. I feel torn between fitting in and doing right. I can decline politely, and often a friend quietly feels relieved that someone said it.
After a big fight, neither of us wants to speak first. Pride is the barrier. The wiser one offers a small gesture like sharing a snack. Saying sorry does not mean I lose; it means I value us.

My younger brother used my sketchbook without asking, and I shout. My anger is fair, since my things are mine. Wise: tell him calmly, ask a parent to set a rule, and lock away precious things. Hitting or breaking his toy solves nothing.
My little sister follows me everywhere and touches my stuff. It irritates me, but she looks up to me. A wise older sibling sets kind limits: this is mine, but we can play together at five.

I feel my parents love my sibling more because they give them more attention. Often it is different needs, not less love. I ask for one-to-one time and say what I feel, rather than trying to become the trouble child.

When I am ill I cling to Mummy and do not want her to leave. I feel afraid and helpless. Wise: she stays close when she can and tells me when she will be back. Clinging is a request for safety, not naughtiness.
My sibling is sick and gets all the attention and treats. I feel jealous and even wish I was sick too. This is normal. A wise parent gives me some care time and explains the sick child needs rest.
I am scared of the doctor's needle and cry. My heart thumps. A wise adult tells me the truth: "it will pinch for a second and I am here". Lying that it will not hurt makes the next visit harder.
I have a fever and Mummy holds me and sits by my bed. I feel small, warm and safe. Being cared for while sick teaches that I can be weak and still loved, and that resting is okay.
Studies why they won and improves offering; treating competitors as teachers keeps motivation constructive.
Spreads negativity and loses focus on customers; obsession with rivals can ruin both business and character.

Your smaller firm fears a bigger competitor's tactics. Focus on niches and customer relationships where you are better, and protect key clients and staff. Fear can push improvement, but must not push unethical shortcuts.
You lose a bid and feel envy at the rival's win. Ask what they did better: price, trust, service. Study and improve. Public sneering or bad-mouthing them harms your own credibility.
I am proud to be different and refuse to fit in. Wise: enjoy it while remaining open to others. Harmful: using superiority as armour against connection.
I use charm and gossip to climb the social ladder. It works, and I feel hollow. Wise: recognise the cost to trust and choose honest ways to belong.
I am popular and sense envy behind compliments. Wise: stay kind and honest, do not assume all attention is friendship, and keep close a few real friends. Harmful: cruelty to stay on top.
I am mocked as weird or poor or fat. It is unfair and not my fault. Wise: protect my self-respect, find spaces where I fit, and report harassment. Harmful: believing their story.
Feels devotion, wonder and belonging while participating; faith is absorbed through stories, music and ritual before argument.
I thank God for my family and food before eating. The feeling is warm and simple. Gratitude can also become action, like sharing my food with someone who has less.
At the gathering I am told I cannot join because of who I am. It hurts and confuses me. It is not my fault; I can tell a trusted adult and know that real faith does not shut a child out.
I listen to the religious teacher's stories and believe them fully. Trust is natural at this age; over time I learn to notice whether teachings promote kindness and never fear, cruelty or secrecy.
Confuses jealousy and monitoring with love; learns to spot control, isolation and guilt-tripping as warning signs.
Feels shattered and embarrassed after a "no"; healing comes from time, support and remembering that rejection is not a verdict of worth.

I see my crush as flawless and hang on every word. It feels wonderful and blinds me. Wise: enjoy the feeling, remember they are an ordinary person, and keep my own life going. Harmful: rebuilding myself for them.
Idealizes the person and checks their profile constantly; reality check comes from talking with friends and noticing their actual behaviour.
My parents sigh over my marks and compare me to a cousin. I feel small. It is not my fault they are anxious; I can say I will try harder and ask for help without losing my self-respect.
My parents beam and tell everyone about my marks. I feel happy but also pressure to do it again. It helps to enjoy their joy while remembering that my worth is more than my rank.
I got fewer marks than I hoped and think I am stupid. One result is not a verdict on me; a wiser view asks which topics went wrong and how to practise them.
My friend topped the class and I feel a sting in my stomach. It is normal; asking what helped him study turns envy into learning, while running him down only hurts us both.
I see my ex happy with someone new and feel a stab of jealousy. I let the feeling pass without stalking their profile, remember my own reasons for leaving, and put attention into building my life.

I compare my current partner with my ex and feel dissatisfied. I see that memory is edited and that I am comparing a real person with a highlight reel; I appreciate present strengths and speak honestly about needs.
Years later I feel ready to forgive an ex. I release resentment for my own peace and can say so briefly if it helps, without reopening the relationship or needing their apology first.
I still feel angry at how an ex treated me. I acknowledge the wrong, seek support from friends or a counsellor, and avoid revenge posts or messages; carrying rage keeps me tied to them.
My grandmother died and the house feels empty. I miss her stories and her hands. Grief comes in waves; letting myself cry and remember her is a way of loving her still.
I do not understand where my grandfather has gone and adults give different answers. It is okay to ask questions and to hear that people have different beliefs and that nobody knows everything.
Relatives gather for prayers and rituals after the death. The songs and food give me a sense of belonging. Whatever our beliefs, rituals help families carry sorrow together.
I discover that the preacher I admired lives against his own words and earns from followers. I feel foolish and angry. Wise: keep the teachings that were true, and not blame myself for hope.
Their community welcomes me warmly when I feel unseen at home. The warmth is real, yet warmth alone is not proof of truth. Wise: also build offline friendships.
I start believing this preacher has all the answers and see others as lost. Harmful: a single voice takes over my thinking. Wise: stay curious, keep diverse friends, and check claims.
I argue with my parent about a preacher they trust and I doubt. Wise: ask what they find helpful, share specific concerns, and avoid ridiculing them.

Watching a peer rise stirs comparison and a sour stomach. Mature response: congratulate honestly, study what they did well, and measure your path against your own goals. Harmful: undermining them or spreading doubts.
A boss who explains honestly why someone else got the role is offering respect. Take the feedback without defensiveness, note what is fair, and ask what would change the decision next cycle.

The mind says: I am not good enough. Wise action: separate performance from worth, list evidence of growth, and decide whether to push here or move on. Harmful: quitting in a rage or drowning in comparison scrolling.

Feels the years of effort were ignored and burns quietly. Wise move: ask for specific criteria and a timeline, separate the sting from the facts. Immature: sulking, withholding effort, gossiping to peers.

The polite "we are moving ahead with other candidates" mail stings and feels personal. Wise: it is one hiring decision, not a verdict; ask once for feedback, note one fix, apply again. Harmful: stop trying or rehearse it for weeks.

In a group discussion I see others as obstacles and want to shout them down. Wise: contribute clearly, credit a good point, let the panel see a person who can work with others. Harmful: talking over people to look strong.

My friend got the offer and I did not, and I feel warmth and a sour twist together. Wise: admit the envy privately, congratulate honestly, ask how they prepared. Harmful: quietly hoping they fail or sneering at their company.

Before the panel my hands are cold and I fear being exposed as not good enough. Wise: prepare a few real stories, breathe, say "I don't know, but here is how I'd find out". Harmful: bluffing, which collapses on the next question.
The child may hug, kiss or bring a toy to another toddler with pure delight. Encourage it gently and respect when the other child pulls away, teaching early that bodies have limits.
Being bitten or shoved by another toddler frightens the child, who cries and clings. Caregiver should comfort, check for injury, and say that was not okay, not blaming either child.
Two toddlers play side by side without interacting: parallel play, normal at this age. Caregivers need not force sharing or friendship; keep enough toys and stay close.

A toddler pushes, bites or grabs because words are missing and the wish is overwhelming. Caregiver should stop it calmly, comfort the hurt child first, name the feeling, and offer a word like mine or stop.

Your partner's promotion or rank makes you feel smaller though you love them. Wise: admit the envy privately, celebrate anyway, and work on your own path. Immature: undermining or mocking their achievement.
A late reply, a like or a new friend sets off doubts. Wise: separate evidence from anxiety and ask calmly instead of spying. Harmful: checking their phone or messages secretly.

You feel a hot pang when they laugh with someone else. Wise: name the insecurity behind it and share it as your feeling, not an accusation. Immature: interrogating, demanding passwords or forbidding friends.
Partner's close friend of the other gender makes you uneasy. Wise: get to know them and share the feeling without ordering a distance. Immature: ultimatums that force them to choose.

Friends bring food and sit silently with you. Accept the help, even if you cannot speak. Their steady presence, not wise words, is comfort. Tell them what you need in the weeks after, since support fades quickly.

A workplace expects quick return and speaks little of your loss. It hurts to feel invisible. Use leave, tell one trusted colleague, and set limits. Ask your manager for reduced load rather than forcing normal.

Grief sparks fights over rituals, property and blame among relatives. Remember everyone is hurting. Delay legal talk, get elders or a neutral mediator, and keep the dead person's memory from becoming a battlefield.
Experiences numbness, anger, guilt or relief; accepts each as normal, keeps rituals and support, and allows a long timeline.

My best friend shared my secret with others and I feel humiliated and enraged. I tell them clearly what happened and how it hurt, watch how they respond, and decide the friendship's future by their repair and not by my anger.
I repeated a friend's secret to others and now feel sick with guilt. The honest path is to tell them before they hear it elsewhere, apologise without excuses, and accept whatever distance they need.

My friend does something wrong or is cheating on a partner and confides in me. I feel torn. I tell them honestly what I think and refuse to lie for them, without publicly exposing them or cutting them off.

A friend only calls when they need money, favours, or a place to stay, and I feel used. I can give within limits, say no without long explanations, and notice that a friendship without mutual care is thin.
My dog died and I cry and ask where he has gone. I feel a big empty hole and may not understand it is forever. Wise adults tell the truth simply, allow crying and let me draw or say goodbye.
My parent hugs me and says "it is okay to be sad, we loved him very much". I feel understood. Not being told to stop crying or to just get a new pet lets grief take its natural path.

My friend says "it is just a dog, get another". I feel hurt and misunderstood. Children may not know what to say. A wise response is to tell them "he was my friend"; adults can teach children gentle words.

I think it is my fault because I once forgot to feed him or was angry at him. Young children believe their thoughts can cause things. A wise adult says clearly "it was not because of anything you did".
I imagine how it feels to be the talked-about one. Empathy stops me repeating hurtful stories. I can say what if it were about you, and kindly change the subject.
I discover a rumour about me is everywhere, and I feel exposed and want to disappear. It is not my fault. I tell a trusted adult, ask the source to stop, and hold onto friends who know me.
I fear that if I do not gossip, they will gossip about me. Fear of exclusion drives many kids. A friend who requires cruelty is not safe. Wise: stay polite, stay out, find kinder friends.
Everyone whispers about a girl's family trouble and I want to know too. Gossip feels like belonging, but it is built on someone else's pain. I can listen less, change the topic and not pass it on.
Classmates ask me to share my answers and call me selfish if I refuse. Wise: refuse kindly, offer to study together, and accept some anger. Harmful: giving in to be liked.
A friend confides they cheated and asks me to keep it secret. Wise: listen without judging, say I cannot approve, and encourage them to fix it. Harmful: acting as their alibi.
I report cheating and feel like a traitor, then friends turn on me. Wise: acting on principle can cost belonging; accept it with steadiness and seek supportive people.
A teacher asks who cheated. Wise: weigh fairness to honest students against loyalty, and speak to the teacher privately when needed. Harmful: gossiping about it or lying outright.
You dread a moody boss and stay quiet in meetings. Wise: prepare, communicate in writing, and do not take moods personally. Immature: hiding problems until they blow up.
You respect your first manager who guides you. Wise: ask for feedback, own your work, and bring solutions. Immature: pleasing without speaking up.
You are made to work late unpaid with vague promises. Wise: recognise the pattern, set boundaries, seek advice from trusted seniors, and know your rights. Harmful: silent burnout.
A colleague gets recognition you wanted. Wise: study what they did well, keep your own pace, and avoid gossip. Immature: undermining them.

The class laughs when I mispronounce a word. I feel small and hot. A wise adult says "everyone is learning". I can laugh gently or say "that is unkind". Laughter that hurts is not the same as laughing together.

After I spill juice at a guest's house, my parent says "accidents happen, let us clean up together". I feel relieved and loved. A parent's calm response teaches me embarrassment passes and mistakes can be mended.

I wet my pants in class and want to vanish. My face burns and I cry. A wise teacher helps quietly, gets a change and does not draw attention. It is an accident, not a failure, and I am not alone in this.
The teacher makes me stand and show my mistake to the class. I feel hot and want to cry. It is not my fault. Telling a parent helps, and a good school lets a child feel safe to make mistakes.
I see a stray dog thirsty in the heat and put out water. Small kindness to animals grows my heart, and I learn to be careful and tell an adult first.
I learn how a farmer grows my food and how a sweeper keeps streets clean. Respect for those who work with their hands makes me waste less and thank them.
I hear about climate change and become anxious about the future. That is understandable. I can talk to an adult and focus on small steps that are within my control.
I watch rain or a big tree and feel amazed. Wonder makes me want to protect nature, and simple things like planting a sapling connect me to it.

A teacher's kindness helped me through a dark year, and I feel deep thanks. Wise: gratitude can coexist with clear eyes; support the good, keep thinking. Harmful: feeling that thanks means never questioning.

My friend has cut off his family for the ashram and I worry about him. Wise: keep the door open, stay warm, ask curious questions, avoid attacking his teacher. Harmful: ultimatums that push him deeper.
Finds peace and direction in devotion; stays alert to signs of exploitation such as demands for money, isolation from family or suppression of questions.

I ask my teacher before every decision and feel lost without him. Wise: a good guide builds my judgement, not my dependence; make small choices alone and see that I can. Harmful: outsourcing my whole life.
I noticed something wrong earlier and said nothing, and now it is bigger. Wise: speak up now, acknowledge the delay, and let the facts lead. Harmful: staying silent because I already stayed silent.

I reported and nothing happened, and I feel cynical about all systems. Wise: try another channel, connect with groups that know the process, and keep some faith in change. Harmful: deciding nobody can be trusted.

After I reported an issue, my boss turned cold and colleagues stopped speaking to me. I feel punished for doing right. Wise: document retaliation, lean on outside support, and remember that integrity has costs and value.

I found evidence of fraud in my workplace and I am afraid of losing everything. Wise: keep copies safely, learn whistleblower protections, seek legal advice, and choose the safest right channel. Harmful: acting impulsively or leaking in anger.
Sometimes the older toddler hands a toy over to the crying baby and pats him: early empathy. Caregivers should notice and warmly name it, without demanding it every time.
The older child feels the baby gets everything and grabs to test whether he still matters. Parents should give one-on-one time and separate turns, not shame him as selfish.
Grabs back, shouts or bites; learns through adult labelling ("you are angry") that feeling is allowed but hitting is not.
The small one clutches the toy and screams, having no words for mine. Caregivers should step in gently, name the feeling, and offer another turn rather than forcing sharing at once.
My team follows my direction and thanks me and I feel proud yet unsure. I keep asking for honest feedback, share credit, and stay approachable so respect does not slide into fear or flattery.

I have just become manager over former peers and fear they think I don't deserve it. I am honest about what I don't know, listen more than I prove myself, and let results build authority rather than acting bossy.

Former peers who wanted the promotion are cool or sarcastic toward me and I feel hurt. I stay generous, acknowledge their strengths, give them meaningful work, and let time settle it rather than demanding warmth.

I feel lost as a new manager and hesitate to ask my own boss for help. Asking for coaching early is a strength; I bring specific problems and options, not just worry, and learn from more experienced leaders.
Others from my home community welcome me warmly, and I feel safe. Wise: enjoy the comfort while also making friends beyond it. Harmful: treating outsiders with suspicion.

People are polite but never invite me in, and my accent makes me feel like an outsider. Wise: keep showing up in clubs, classes and small talk; belonging is built slowly. Harmful: assuming all locals dislike me.

I miss home food, language and family and cry in secret. Wise: schedule calls, cook familiar meals, find fellow migrants, and know that it eases with time. Harmful: isolating or judging myself for missing home.

In a new city or country I fear making mistakes with language, food and rules. Wise: ask, watch, be patient with a learning curve, and find a small community. Harmful: staying only in a bubble that never lets me learn.

My sibling broke my drawing and I hit back. I feel the anger in my whole body. A wise child says "you broke it, I am mad" and gets help. Hitting brings a punishment and my sibling then feels angry too.

On the playground someone bothers my brother and I stand next to him even though we fought at home. Sibling love can be stronger than sibling fights. Wise loyalty means telling a teacher, not fighting.

We race to be first for everything and both want Papa's attention. I feel proud when I win and crushed when I lose. Wise families let each child have their own special time and praise effort, not who is first.

After we both cried, I hand my sibling a toy and say sorry. I feel light again. Saying sorry and doing something kind is a lovely repair, while forced sorry with no feeling teaches only how to say the word.
I believe I am not good at anything special. At this age, talents unfold slowly; trying different things and enjoying them is more valuable than being the best.
My parents say, look at your cousin, he is so good. I feel crushed. I can say that I am trying in my own way and ask them to notice what I do well.
A classmate draws or sings beautifully and I am amazed. Admiring others opens my heart, and I can ask how she practises instead of thinking I could never do it.
I won a prize for my talent and love the applause. Pride is healthy; I stay humble by thanking those who taught me and helping others who are learning.

Demands for donations, unpaid labour, cutting off family, or secrecy are signs of exploitation. It is not your foolishness; these groups target sincere seekers. Step back, consult trusted family, and seek outside counsel.
The satsang feels like a family that finally accepts you. Enjoy it, and also keep outside friendships and questions alive. A healthy community allows you to leave, disagree and still be respected.

A friend is giving all savings and time to a group, and you worry. Stay warm, ask open questions, and do not attack their belief. Keeping the friendship alive is what lets them turn to you when doubts rise.

You discover the teacher lives differently from what they preach or hides wrongdoing. Grief and anger are natural. Separate the good you learned from the person, report abuse, and do not conclude that all sincerity is fake.
My friend is secretly chatting with a stranger who asks for photos. Being loyal means telling a trusted adult, even if she gets angry, because her safety matters more than the secret.
A person messages me and seems interesting, and I want to reply. Curiosity is natural, but I check with a parent before chatting, and I never share my school, address or photos.
A stranger says he knows where I live and I freeze. It is right to be scared. I save the messages, do not answer and immediately tell a trusted adult; help is available.
I chatted with someone I should not have and I am afraid to tell my parents. Shame keeps children silent; telling them early is the bravest and safest step, and they are on my side.
Finds meaning and support in community and remains open to those outside it.
You feel thanks for daily blessings, hard times survived, and those who helped. Let gratitude show as generosity and humility. Devotion without kindness to people around you is incomplete.
Combines faith, rituals and service with critical thinking, staying wary of groups that demand blind obedience or funds.
Feels used and considers exposing them; a measured approach is to document contributions, speak to the colleague, and escalate with facts if needed.
Your idea or work is presented as theirs. Wise: raise it calmly with evidence, share updates in writing in future, and clarify roles early. Immature: public blowups or sulking.
Notices that the credit-taker gets promoted and feels bitter; learns to make own work visible instead of resenting.

A post of yours goes viral for the wrong reasons and thousands attack you. It is frightening and isolating. Step away from notifications, tell trusted people, save evidence of threats, report them, and do not respond in panic.

Strangers call you names and dig up your past, and you feel worthless. Remember mobs act on fragments, not on your whole life. Correct facts once if needed, then mute; seek support, and let the storm pass.
Separates valid criticism from abuse, replies calmly or not at all, and avoids trading insults.

A friend is being trolled and is sinking. Message privately, ask what help they want, offer to check the messages for them, and avoid piling advice. Being present can matter more than defending them publicly.
The doctors are helping my grandfather and I try to trust them. I can ask my parents what they are doing in simple words. Understanding a little cuts down my fear. I also prepare for uncertainty.
My grandfather is in the hospital and I am afraid he may die. Fear like this is natural. I ask an adult honest questions and draw or pray or sit with him. Not being told anything is scarier.
My grandfather has died and I feel empty, angry and confused. All of those are grief. I can cry, ask questions, share memories and take part in the rituals if my family does. Grief comes in waves.
I sit near my grandmother and read to her while she rests. Small caring acts matter to sick people. I do not have to fix anything; being present is enough.
I keep thinking about the game while at school and get upset when I must stop. This is a sign to loosen my grip. I can agree with my parents on time limits and balance it with outdoor play.
My friend and I are fiercely competing for game ranks. Rivalry is exciting, but if I cannot stand losing or start sulking, I should take a break and remember he matters more than the score.
The game keeps offering purchases to look cool or win. It is designed to tempt me. I can ask a parent before spending, and remember that real friends do not care about my skins.
A stranger in the game asks if I am okay after I lose badly. It feels nice, but kindness online still needs care; I stay friendly and never share private information.

My parent is unwell or money is tight and I worry constantly, hearing whispers. Wise: ask what is happening, take small helpful jobs, and still keep studying and friends. Harmful: silently carrying adult burdens.
A friend's family is struggling and I want to help. Wise: offer time, notes, and company without making them a charity case. Harmful: gossiping about their problems.
I see my parent's sacrifices and feel gratitude and pressure to succeed. Wise: say thanks and take on fair responsibility. Harmful: believing I must give up my own dreams to repay them.

I hide our situation from friends and refuse invitations I cannot afford. Wise: speak to one trusted friend, avoid pretending, and know that money does not measure me. Harmful: lying or stealing to keep up.

After the teacher praises me, a classmate frowns and says "you are not that good". I feel confused and a little sad. A wise response is to stay kind and not brag; the classmate's feeling is envy, not proof I did wrong.

I tell my friend "your drawing is so good". I feel happy giving kind words and want to learn how they did it. Admiring without envy is a lovely early skill, and asking "will you show me?" is a wise next step.
My parent hugs me and says "I am proud of you" after I tie my shoes. I feel safe and loved and eager to show more. I learn I am loved for who I am, not only for what I do.

My teacher says "well done, you tried so hard" and gives me a star. I feel tall and happy. Praise for effort makes me want to keep trying, while praise only for being the best can make me fear mistakes.
I made a serious mistake at work and feel ashamed and afraid my manager will give up on me. I own it fast, bring a fix, and ask for guidance; hiding errors is the real danger, not the error itself.
I cover for my junior's mistakes to shield them from blame. A little cover early can help, but if I hide problems they never learn; I coach them to own their errors and I stay honest with my boss.

I trusted a junior with a big task and they failed, and now I doubt my ability to delegate. I review what I explained, adjust the scope and check-ins, and delegate again in smaller steps instead of taking everything back.
Feels tempted to take the task back; learns that doing it for them stunts growth.
My grandfather says we children never talk to him because of phones. I feel guilty. Putting the phone away for a story-time chat gives us both something we need.
My friends only want to play online now and I feel lonely if I do not join. I can invite them to play outside, and notice how I feel after long screen time.
My mother says I look tired and stares at my screen habit. She is worried, not being mean. Listening to her and setting a limit together shows I can take care of myself.
My brother and I fight over the TV remote. Taking turns with a timer, or asking a parent to decide, is fairer than shouting or grabbing.
You cover for a sibling with parents. Wise: protect their privacy but not harmful behaviour. Immature: lying that costs you your integrity.
A sibling seems to be the favourite or more successful. Wise: talk to parents and sibling about how it feels; compare less. Immature: sabotaging them or competing for approval.
Distance makes you realise how much you rely on them. Wise: say it out loud and show up in small ways. Immature: assuming they know.
One sibling handles ageing parents or money more than the other. Wise: have an honest conversation about fair shares. Immature: keeping score in silence until it explodes.
I am afraid the teacher will notice my glance at another paper. Fear of getting caught is not the same as caring about honesty, and I can ask myself what I would do if nobody ever found out.
A friend says, just show me your answers, we are friends after all. I feel pulled between loyalty and honesty. A real friend won't make me risk trouble; I can say no and offer to help him study.
I feel superior to a classmate who cheats and tell everyone. Being angry at dishonesty is fair, but gossip does not help; reporting to a teacher quietly, if needed, is more mature.
I copied once and got away with it, but I feel uneasy. That unease is a sign of my conscience. Admitting it or deciding not to repeat it is better than pretending nothing happened.
A doctor who explains options honestly earns your trust. Share full information, follow the plan, and ask if you do not understand. Trust is not blind: you are a partner in your treatment.

Prayer, ritual or spiritual community brings solace in illness. Let it hold you, and also follow medical advice. Faith and treatment can coexist, and miracle promises that replace treatment are dangerous.

A serious diagnosis brings fear about the future and family. Bring someone to appointments, write down questions, ask for second opinions, and take it in stages. Panic searching at night rarely helps; trusted sources do.

Why me feels bitter and unfair, especially at young age. Anger is a natural response to loss of control. Let it out safely through talk, writing or movement, and avoid taking it out on those caring for you.
Two older cousins play together and leave me out. It stings. I can ask to join, suggest a game, or play with another cousin. If they still exclude me, I tell an elder without being dramatic.
I want to show my cousin that I am better at cricket and at studies. Friendly competition can push me. If I need her to lose, something is off. I aim to enjoy and learn from her strengths.
My small cousin is being teased by neighbourhood kids and I step in. Family loyalty feels strong. Wise: stand beside him, speak calmly and get an adult if it grows. Fighting is a last resort.
Relatives compare my marks with my cousin's and I feel small. Comparison hurts. I can tell my parents I feel bad and remember I am not a rank. My cousin may feel judged too.
I hide a loan, purchase, or savings from my partner, fearing their reaction. Hidden money damages trust more than the money itself; disclosing early with a plan is the mature choice.
My partner depends on me financially and I feel both protective and burdened. I talk openly about shared goals and their route to independence, without shaming them or using money as leverage.

I feel I owe my partner because they backed my career or paid for my studies. Gratitude is healthy; I show it through respect and reciprocity, not by giving up my voice or letting the debt become a leash.
I quietly resent my partner over who earns more or who sends money home to parents. I say it aloud kindly, treat it as a shared decision, and avoid keeping a silent ledger of grievances.
I want to fit in so much that I change how I talk and dress. Wise: adapt lightly, but keep my core; friends who need me to hide aren't yet home.
I feel proud of where I come from, my language and culture. Wise: pride can live alongside curiosity for other people and needn't require putting anyone else down.
I meet a classmate whose life is very different from mine. Wise: ask respectfully, listen more than assume, and let differences teach me.
Classmates tease me for my accent, name or manner. Wise: I need not shrink; tell a teacher if it continues and find people who value me as I am.
A teacher insults me in front of the class. I feel shame and rage. Wise: keep composure, speak to a parent or another trusted teacher, and report if it repeats. It is not my worth.
A teacher believes in me and I work hard to earn their respect. Wise: use their belief while building my own drive. Risk: crushing dependence on their approval.
I choose to report unfair treatment through the proper route, believing the school can fix it. Wise: be factual, bring a friend or parent, and give it time. Harmful: posting it online first.
Years later I see that the hard teacher pushed me well. Wise: thank them. Harmful: assuming that harshness is always good just because it worked once.

My big brother helps with my bag and says "you owe me a sweet". I feel unsure. Wise families let older siblings help for love, without bargaining. I learn to say thanks and to help back in my own time.
I keep asking the teacher to do it for me because I fear failing. I want to be safe. A wise teacher says "try one step and I will be here". Too much help stops me learning, and too little scares me.
Papa helps me with my buttons and I say "thank you". I feel loved and a bit proud to be learning. Wise adults help just enough so I can finish myself, and I learn that needing help is normal.
I laughed along at someone and later feel sick about it. Guilt shows my conscience works. I can apologise to him, and next time refuse to join. Guilt that turns to defensiveness teaches nothing.
I tease others about their looks because I dread being teased myself. Fear of being the target drives me to attack first. A wiser way is to build real confidence and find kinder friends.
I pick on a quieter boy because it makes me feel big and gets laughs. Underneath I may feel small or copy how I am treated at home. Wise change: notice the hurt on his face and stop, then apologise.
The boy I tease flinches when I come near. Seeing his fear should make me uncomfortable, not proud. The mature step is to stop, say sorry and mean it. Pretending it is only a joke keeps hurting him.

My manager gave the credit or the promotion to someone else and I burn with anger. I let the first surge pass, collect facts, ask for a private explanation, and decide whether to stay; a public outburst rarely helps.
Weighs loyalty to a manager against honesty to the organisation; loyalty never justifies deceiving customers or colleagues.

I know a decision is unfair but I am afraid to speak because I need the job. I weigh risk honestly, find allies, raise concerns in writing calmly, and accept that silence is a choice with its own costs.
My manager belittles people in meetings and I feel humiliated and unsafe. It is not my fault. I document incidents, seek support from HR or a trusted senior, and protect my dignity and health.
You control because you fear abandonment. Wise: admit this, work on it with a counsellor or friend, and let go of control. Harmful: calling it love.
They deny events you clearly remember and call you oversensitive. Wise: write things down, check with a trusted friend, and see that doubt is the aim. Seek counselling.
They slowly make you distance from friends and family. Wise: keep at least one outside connection and see isolation as a warning sign. Reach out to someone you trust.
Intense adoration turns into silence when you set limits. Wise: notice the swing and judge by steady behaviour, not grand gestures.

A talented junior threatens you with faster progress. Notice the sting, then decide: share opportunities, give credit, and keep growing your own skills. Holding them back protects your ego but hurts the team and you.

A younger colleague looks up to you and copies your habits. It is an honour and a responsibility. Be honest about your failures, model integrity, and do not seek adoration or use their trust for your ego.
Seeing your mentee grow makes you proud, and slightly wistful. Celebrate them without claiming credit, and be glad when they surpass you. Good mentors work towards being no longer needed.
A mentee keeps asking you to decide everything. Help them build judgment: ask what they think, offer options, and celebrate independent choices. Rescuing them each time weakens them and burdens you.
I notice that officers treat rich kids gently and poorer boys roughly. I feel anger and helplessness. Wise: record what happened, seek an adult or legal aid, and channel anger into knowing my rights.
I have seen bad police behaviour and I now see every uniform as a threat. Wise: stay careful without hating everyone, and know that many officers do their duty properly.
A friend brags about talking back to police. I feel the pull to copy. Wise: courage is knowing when to stay calm; a video for likes can cost me my safety.
My parent is frightened after I was questioned and turns strict. Wise: listen to the fear, share the full story, and agree on safe habits like sharing locations.
I am scared of the dark and imagine things in the corner. Fear is real even if the danger is not. Talking about it and having a small light helps, and it fades with time.
A friend laughs that I am a scaredy-cat. It stings. Being afraid does not mean I am weak; I can say everyone is afraid of something, and choose friends who do not tease.
My mother sits beside me after a nightmare and says I am safe. Her calm makes my heart slow down. I learn that fear shared becomes smaller.

I see the other side as stupid or evil and enjoy mocking them. Wise: understand their fears, argue the issue and not the person, and keep the moral high ground by being fair. Harmful: dehumanising anyone.
A leader keeps asking for more money and says doubters are traitors. Wise: real movements welcome transparency; ask how funds are used and treat forced unity as a warning sign.

The group is like family, and I hesitate to speak when it makes a bad tactical or ethical choice. Wise: dissent within a movement is loyalty too; say it early and kindly. Harmful: silence that leads to harm.

I give time, energy and hope to a cause I believe in, and it gives my life direction. Wise: keep sleep, studies and relationships intact so the commitment lasts. Harmful: burning out or seeing all non-members as enemies.
I feel I will die without them and need constant reassurance and check-ins. Wise: see this as anxiety and not love, seek support, and build my own interests. Harmful: monitoring or controlling them.
They demand my passwords, tell me what to wear, and get angry when I see friends. It is control and not proof of love. Wise: name it, keep friends close, and tell a trusted adult.
I like them and we both can say no, keep friends, and enjoy the time. Wise: keep communicating openly and treat consent as always on. It grows because neither owns the other.
When I resist, they say I am selfish or that they will fall apart. I feel responsible for their feelings. Wise: care without giving in, and get help from a counsellor or elder if it continues.
I catch someone cheating against me and feel furious. Wise: tell the referee or an adult calmly instead of accusing loudly or retaliating. Cheating back turns me into the same thing.
I could bend the rule and nobody would notice. Winning feels big and losing feels small. A wise child knows a win by cheating feels empty and would need to be hidden. I play fair.
I cheated and won, and the trophy feels heavy. Guilt is my conscience working. I can admit it to the coach, accept a consequence and start clean. Hiding it makes it grow.
Hiding EMIs and credit card dues from family adds isolation. Face the actual numbers on paper, prioritise high-interest debt, and tell one trusted person. Shame keeps debts growing.

You took a loan partly to support family expectations, and now feel trapped between duty and survival. Talk openly with them about limits, set a repayment plan, and avoid pretending to be richer than you are.
Easy credit, buy-now-pay-later and status spending feel harmless. Track small EMIs, ask if the item is a need, and delay purchases for a week. Debt for lifestyle steals future freedom.
You lent a friend money and they keep dodging you. You feel used. Ask once, clearly, propose a plan, and decide how much of the friendship you value. Lend only what you can afford to lose.

I fear that the other side's victory will destroy what I value. The fear is sincere. Wise: check facts from varied sources, notice when fear is being sold to me, and act through voting and local work. Harmful: seeing all opponents as enemies.
Asks "how did you come to that view?" and finds shared values beneath disagreement.
I admire a political leader and feel proud when he speaks. Wise: support policies on evidence, and stay able to criticise my own side. Harmful: treating criticism of the leader as an attack on me.

A relative at a family dinner shouts that my views are "brainwashed". I feel insulted and want to retaliate. Wise: decline to debate while heated, say it calmly, and change the subject. Harmful: escalating until dinner is ruined.
I want to hit back with something equally cruel. Wise: the impulse is human, but revenge often makes things worse; choose evidence and reporting.
I dread going to school because of what's online. Wise: fear is a signal, not weakness; tell a parent or counsellor, and request the school to act.
An anonymous account sends nasty messages and I obsess over who it is. Wise: preserve evidence, report to platform and school, and don't let guessing consume me.
Classmates post memes or edited photos to mock me. I feel hurt and exposed. Wise: don't retaliate, save screenshots, block, report, and tell a trusted adult; it is not my fault.
After being lied to many times, you trust no news at all. Total distrust is as manipulable as blind trust. Keep a small set of sources with track records of corrections, and hold conclusions loosely.

Campaigns use edited clips and fear-based rumours to steer emotion. Notice who benefits, check multiple sources, and be cautious about content that flatters your side. Media literacy is a civic skill.

Your feed keeps you angry and hooked, and you notice worse mood and warped views. Curate sources, schedule offline time, read long-form, and remember outrage is what platforms reward. You are shaping your mind with your attention.

You shared something false and it caused panic or hurt someone. Delete it, post a correction to the same audience, and apologise if named. Building the habit of checking before sharing repairs more than shame does.

My mum's new partner tries to be friendly and I refuse. I fear he will replace my dad. It is fine to go slowly. I stay polite, be honest about feelings, and let trust grow without being forced to love.
When my parents separate, I miss the old family and cry at odd times. Grief is normal even though nobody died. I keep routines, talk about it, and let myself be sad without hurrying to be okay.
I keep hoping they will get back together and imagine plans to fix it. This is common, but I cannot fix their marriage. Accepting slowly frees me to enjoy time with each parent as it is.

I am angry at both of them for ruining our home. Anger covers sadness. Wise: say it in words, maybe draw or run. Slamming doors is natural, but hurting others or blaming one parent unfairly will hurt me more.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: You explore new customs, foods and ways of working with interest. Adapt where it helps and stay rooted where it matters. Learning does not mean betraying your own culture or copying blindly.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: You face stereotypes, accent mockery or being left out. It hurts and can shake confidence. Name it to yourself, find supportive people, address it calmly when safe, and report discrimination. Their bias is not your defect.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: You live far from ageing parents and feel torn between career and duty. Set regular calls, plan visits, arrange local support, and be honest about limits. Guilt without action helps no one, and love can travel.

rows.subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
rows.description: In a new city or country, you miss home food, language and easy jokes. Loneliness is normal at first. Join clubs, meet colleagues outside work, keep calls with family, and give yourself months, not weeks, to belong.

My child is being held back or hovered over by an anxious parent. As their parent I feel my own worry shape how I act; I consciously allow small risks so they learn courage and my fear does not become theirs.

My child looks at me as their hero and copies everything I do. I feel warm and weighed down. I stay honest about mistakes, model apology and kindness, and remember that they will one day see me as human and still love me.

My partner and I differ on discipline and argue in front of our child. We agree privately on a few shared rules, back each other publicly, and avoid one parent becoming the harsh one and the other the friend.

My child is screaming at me in a tantrum and I feel embarrassed and furious in public. I stay calm, keep them safe, and wait it out; the child needs me steady, and I gently repair later if I lost my temper.

You worry AI will make your career obsolete. Take it seriously and act: learn the tools, focus on judgment, relationships and domain depth, and keep upskilling. Panic or denial both waste the time you have.
Coworkers accuse you of cheating because you use AI well. Be open about how you use it, take responsibility for the output, and help others learn. Skill lies in framing problems and checking results.

The answers are fluent and confident, and you accept them. Fluency is not accuracy. Verify facts, code, and legal or medical advice with reliable sources and people. Trust tools in proportion to how easily you can check them.

You are tempted to pass AI work off as fully your own in a place where that is not allowed. Follow the rules, disclose when required, and understand what you submit. Being caught is less costly than lacking the competence you claimed.

After a loss I ask why God let it happen, and prayer feels empty. Wise: doubt is common in many traditions and can deepen or reshape faith; stay honest, read, ask elders. Harmful: forcing a fake certainty.

People in my temple, mosque or church go cold when I question things. I feel lonely. Wise: find one or two open-minded elders or peers, and value people over doctrine wins. Harmful: cutting all ties in anger.

My parents fear that my questions mean I am losing my way and my values. Wise: reassure them I still love them, share questions gently, and avoid mocking their beliefs. Harmful: open contempt for family rituals.

I am angry at God for suffering I did not deserve. Wise: many prayers and texts contain protest; let the anger speak, and let time and community hold me. Harmful: suppressing it until it turns to numbness.
I see someone litter near the flag or a monument and feel uneasy. Civic respect means caring for shared places too; I can pick it up or gently remind someone.
I giggle during the anthem because friends do. It is easy to copy others; I learn that respect for shared symbols matters to many, and that I can save jokes for another time.
I hear a story of a soldier or freedom fighter and feel awed at their courage. Admiration can inspire me to serve in my own small ways, like honesty and helping the community.
I stand tall for the anthem and feel goosebumps on Republic Day. Pride in the country feels warm; a wise child also learns that love for one's land includes caring for all its people.
As the parent I favour the child who is like me and never notice the other shrinking. Wise: for a teen, understand this is usually blindness and not hatred, and tell them plainly what I need.
Being treated as the golden child, I feel guilty when my sibling is snubbed. Wise: gently include them and refuse to compete for the parent's approval. It is not my fault, but my behaviour matters.
I watch my brother or sister get gifts, trust, or praise I never get and feel invisible. Wise: tell a parent what I notice without attacking the sibling. Immature: making the sibling pay.
My sibling hates me for being preferred and says cruel things. Wise: see the pain underneath, avoid retaliating, and ask parents to fix their behaviour. Harmful: rubbing it in.
Handles money, chores or in-law disagreements by choosing timing, stating needs, listening fully and agreeing on a next step instead of keeping score.

I roll my eyes and mock my partner's habits, feeling superior and tired. Contempt is the most corrosive habit in marriage; the wise move is to name the hurt underneath and ask for what I need, not score points.
Uses small gestures, humour and apologies to repair after fights; successful couples repair fast, not fight less.

I am flooded with anger at my partner, heart racing, and I want to say the cruelest true thing. Mature action is to pause, cool off, and speak about my feeling and request; the harmful pattern is wounding words that cannot be taken back.
Wants revenge and imagines hurting the bully; a healthy path is to acknowledge the anger, tell an adult, and avoid retaliating.
Feels shame at teasing and withdraws; learns to answer calmly, walk away and seek support instead of fighting.
Realizes that a bully may be hurting at home; understanding explains behaviour but does not excuse it or remove the need for boundaries.
The toddler folds hands, rings the bell, claps or bows because the family does, drawn by sound, lamp and loved faces. It is imitation and belonging, not belief. Keep it warm and never forced.
Sitting on a grandmother's lap during aarti or bedtime prayer, the child feels loved and part of the family. Rituals shared with warmth become safe memories, not obligation.
Flickering diya, incense, chanting or a gurudwara or church hush hold a toddler's gaze with wonder. Caregivers let the child watch and take part gently, whatever the faith at home.

Told to leave after loyal service, you feel discarded and lied to. Feel it fully, then get the terms in writing, ask for references, and keep bridges intact. Immature: angry emails, leaking documents, or burning every contact.

Being laid off feels like a verdict on your worth, and you hide it from parents. Reality: it is usually a budget decision. Tell one trusted person, set a daily routine, and treat the search like a job.
Parents or a spouse rely on your income and are anxious. Be transparent about savings and plan, involve them without hiding, and accept that their worry is love in an ugly shape, not an accusation.
Rage at leadership for cuts made after record celebrations is understandable. Channel it into precise questions on severance, notice and rights, not a public tirade that shrinks your future options.
At a party, friends offer cigarettes, vape or alcohol and say don't be boring. Wise: a simple no with a joke or an exit works; real friends respect it.
An older boy offers free vapes, pills or sweets to draw me into his circle or to sell for him. Recognise it: it's a hook. Refuse, leave, and tell a trusted adult.
I am curious about trying something because everyone talks about it. Wise: notice I am reacting to curiosity and image; learn real effects, especially on a developing brain, and choose knowing.
A friend is using regularly and getting worse. Wise: express care without lecturing, encourage help, and tell a trusted adult when their safety is at risk.

I am furious and want to trap the fraudster myself. Wise: give what I have to the police and cyber cell; do not chase him alone, as that risks more loss or danger. Harmful: revenge fantasies that lead to further scams.
I keep it secret because I fear being mocked, which lets the scammer's damage grow. Wise: speaking up early can recover money and stops the loop. Harmful: silence, which scammers rely on.

A friend forwards a "guaranteed profit" scheme he believes in. He is not evil, just caught. Wise: check the source before spreading it, question calmly, and keep the friendship while refusing the scheme.
