rows.description: A boy cannot follow three-fourths until his mother cuts a roti into four parts and gives him three. The picture of real food gives the abstract number a meaning he can hold.

rows.subtype: Approach: memorising the rule without understanding it [Pitfall]
rows.description: A girl learns 'flip and multiply' for dividing fractions without knowing why. She gets the familiar sums right but is lost when the teacher gives a word problem in a new shape.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking the teacher a specific question [Revision]
rows.description: A child notices that guessing has not helped and writes down exactly where he gets lost, which is the borrowing step in subtraction. Next day he asks the teacher to show that one step again.
A child hides in the almirah because an older cousin won there last time. It works this time only because the seeker does not know the cousin's trick.
A child thinks, "If the seeker goes left, I go right around the sofa," and waits to see which way he goes. It is a simple plan about another person's move.
A child of four covers both eyes in the middle of the room and believes nobody can see. The child cannot yet take the seeker's point of view.
Found in seconds behind the door, a child tries behind the curtain next round, then under the bed. Each round of being found or not found teaches which spots work.

rows.subtype: Approach: means-end analysis from company pattern to gap [Thinking]
rows.description: A student reviews the past three years of a target company's rounds, notes aptitude, coding and HR stages, and compares each stage with current ability to find the biggest gap.
Over six weeks, the student fixes ninety minutes for coding problems, forty for aptitude and thirty for speaking practice, and keeps a log of solved problems.

rows.subtype: Approach: memorising answers word for word [Pitfall]
rows.description: A candidate scripts every HR answer from the internet, sounds rehearsed, and freezes when the interviewer changes the question slightly.

rows.subtype: Approach: learning from a rejection debrief [Revision]
rows.description: After failing the technical round, the student writes down each question missed, learns the underlying concept, and finds the next company's questions feel easier.
A child folds the paper in half, draws a cake on the front, writes the friend's name inside, and colours it last. The order makes the card come together.
A child imagines grandmother opening the card and smiling, and decides on her favourite flowers and colours. The imagined reaction chooses the drawing.
The drawing turns out crooked and a child crumples the paper and says "it's ugly," and will not make another card. The wish for a perfect result stops the effort.
Glitter glue smudges the drawing, so a child tries pencil first on a fresh sheet and adds glitter only at the border. The mess teaches an order for the materials.

rows.subtype: Approach: allowing feelings and staying with family [Thinking]
rows.description: After the sudden death of a grandfather, a teen lets herself cry, sits with the family through the rituals, and understands that grief is not something to hurry or hide.

rows.subtype: Approach: adjusting study and exam plans with school support [Action]
rows.description: A teen informs the class teacher, asks for extra time on assignments for a few weeks, and rebuilds a lighter schedule, instead of forcing normal performance immediately.

rows.subtype: Approach: suppressing emotion to seem strong [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy told to be the man of the house hides his tears, throws himself into chores and studying, and weeks later finds outbursts and sleeplessness because the grief was never expressed.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing when grief becomes overwhelming and seeking support [Revision]
rows.description: Months later, a student still cannot concentrate or sleep, so he tells his mother, who arranges a talk with a school counsellor, an appropriate step and not a weakness.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
rows.subtype: Approach: deciding a personal rule for what counts as own work [Thinking]
rows.description: A student decides that AI may explain ideas and check his work, but written answers and graded assignments must be his own, and reads school policy to confirm where the line is.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
rows.subtype: Approach: being open with the teacher about use [Action]
rows.description: A teen tells the teacher she used AI to brainstorm ideas and check grammar, shows her notes, and asks whether this fits the assignment rules, which builds trust and avoids misunderstanding.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
rows.subtype: Approach: copying AI output as homework [Pitfall]
rows.description: A teen pastes an AI-written answer to submit, and later cannot explain it in class or solve a similar problem on the test, since the learning never happened.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
rows.subtype: Approach: testing understanding without the tool [Revision]
rows.description: After noticing he depends on AI, a student closes it and tries a similar problem cold, sees gaps, and adjusts by asking for hints only after a fair attempt.

rows.subtype: Approach: finding out the topics and format first [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy learns that the inter-school quiz covers general knowledge, science and sports, with buzzer rounds. Knowing the format tells him what to prepare and how quickly he must answer.

rows.subtype: Approach: reading widely from newspapers and books [Action]
rows.description: A girl reads the children's page of the newspaper each day and a general knowledge book at night. She keeps a notebook of new facts about places, people and records.

rows.subtype: Approach: trying to memorise everything in the encyclopedia [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child decides to learn all the facts in a thick book. He soon gets tired and confused, and does not know which facts matter or where he is weak.

rows.subtype: Approach: spotting weak topics and giving them extra time [Revision]
rows.description: After a mock round, the team sees that they miss questions on geography. They spend the next week with a map and an atlas, and their score improves.

rows.subtype: Approach: identify the rule and value at stake [Thinking]
rows.description: Asked by a manager to backdate a document for a client audit, the junior analyst asks what it would mean if the record were false, and recalls company policy and personal integrity. Naming the principle clears the fog of pressure.

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of the refusal conversation [Thinking]
rows.description: The employee imagines the manager's reactions and prepares calm wording such as offering to fix the delay honestly instead of falsifying records. Rehearsal makes it easier to stay steady under pressure.

rows.subtype: Approach: comply quietly to avoid conflict [Pitfall]
rows.description: Afraid of losing the job, the employee backdates the document and tells no one. The fear of consequences is real, but the person now carries the risk of an audit and the guilt, and may be asked again.

rows.subtype: Approach: escalate to HR or the ethics channel if pressure continues [Revision]
rows.description: When the manager repeats the request, the employee moves from private refusal to a written report to HR or the ethics helpline, keeping details factual. Escalation is used when direct handling does not work.

rows.subtype: Approach: reading the timetable and packing the night before [Action]
rows.description: A boy looks at tomorrow's timetable, takes out yesterday's books and puts in the right notebooks, lunch box and water bottle. Doing it in the evening leaves the morning calm.

rows.subtype: Approach: using a coloured chart pinned on the wall [Action]
rows.description: A girl makes a weekly chart with each subject in a colour and pins it near her study table. Colours help her see at a glance which books belong to which day.

rows.subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child keeps all books in the bag so he need not check the timetable. The bag becomes too heavy for his shoulders, and he still cannot find the right notebook in the mess.

rows.subtype: Approach: adding a note about changes to the plan [Revision]
rows.description: After the PT shoe mistake, the girl adds a sticky note to her chart reading Wednesday PT shoes. She also checks the school diary each Sunday for changes to the timetable.
A sixteen-year-old lists what he can do, such as fixing phones, drawing or teaching basic Maths, and then checks which are legal and safe for his age and can fit around school.

rows.subtype: Approach: minimum viable version of a small business [Action]
rows.description: The student starts by making ten handmade greeting cards for festival season, sells them to relatives and neighbours, and uses the response to decide whether to make more.

rows.subtype: Approach: taking any offer without thinking [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student accepts a night delivery job with vague terms from a stranger. It looks like easy money, but it is unsafe, may be illegal for a minor and clashes with school hours.

rows.subtype: Approach: buffer and weekly hour cap [Revision]
rows.description: After a dip in marks, the student caps work to six hours a week and blocks exam months completely, agreeing with parents on when to pause the gig.

rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.description: When floodwater enters a rented flat, the person ranks needs: people and documents first, then medicines, phone and power bank, and only later furniture and electronics.

rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.subtype: Approach: following official alerts and evacuation guidance [Action]
rows.description: The person watches local authority alerts, moves family to a designated relief shelter or relatives on higher ground, and avoids risky attempts to save belongings from rising water.

rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.subtype: Approach: ignoring warnings and hoping it passes [Pitfall]
rows.description: Having seen mild floods before, the person dismisses the alert and delays leaving. Roads close overnight, and rescue becomes harder and riskier for the whole family.

rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.description: After the disaster, the person repairs essentials first, then postpones cosmetic work, and adjusts the budget as claims arrive, adapting to money as it becomes known.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing warning signs and taking them seriously [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen sees a friend withdraw, stop eating lunch and say things like nothing matters, and decides these changes are serious enough to act on rather than something he should just wait out.
Before approaching a struggling friend, a student plans simple words such as I have noticed you seem low and I am worried about you, and what to do if the friend gets angry or shuts down.

rows.subtype: Approach: trying to fix everything alone [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student becomes his friend's only support, answers messages through the night and hides how bad it is, until his own sleep and marks collapse and the friend still has no professional help.

rows.subtype: Approach: caring for own limits and feelings [Revision]
rows.description: After several heavy conversations, a teen notices she is exhausted and anxious, talks to her mother about it, and agrees to share the support with adults, keeping a friendly role only.
A child tries one piece after another at the same gap in a jigsaw until one fits, without thinking about the picture on it.
A child says, "Edges first, then the sky, then the house." Sorting flat-sided pieces first makes a frame to work inside.
A child presses a wrong piece down hard and says, "It wants to go here." Liking the idea outweighs the evidence of the shapes not matching, and the piece bends.
Stuck on the last corner, a child asks father, who shows the piece's picture and where the colour continues. The child then finds the next match unaided.
A toddler picks up a star block and pushes it against the circle hole, then the square, then the triangle, testing each hole until one finally accepts it.
Mother drops the star into its slot, and a toddler copies the drop but holds the piece flat, sees it bounce off and starts again from the top.
A toddler hammers a square block on the round hole with a palm again and again. The force feels like effort, but nothing about the shape of the block changes.
The block will not go in, so a toddler rotates it a quarter turn and tries again. The change in angle, rather than the hole, is what the toddler adjusts.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.description: After breaking a neighbour's window with a cricket ball, a boy goes to the door with his father, admits it and offers to help pay, and is surprised to find the neighbour is kind.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: imagining the consequences of each choice [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl who spilled ink on the sofa thinks that a lie may be found and make her parents angrier, while the truth costs a scolding now but keeps their trust.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: blaming a sibling or the dog [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child says his little sister broke the vase to escape punishment, and then feels awful watching her get scolded, and the lie needs more lies to hold it up.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: confessing late after first lying [Revision]
rows.description: After telling his mother he had finished homework, a boy feels bad through the evening, goes to her before bed and tells the truth, and she appreciates it although she still asks him to complete the work.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: pros-and-cons list with a fixed deadline [Thinking]
rows.description: An engineer unhappy in a first job writes what is gained and lost by staying versus leaving, and sets a date, three months away, to decide. A deadline prevents endless brooding.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: find out what exactly is wrong using five whys [Thinking]
rows.description: The person asks why the job feels bad, then why again, and finds that the real problem is a lack of learning and an unclear role, not the pay. Root-cause thinking changes what to ask for or look for.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: quit on the day of a bad meeting [Pitfall]
rows.description: Humiliated in a review, the employee sends a resignation email that evening with no other offer. The impulse feels like freedom, but leaves a gap in income and burned bridges.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: decide to stay with a set review and adjust [Revision]
rows.description: After the trial, the person chooses to stay for six more months with a written goal for skills and pay, and a scheduled review. If the goal is missed, the exit plan is ready.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the target employer [Thinking]
rows.description: A student looks at what recruiters at target firms want to see, and picks two projects that show data handling and deployment instead of ten small tutorial clones.

rows.subtype: Approach: storyboarding the portfolio site on paper [Action]
rows.description: Before coding, the student sketches the home page, project pages and contact section on paper, and decides that each project needs a problem, a role, a result and a link.
The student keeps redesigning the fonts and animations of the portfolio for two months and never publishes it, so no recruiter sees anything at all.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking peers and seniors to critique it [Revision]
rows.description: A senior points out that project descriptions list tools but not outcomes, so the student rewrites each with the problem, what was built and what improved.

rows.subtype: Approach: staying put and waiting to be found [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl separated from her mother at a festival market remembers the rule that lost children should stop moving, reasoning that a parent will search back along the route where they were last together.

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of a lost-child plan made beforehand [Thinking]
rows.description: Before entering the bazaar, the family asks the child what he would do if separated, and he practises saying the plan aloud: stop, look for a shop, tell the number, do not leave the area.

rows.subtype: Approach: following the first friendly adult who offers to help [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy panics and goes off with a kind stranger who says he knows where the mother is, and ends up farther from the meeting spot because he never checked whether the person was trustworthy.

rows.subtype: Approach: switching from wandering to staying and asking [Revision]
rows.description: After walking two lanes and not finding his family, the boy realises moving is making things worse, stops beside a chai stall and asks the owner to phone his father.

rows.subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
rows.description: A toy car stops making its noise, so a toddler carries it to father, holds it up and says "no." The caregiver is treated as the repair service.
A toddler has seen mother call "Dadi!" when something breaks. Now a shoe strap comes loose and the toddler shouts "Dadi" toward the next room.
A teddy is wedged behind the sofa and a toddler screams from the spot, waiting. The caregiver hears the noise but cannot tell what is wrong, so help arrives late.

rows.subtype: Approach: leading the caregiver by hand [Revision]
rows.description: Mother says "wait a minute," so the toddler grabs her finger and pulls her to the sofa, pointing at the teddy. Bringing the adult to the problem fixes the missing message.

rows.subtype: Approach: check safety and call emergency services first [Action]
rows.description: At a road crash scene, a young bystander moves to a safe spot, checks for danger such as traffic, and calls the ambulance and police using the emergency number. Calling trained responders is the priority.

rows.subtype: Approach: stay calm and follow a simple mental checklist [Thinking]
rows.description: The person recalls a first-aid class outline: safety, call for help, do not move a seriously injured person unless there is a danger, and share only what is known. A learned checklist gives structure under stress.

rows.subtype: Approach: freeze and film the scene instead of helping [Pitfall]
rows.description: Shock and habit lead the person to record video while the injured person waits. Nobody calls for help for several minutes, showing how the bystander effect delays action.

rows.subtype: Approach: seek support and review habits afterwards [Revision]
rows.description: Shaken after the event, the person talks with family, sees a doctor for lingering symptoms, and decides to follow stricter rules on helmets, speed and night riding. Learning from the event changes future routines.
A child talks through a doctor game ahead of time, saying "You are sick, I listen to your chest, then give medicine," and acts out the first lines with a doll.
Two children assign roles, gather props such as a toy stethoscope and a bandage, and set the clinic on the mat before starting. Set-up comes before play.
A child insists the game must go exactly as planned and corrects the friend's every line. The friend loses interest and drifts away.
The play stalls after the check-up, so a child announces, "Emergency! The baby has a fever!" A new problem in the story keeps the game going.

rows.subtype: Approach: resource and budget planning with fixed-cost-first split [Thinking]
rows.description: A new graduate with a Rs 30,000 monthly salary lists rent, food, transport and the phone bill first, then sees what remains. Working from the unavoidable costs shows how little is truly free to spend.

rows.subtype: Approach: pay-yourself-first automation using a standing instruction [Action]
rows.description: On salary day the graduate sets an auto-transfer of a fixed amount to a separate savings account and a small SIP, before spending anything. Saving becomes a default rather than a daily decision.

rows.subtype: Approach: spend freely and see what is left [Pitfall]
rows.description: A first-job employee treats the credited amount as abundant, buys a phone on EMI and eats out often, and finds the account empty by the 20th. The plan fails because no total was ever set against the month.

rows.subtype: Approach: track spending for a month, then set category limits [Revision]
rows.description: After running short, the employee notes every UPI payment for a month, sees food delivery is the largest leak, and sets a weekly cap. Evidence from real data replaces a guessed budget.

rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: reading the notice carefully and noting the deadline [Thinking]
rows.description: On receiving a tax department email, the person reads who sent it, what is asked and the last date to respond, and does not react until the facts are clear.

rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: verifying authenticity through official channels [Action]
rows.description: Aware of frauds using fake notices, the person logs in to the official portal directly and checks whether the same notice appears there, rather than clicking email links.

rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: ignoring the notice from fear [Pitfall]
rows.description: The person puts the letter in a drawer, hoping it is a mistake. The deadline passes, penalties are added, and a simple mismatch becomes a bigger problem.

rows.subtopic: Handling a legal or tax notice
rows.subtype: Approach: revising record-keeping after the episode [Revision]
rows.description: After resolving the matter, the person starts tracking side income and receipts monthly, so that the next filing has complete records and fewer mismatches.

rows.subtype: Approach: taking turns by the clock [Action]
rows.description: Two brothers share one tablet and use a kitchen timer so each gets thirty minutes. The fixed time stops the argument about who has been playing for longer.

rows.subtype: Approach: agreeing to a plan with days for each [Thinking]
rows.description: Siblings agree that Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays are for one, and the rest for the other. They think about fairness and note that some days will suit one child's homework better.

rows.subtype: Approach: grabbing it first and refusing to hand over [Pitfall]
rows.description: An older sister takes the remote and hides it because she got there first. Her brother complains, the parents are upset, and the sharing turns into a fight over power.

rows.subtype: Approach: changing the plan when exams come [Revision]
rows.description: When the older sibling has exams, the children notice the schedule is unfair. They talk and agree that the younger gets more time for two weeks and it will balance later.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the date [Thinking]
rows.description: For a Diwali cultural evening, the student fixes the date, then counts back to book the hall, invite guests, rehearse performances and finalise food, so each step has a deadline.
The organiser lists all expected costs, sets a limit of what each classmate can contribute, prices alternatives such as home-made snacks, and tracks spending in a shared sheet.

rows.subtype: Approach: last-minute leaving everything to the day [Pitfall]
rows.description: Assuming things will work out, the organisers wait until the final day to arrange sound and seating. Equipment problems and missing chairs cause chaos and disappoint the guests.

rows.subtype: Approach: adapting when things go wrong on the day [Revision]
rows.description: When the chief guest is late, the organiser moves the performance forward and adjusts the order, keeping the audience engaged. Later the team notes a buffer would have helped.

rows.subtype: Approach: identifying the underlying concern behind the demand [Thinking]
rows.description: A wife notices her mother-in-law's insistence on cooking for the family comes from a wish to feel needed. She considers ways to include her rather than only resisting.

rows.subtype: Approach: agreeing with the spouse before speaking to parents [Action]
rows.description: The couple first decides their shared position on visits and holidays. Only then does the husband talk to his parents, so the family sees a united couple, not a spouse against them.

rows.subtype: Approach: avoiding the issue and building resentment [Pitfall]
rows.description: The wife says nothing about frequent unannounced visits. Resentment builds, and one day a minor comment leads to an outburst that hurts everyone far beyond the original matter.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing what worked after the festival season [Revision]
rows.description: After a tense Diwali, they note which arrangements helped and which did not. They change next year's plan by hosting one meal and travelling for the other, staying kinder to all.

rows.subtype: Approach: repeating the list aloud again and again [Action]
rows.description: A girl told to bring seven items for a craft class chants them over and over on the way home. It works for a short time, but she forgets two after being interrupted by her brother.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking a parent to remind him at night [Action]
rows.description: Knowing he tends to forget, a boy asks his father to ask him in the evening what is needed. This uses another person as a memory helper for a one-time, important list.

rows.subtype: Approach: trusting memory and not writing it [Pitfall]
rows.description: A girl feels sure that she will remember four items for the school trip. By evening she recalls only three, and has to call a classmate, who is unavailable.

rows.subtype: Approach: testing himself by covering the list [Revision]
rows.description: After checking, a girl finds she missed two items. She covers the list and tries to say all items again, repeating until she can say them all, and then she sleeps on it.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.subtype: Approach: thinking of how the owner must feel [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy finds a wallet on the bus and imagines his own father losing one, so he decides the money matters less than getting it back to the owner.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.subtype: Approach: pros and cons of keeping it [Thinking]
rows.description: A child lists that keeping the money buys a cricket bat, but the owner might need it for medicine or rent, and that he would feel guilty every time he used it.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.subtype: Approach: keeping it because nobody saw [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy pockets a hundred rupee note on the street thinking no one will know, then spends the day uneasy and is caught by the guilt more than by anyone's eyes.

rows.subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
rows.description: At first the girl decides to keep the money, but after talking with her friend who says the owner may be poor, she reverses and gives it to the shopkeeper to look after.

rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising urgent versus important tasks [Thinking]
rows.description: Facing two assignments, a lab file and a club event in one week, the student sorts by deadline and marks, and drops the least valuable item.

rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: weekly schedule with time blocks [Action]
rows.description: On Sunday the student blocks classes, study slots, meals, gym and sleep in a calendar, and keeps buffer space for surprises.

rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: planning fallacy about assignment length [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student assumes a report will take two hours, starts late, and needs a whole night, and the same underestimate repeats every week.

rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: adding a buffer after past overruns [Revision]
rows.description: Having seen that tasks took about double, the student multiplies estimates by one and a half and starts earlier, and deadlines stop being panics.

rows.subtype: Approach: implementation intention with a fixed cue [Thinking]
rows.description: The young professional decides: after I brush my teeth in the morning, I walk for 20 minutes. Linking the habit to an existing routine removes the daily decision.

rows.subtype: Approach: start with a tiny version that can be done on bad days [Action]
rows.description: The person begins with ten minutes of stretching and a short jog rather than a one-hour gym session, and adds time each week. Small steps build consistency before intensity.

rows.subtype: Approach: all-or-nothing plan with a five-day-a-week gym [Pitfall]
rows.description: Motivated on 1 January, the person signs up for a year and plans daily hard workouts. A cold and a busy week break the streak, and the person drops the whole plan feeling like a failure.

rows.subtype: Approach: track and adjust after a missed week [Revision]
rows.description: After missing a week, the person does not scrap the plan but notes that late evenings fail and moves sessions to mornings, with a rule of never missing twice in a row. Treating a lapse as data keeps the habit alive.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the exam date [Thinking]
rows.description: A candidate counts weeks to the exam, subtracts revision and mock periods, and sees how many days are left for each syllabus block, which shows that the plan needs a cut.
Analysing past papers, the aspirant sees which topics carry the most marks and starts with those, leaving rarely asked topics for the end.

rows.subtype: Approach: collecting resources instead of studying [Pitfall]
rows.description: The candidate joins many groups, downloads dozens of PDFs and switches teachers, feeling busy, but never finishes one book, so there is little retention.
Noticing that scores dip after sleepless weeks, the aspirant adds fixed sleep, a short evening walk and one free evening weekly, and finds accuracy improving.
A child watches another child join a group by asking, "Can I play too?" and repeats the same words the next day at the sandpit, with a smile.
A child offers a friend the first turn on the new bicycle in return for playing tag afterwards. Trading what the friend wants for what the child wants opens the play.
A child says, "You have to play my game or I won't be your friend," and the other child walks away. Demanding works less well than offering.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a packing and route list [Action]
rows.description: A girl helps plan a visit to her grandparents by listing tasks: book tickets, pack clothes, arrange food for the train, and tick them off with her mother the week before.

rows.subtype: Approach: comparing travel options by cost and comfort [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy compares train, bus and car for a trip to Agra, noting the train is cheaper and safer at night while the car allows stops, and helps the family choose the train.

rows.subtype: Approach: making a wish list without limits [Pitfall]
rows.description: The child suggests visiting six places in two days, and only when his father points at the map and clock does he see that travel time makes the plan impossible.

rows.subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan to fit the budget [Revision]
rows.description: After learning the family can spend only ten thousand rupees, the girl removes the water park and keeps the fort and museum, which cost less and everyone still enjoys.

rows.subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
rows.description: A toddler brings an empty katori to mother and taps it, saying "aur." Handing over the bowl says more than the word does.
A toddler tugs at the kitchen cupboard where biscuits are kept, then at the fridge handle, then points at the counter. Each try shows what can be reached.
A toddler wanted a biscuit and gets offered a banana. The toddler pushes it away and cries, because the goal was fixed on one thing and the request was not clear.
After crying for a biscuit, a toddler sniffs, looks at the banana, and takes it. Hunger wins out, and the plan changes from getting a specific food to getting some food.
A student in Class 11 adds up school, three coaching batches, travel and homework, finds 62 hours a week and no rest, and sees that the problem is total load and not lack of effort.

rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising the classes that add most [Action]
rows.description: The student compares which batches clarify concepts versus repeat school content, keeps the two that help most, and uses the freed time for self-study and sleep.

rows.subtype: Approach: attending everything out of fear of falling behind [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student stays in all batches because peers do. Constant sitting leaves no time to absorb the material, and marks stay flat despite exhausting days.

rows.subtype: Approach: adding rest and exercise as fixed items [Revision]
rows.description: After noticing exhaustion, the student blocks a 30-minute walk and a free Sunday afternoon in the calendar, treating rest as a scheduled part of study rather than a reward.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.subtype: Approach: choosing one course and finishing it [Action]
rows.description: A student picks a single beginner Python course, sets a goal of one lesson a day, and resists starting other courses until it is completed and a small program of his own is written.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.subtype: Approach: joining a study group for accountability [Action]
rows.description: A student teams with two classmates to solve one problem a week, present solutions to each other every Friday, and nudge whoever has skipped, which keeps all three going through dull weeks.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.description: A student watches video after video, feels he is learning, but when given a blank editor cannot write even a loop because he only ever followed along and never typed his own code.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing progress and changing method [Revision]
rows.description: After noticing three weeks without new skills, a student reviews what he did, sees he only watched videos, and switches to solving small exercises first and using videos only when stuck.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: writing down each partner's priorities separately [Thinking]
rows.description: A couple facing a job offer in another city each lists what matters most: career growth, closeness to family and finances. Seeing the lists reveals shared values beneath the disagreement.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: exploring the options as a joint decision matrix [Thinking]
rows.description: They score staying, moving, or a trial year against agreed criteria and weights. The score is not final, but it turns an emotional argument into an organised discussion.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: winning the argument through pressure [Pitfall]
rows.description: One partner repeats reasons more forcefully and uses guilt. The other gives in, but resentment lingers and reappears months later in unrelated fights.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: revisiting the decision after the trial period [Revision]
rows.description: At the six month review they note what improved and what hurt, such as long weekends apart. They adjust by adding a shorter commute and a visit schedule rather than reversing everything.

rows.subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy wants a Rs 600 remote-control car and gets Rs 50 a week. He divides and works out twelve weeks, and decides to keep going because the number seems reachable.

rows.subtype: Approach: earning extra by doing jobs at home [Action]
rows.description: A boy asks his parents whether he can earn Rs 10 for washing the family car on Sundays. The extra income shortens his wait from twelve weeks to eight.

rows.subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child gets money each week but buys chips and stickers at the shop near school. After a month the jar is nearly empty because small spends were never counted.

rows.subtype: Approach: setting a smaller first target [Revision]
rows.description: Noticing he feels discouraged, the boy sets a first goal of Rs 200 and celebrates when he reaches it. Smaller steps rebuild his patience and he carries on toward the full price.

rows.subtype: Approach: choosing the right moment and mood [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy wants permission for a sleepover and waits until his father has relaxed after dinner, rather than asking when he is tired or on a call.

rows.subtype: Approach: preparing reasons and answers to objections [Action]
rows.description: Before asking for a bicycle, a girl lists why she needs it, how she will be safe, and what she will do to earn part of the cost, so she is ready for questions.

rows.subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child asks for a mobile phone every day and cries when refused, and the parents become firmer, because pressure without reasons builds resistance.

rows.subtype: Approach: accepting a no and asking what would change it [Revision]
rows.description: Told no to a late outing, a boy calmly asks what he would need to show, and the parents say trust with earlier smaller outings, giving him a clear step to work toward.
A child stacks wooden blocks into a tower, watches it fall at the sixth block, and simply builds it again with the blocks in a slightly different order.
A child tells herself, "First the big blocks, then the small ones, then the flag on top," and builds in that order. The list keeps the tower's shape in mind as it grows.
A child says "stay up" to the tower and insists the red block is lucky, so it goes on top. When the tower wobbles anyway, the child blames the block rather than the narrow base.
After three collapses a child decides, "If it wobbles, make the bottom wider," and uses the rule on the next tower. A tested rule replaces the guess.
After noticing tension at home, the teen gently asks what has changed and learns that the father's income has dropped, which turns vague worry into a clear problem with specific limits.

rows.subtype: Approach: exploring scholarships and school support [Action]
rows.description: The teen asks the class teacher about fee concessions and scholarships, gathers documents with parents, and applies before the deadline, using formal help that exists for such situations.

rows.subtype: Approach: hiding worry and carrying it alone [Pitfall]
rows.description: The teen says nothing and pretends everything is fine, while stress builds and marks fall. Parents, unaware of the burden, cannot offer reassurance or help share the load.
After tutoring hours cut into sleep and revision, the teen and parents reduce the sessions and look for another aid source, deciding that education remains the long-term priority.

rows.subtype: Approach: watching how others behave before joining in [Thinking]
rows.description: A new girl in Class 6 observes the first days quietly, noticing where children sit and what they play at recess. She uses the time to understand before choosing whom to approach.

rows.subtype: Approach: introducing himself and asking someone to play [Action]
rows.description: A boy walks up to a group at lunch, says his name and that he moved from Kanpur. He asks if he can join their game, and the friendly response makes him feel welcome.

rows.subtype: Approach: staying alone and waiting for others to come [Pitfall]
rows.description: A shy child sits by herself at lunch, hoping someone will invite her. Classmates think she prefers to be alone, so they do not approach, and she feels lonelier every day.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing what is not working and changing the approach [Revision]
rows.description: After a week of bragging without friends, the girl notices classmates go quiet around her. She starts asking questions and listening about them, and gets invited to sit together.
A toddler sitting on the floor says "Amma" repeatedly and points at a fallen ball while mother chops vegetables. Voice and gesture are the whole plan.
A toddler tries babbling, tapping the table and carrying over a cup, and watches which one makes father look up from his phone. The one that works becomes the favourite.
Loud crying once brought mother running, so a toddler cries at full volume whenever she is busy. The method works, but it escalates and the adult starts to answer only to loudness.
Calling from across the room brings no answer, so a toddler walks over, puts both hands on the caregiver's knee and looks up. Moving closer is the change made after the first plan failed.

rows.subtype: Approach: choosing a fixed slot in the weekly timetable [Action]
rows.description: A boy who wants to learn chess fits an hour on Tuesday and Saturday evenings after homework, and tells his family so the time is respected.

rows.subtype: Approach: starting small and building up [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl beginning drawing decides on ten minutes a day, thinking a small habit that continues is better than a big plan that stops after three days.
A child spends a week making a colourful timetable and buying supplies for painting, but does no actual painting, mistaking planning for progress.

rows.subtype: Approach: dropping the routine when exams come [Revision]
rows.description: With exams coming, a girl reduces her painting time to Sunday only, planning to return at full pace afterwards, adapting the routine to her main priority rather than quitting.
A child tidies in an order: books to the shelf, then toys to the box, then clothes to the basket. Doing one kind at a time keeps the mess from feeling endless.
A child follows the rule, "If it has wheels, it goes in the blue box," and sorts cars, trucks and a scooter without asking each time.
Faced with toys everywhere, a child sits in the middle and starts to play with one, so nothing gets put away. The size of the job is too much to start on.

rows.subtype: Approach: identifying what voters actually need [Thinking]
rows.description: A candidate for school captain asks classmates about canteen queues, sports equipment and library hours, and forms a platform on concrete issues instead of general promises of change.

rows.subtype: Approach: writing and rehearsing the speech [Action]
rows.description: The candidate drafts a two-minute speech with one clear promise and one story, practises in front of a mirror and a friend, and trims filler after timing it.
A well-liked student assumes friends will vote for him and makes no plan. Rivals with clear proposals talk to more classes, and he loses despite having a lot of goodwill.

rows.subtype: Approach: learning from a loss and following through [Revision]
rows.description: After losing by a few votes, the student congratulates the winner, asks for feedback and offers to lead a canteen committee, turning the defeat into a way of doing the promised work anyway.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
rows.subtype: Approach: weighing values of loyalty and honesty [Thinking]
rows.description: A student who saw his close friend copy in a test lists what matters, friendship, fairness to others and his own integrity, and notices the conflict is real rather than simple.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
rows.subtype: Approach: talking to the friend first [Action]
rows.description: A teen privately tells her friend that copying worries her, asks why it happened, and gives her a chance to fix it herself, such as confessing to the teacher.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
rows.subtype: Approach: staying silent to avoid conflict [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student tells himself it is not his business, and the friend keeps copying, gains marks over honest classmates, and the student feels uneasy each time he sees the result.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
rows.subtype: Approach: reconsidering after seeing the friend's reasons [Revision]
rows.description: After learning that the friend was under heavy pressure from home, a teen still insists on stopping the cheating but also helps him ask for tutoring, changing how the problem is approached.

rows.subtype: Approach: starting with the junior's actual goal [Thinking]
rows.description: A final-year student asks the junior what they want, such as a first internship, and tailors advice to that goal rather than repeating what worked for themselves.

rows.subtype: Approach: breaking learning into small steps [Action]
rows.description: The mentor turns learn programming into a weekly plan of one concept, one exercise and one small program, and reviews the work with the junior every Saturday.

rows.subtype: Approach: giving the answer straight away [Pitfall]
rows.description: Wanting to be helpful, the mentor solves every problem for the junior, who becomes dependent and cannot work through a problem alone.

rows.subtype: Approach: recognising own limits and referring on [Revision]
rows.description: When the junior asks about a field the mentor does not know, the mentor says so, and introduces a senior from that field instead of pretending.

rows.subtype: Approach: discussing timing, finances and roles with the partner [Thinking]
rows.description: A couple talks about when to start a family, how leave will work, who will take time off and what changes in spending. They treat it as a joint plan rather than an assumption.

rows.subtype: Approach: checking employer leave policy and planning finances [Action]
rows.description: They read the company's maternity and paternity leave rules, estimate months of reduced income, and build a savings buffer over a year before trying.

rows.subtype: Approach: assuming grandparents will handle childcare [Pitfall]
rows.description: The couple takes for granted that parents will move in to help. When the grandparents say their health and home make that difficult, the couple has no plan and scrambles.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing the plan after the baby arrives [Revision]
rows.description: After the first month, the plan of the mother handling nights proves exhausting. They change to alternating nights and hire part-time help, and keep talking about how each is coping.
A child drags a chair to the cupboard to reach a jar of sweets, tries standing on it, and finds it still too short. Then a stool is added on top.
A child says, "Papa, can you get the jar down?" and points to the shelf. Asking is quick and safe, and the child's own plan is only needed if nobody is home.
A child stretches and stretches, believing that arms can grow long enough with effort. Wanting the jar overrides a plain look at the distance.
A stacked stool starts to wobble, and the child steps down and calls for help. Feeling the danger changes the plan from climbing to asking.

rows.subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: disclosing quickly and owning it [Action]
rows.description: After deleting a customer table by mistake, the engineer tells the lead within minutes, explains exactly what happened and what data is affected, so the team can start recovery at once.

rows.subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
rows.description: The employee asks what can still get worse, stops the scheduled job, restores from backup and informs affected customers, and leaves blame and analysis for after the fire is out.

rows.subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: hiding the mistake and hoping it goes unnoticed [Pitfall]
rows.description: The employee quietly patches the error and says nothing. When it appears later in an audit, the concealment damages trust far more than the original mistake would have.

rows.subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: rebuilding trust with small reliable deliveries [Revision]
rows.description: Over the next months, the employee delivers tasks on time, communicates delays early and keeps the team informed, and gradually regains bigger responsibilities.
Two children argue about a toy car and one runs to the teacher, who listens to both and helps them agree. The adult acts as the judge.
A child says, "You have it now, I have it after lunch." Splitting the time between them ends the shouting with each getting a turn.
A child turns away and pretends the fight is not there, in the belief that it will go away. The hurt stays, and the friend is puzzled by the silence.
A third child suggests tossing a coin for the toy and both accept. The first child remembers the idea and suggests it at the next quarrel.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
rows.description: A toddler stands under a low shelf, rises on tiptoe and stretches one arm toward a stuffed elephant, grunting, then tries the other hand when the first falls short.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
rows.description: A toddler tries jumping, tugging the shelf edge and pulling the rug under the toy, one after another, and keeps repeating whichever move makes the elephant shift even a little.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
rows.description: A toddler keeps stretching at the same spot for several minutes and ignores the stool close by, until tears come. Repeating one failing action leaves no room to notice other options.

rows.subtopic: Reaching a toy on a shelf
rows.description: Frustrated, a toddler sits down and whimpers, then looks around for mother, points at the shelf and lets her lift the toy down. The toddler switches from doing it alone to asking.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from months of cash left [Thinking]
rows.description: A founder with savings for nine months counts back from the last salary date and asks what must be proven by month six to raise money. Every task is then judged against that date.

rows.subtype: Approach: building a minimum viable version in six weeks [Action]
rows.description: Two founders ship a bare-bones invoicing tool for Kirana shops using no-code tools, and put it in front of twenty shop owners in Lucknow before writing any custom backend.

rows.subtype: Approach: polishing the product before showing anyone [Pitfall]
rows.description: A founder keeps refining the app design for five months out of fear of a weak first impression. Cash drains while no real customer feedback arrives, and the runway shrinks to three months.

rows.subtype: Approach: weekly burn review with a kill threshold [Revision]
rows.description: After each Friday the founders compare spending with signups. When cash falls below four months with no paying user, they cut the paid tools and freelancers and shift to selling personally.

rows.subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
rows.subtype: Approach: thinking of what is still possible [Thinking]
rows.description: During a night power cut, a girl notes she cannot use the tablet but can read by candle light, tell stories or play antakshari with her family.

rows.subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
rows.subtype: Approach: finishing homework before the battery dies [Action]
rows.description: When the weather forecast warns of a storm, a boy completes the online task early and prints notes, so an outage does not leave him stranded before the deadline.

rows.subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
rows.description: A boy whose picnic is rained off sits angry and says everything is spoiled, so he misses the chance to enjoy the cosy day the family attempts to arrange.

rows.subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
rows.subtype: Approach: switching to an indoor activity [Revision]
rows.description: When rain cancels the cricket match, the children decide to play carrom and ludo indoors, and treat it as a different fun day rather than a lost one.

rows.subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
rows.subtype: Approach: pre-departure checklist and task decomposition [Action]
rows.description: A teen lists documents, admission papers, bank access, medicines, clothes and contacts, ticks them off over two weeks with a parent, and packs the essentials last.

rows.subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
rows.subtype: Approach: researching housing and neighbourhood safety [Action]
rows.description: With parents, a student compares hostel and paying-guest options, reads reviews, asks seniors about commute time, food and safety, and visits before paying any deposit.

rows.subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
rows.subtype: Approach: expecting the new place to feel like home instantly [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student assumes he will fit in within days, feels panicked when he is lonely by the third week, and wants to drop out, not realising that adjustment usually takes months.

rows.subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
rows.subtype: Approach: adapting routines after early problems [Revision]
rows.description: After skipping breakfast and struggling to focus, a student changes to a fixed schedule, finds a nearby tiffin service, and shifts study time to when the hostel is quieter.
A family walks through the flat one evening, tracing the path from each bedroom to the stairs, and the children practise crawling low and feeling doors before opening them.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the safe meeting spot [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl decides that the goal is to stand at the neighbour's gate, then figures out each step back from there: out the door, down the stairs, avoiding the lift, leaving belongings behind.

rows.subtype: Approach: going back for a favourite toy [Pitfall]
rows.description: In a practice drill, a boy runs back to fetch his pet's cage, and his parents use it to teach that belongings and even pets are secondary once the alarm sounds and adults must lead rescue.

rows.subtype: Approach: fixing a blocked exit found in the drill [Revision]
rows.description: During practice the children see the balcony door is stuck and a cupboard blocks the passage, so the family clears the way and repeats the drill until it takes under a minute.
A child follows a picture chart on the wardrobe door: vest, shirt, shorts, socks, shoes. Each step is ticked off in order.
A child recites, "If it is Wednesday, I wear sports shoes." Attaching the action to the day means the child needn't ask every morning.
A child cannot find the second sock, climbs back into bed and says "I'm not going." One missing item ends the whole plan for the morning.
Buttons are done up one hole out, and the child sees the shirt hang crooked, undoes it and starts again from the bottom button. The mistake is spotted and fixed.
The teenager asks why parents refuse late evenings out and learns the concerns are safety and late-night travel, not distrust, which allows a plan that addresses those specific concerns.
The teen proposes going to a friend's house until 8 pm, sharing the address and location, phoning on arrival and being picked up by a parent, offering a trial for a month.
The teen shouts that everyone else is allowed and that parents are too strict. The argument turns into a power struggle, parents dig in and the request for freedom is refused outright.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing after a broken agreement [Revision]
rows.description: After coming home late once, the teen owns up, explains the reason without excuses and proposes a stricter check-in for two weeks, showing that trust can be repaired rather than lost.

rows.subtype: Approach: finishing homework first, then playing [Action]
rows.description: A boy makes a rule that games start only after homework, and finds that with work done he enjoys the game more without worry in the back of his mind.
A girl sets a timer for forty minutes of gaming on weekdays, and when it rings she stops, making the limit feel like her own rule rather than a parent's.
A child tells himself only one more round, then another, and suddenly it is ten p.m. with unfinished maths, showing how a fun activity without a stopping point expands.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing tiredness and changing the routine [Revision]
rows.description: After falling asleep in class from late gaming, the boy realises the cost, moves gaming to the afternoon and puts the console away by nine at night.

rows.subtype: Approach: acts quickly when time is short and the situation is urgent [Thinking]
rows.description: A student sees a friend faint at a hostel event and acts at once, calling for help, since there is no time for a detailed plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: takes time and sleeps on it when the decision is slow and important [Thinking]
rows.description: A student weighing whether to pursue further study lets the decision take a month, gathering facts and talking to family, since no deadline forces speed.

rows.subtype: Approach: uses one method for every problem out of habit [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student who likes detailed timetables uses them even for creative work, where a loose start would suit better, and feels blocked.

rows.subtype: Approach: pausing and recognising pressure tactics [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen gets a call saying his father's account will be blocked in ten minutes unless an OTP is shared, notices the urgency and fear, and treats the pressure itself as the warning sign.

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of scam scripts [Thinking]
rows.description: After reading examples of common frauds, a teen rehearses aloud what she would say to a fake officer or a fake job offer, so a calm refusal is ready when a real call arrives.

rows.subtype: Approach: trusting a caller who knows some personal details [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student believes a caller because he knows her school name and her father's name, not realising such details are easily collected, and starts sharing more information to be helpful.

rows.subtype: Approach: containing the damage after a slip [Revision]
rows.description: Realising he entered his login on a fake page, a student changes the password at once, logs out other devices, turns on two-step verification, and tells a parent so the bank can be warned.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: list all demands and rank them by urgency and importance [Thinking]
rows.description: A final-year student lists hospital visits, exams, assignments and household tasks, and decides that treatment appointments and the coming exam are the top priorities. Ranking gives a way to say no to the rest.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: share the care schedule with siblings and relatives [Action]
rows.description: The student writes a weekly rota for hospital stays, medicine pickup and cooking and asks a sibling, an aunt and a neighbour to take fixed slots. Sharing the care prevents burnout of one person.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: take on everything alone to prove devotion [Pitfall]
rows.description: Feeling that asking for help is disloyal, the student does every task and sleeps four hours. Exhaustion leads to a failed test and short temper, which makes the care worse.

rows.subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
rows.subtype: Approach: notice signs of caregiver fatigue and step back [Revision]
rows.description: Realising that irritation and poor sleep are constant, the student asks an aunt to take two nights and books a counselling session. Recognising limits keeps the care sustainable.
A child swaps the toy truck for a turn with the friend's doll. Both get something they want, so the trade feels fair to both.
A child reasons, "If I share the truck, then Aarav shares his cars." The rule ties giving to getting, and makes it less costly to hand the toy over.
A child fears that the toy will be "used up" or will change once a friend touches it, and hides it. The fear has no basis but decides what the child does.
Two children pull on one toy until a teacher is asked, and she proposes a sand timer for each turn. The child follows the rule the timer sets.

rows.subtype: Approach: sort out runway with a cash and expense count [Thinking]
rows.description: After a layoff at a startup, the employee counts savings, essential monthly costs and expected severance to see how many months of runway exist. The number turns a vague fear into a bounded problem.

rows.subtype: Approach: structured job search with weekly targets [Action]
rows.description: The employee sets a weekly plan: update the CV, apply to ten roles, message five former colleagues and practice one mock interview. A routine gives a sense of progress even when replies are slow.

rows.subtype: Approach: take the first offer accepted out of panic [Pitfall]
rows.description: Fearing the gap, the employee accepts a role with lower pay and a poor fit without asking about terms. Within three months the person is looking again, showing how fear can override checking the match.

rows.subtype: Approach: revise the plan after two months without offers [Revision]
rows.description: With no offers after two months, the person reviews the applications, finds the CV lacks results-oriented lines, asks a mentor for feedback and widens the search to adjacent roles. Reviewing evidence prevents repeating a failing approach.

rows.subtype: Approach: ignoring the teasing at first [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy hopes that if he does not react the bully will get bored, and for some days it works a little, though it also shows the limits of ignoring when the teasing continues.

rows.subtype: Approach: rehearsing a calm firm reply [Thinking]
rows.description: In front of a mirror, a boy practises saying stop it in a steady voice and walking away, imagining how the bully will react so he is less shaken in the moment.
A boy pushes the bully during recess and ends up in the principal's office too, learning that revenge can turn a victim into a person also in trouble.

rows.subtype: Approach: changing the plan when the first step fails [Revision]
rows.description: When ignoring the teasing does not stop it, the girl chooses to tell her parents, who meet the teacher, and the school separates the seating and watches the group.
A child looks for a lost shoe by going back through the day: the bedroom, the verandah, the gate where she played. Going in order narrows down where it could be.
A child says, "Mummy, I can't find my shoe," and mother asks, "Where did you last have it?" The adult's question gives the search a structure.
A child insists that the shoe "ran away" and that it will come home if she waits at the door. Waiting replaces searching.
A friend says, "Check the last place you played," and the child goes to the balcony where the shoe lies. The hint changes the search from random to reasoned.

rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.subtype: Approach: preparing facts, cause and options first [Thinking]
rows.description: Before telling a hospital client that go-live will slip by three weeks, the account lead gathers the cause, the new date and two ways to reduce impact, so the message has substance.

rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of likely reactions [Thinking]
rows.description: He imagines the client being angry, asking whom to blame, or asking for a discount. He drafts calm, honest replies for each so he is not pushed into rash promises.

rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.subtype: Approach: delaying until a fix is found [Pitfall]
rows.description: Hoping to solve it quietly, the manager waits two weeks before telling the client. When the delay is finally revealed, trust suffers more than the delay itself would have caused.

rows.subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing the call and adjusting communication cadence [Revision]
rows.description: After the call the team notes the client wanted more frequent updates. They switch from weekly emails to short Monday and Thursday notes, and the relationship steadies.

rows.subtype: Approach: gathering specific examples before speaking [Thinking]
rows.description: A lead lists what actually happened: three late tasks and two untested changes over a month. He avoids labels like careless, so the discussion stays on observable work.

rows.subtype: Approach: root cause analysis with the junior [Thinking]
rows.description: In a private talk she asks what is making tasks hard. The junior explains he does not understand the codebase and fears asking, so the problem is support, not effort.

rows.subtype: Approach: doing the junior's work quietly [Pitfall]
rows.description: To meet deadlines the lead rewrites his code at night without telling him. He never learns what was wrong, and she burns out while his performance stays the same.

rows.subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan when the fit is wrong [Revision]
rows.description: After six weeks progress is patchy on backend but strong on testing. With the manager's agreement, the lead moves him to a quality role that suits his strengths.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the loan end date [Thinking]
rows.description: A graduate with a Rs 6 lakh education loan takes the bank's repayment period and works backward to the monthly amount needed, then checks it against the expected salary. The goal date sets the size of each step.

rows.subtype: Approach: list loan terms and interest rate before deciding [Action]
rows.description: The borrower collects the sanction letter, notes the interest rate, moratorium end, EMI and any prepayment charges, and asks the bank to explain anything unclear. Knowing exact terms comes before choosing any strategy.

rows.subtype: Approach: ignore the letters until the first EMI is overdue [Pitfall]
rows.description: Anxious about the size of the loan, the graduate avoids opening bank messages during the moratorium. The first EMI is missed, a late fee is added and the credit record suffers. Avoidance turns a manageable task into a bigger problem.

rows.subtype: Approach: talk to the bank about restructuring before missing a payment [Revision]
rows.description: When a job start is delayed, the borrower meets the bank branch early, explains the situation and asks about options such as a longer tenure. Acting before default keeps choices open and shows good faith.
Five friends list transport, stay, food and entry costs for a Manali trip, add a ten percent cushion, and divide by five to see what each must save.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from dates and exams [Thinking]
rows.description: Given exam dates and holiday days, the group finds the only free window, then books trains first because the rest depends on it, and fixes stays afterward.

rows.subtype: Approach: leaving planning to the last moment [Pitfall]
rows.description: The group keeps saying it will figure it out later, so prices rise, trains fill up, and the trip is cut short or dropped, which leaves people disappointed.

rows.subtype: Approach: replanning when money runs short mid-trip [Revision]
rows.description: On day two the group sees spending is higher than planned, so they skip a paid activity, cook one meal, and choose free viewpoints instead of dropping the trip.

rows.subtype: Approach: notice the pattern through a mood diary [Thinking]
rows.description: A final-year student who feels flat for weeks jots down sleep, appetite and mood each day, and sees a link with late nights and isolation. Writing makes the pattern visible and gives something concrete to share with a professional.

rows.subtype: Approach: tell a trusted friend or family member [Action]
rows.description: The student tells a close friend and later a sister that things have felt heavy for a month. Saying it aloud reduces isolation and brings in someone who can help with next steps.

rows.subtype: Approach: push through and hide it [Pitfall]
rows.description: Believing that admitting struggle looks weak, the person keeps a cheerful face, skips meals and stops replying to friends. Suppression drains energy and delays help.

rows.subtype: Approach: build a wider support net with roles [Revision]
rows.description: After the roommate's fatigue, the student adds a counsellor, a weekly call with family and a walking group, and agrees with each on how they can help. Spreading support makes it sturdier.

rows.subtype: Approach: deciding purpose and audience first [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen asks why she is posting, chooses to share art with friends and family only, and sets her account to private so the purpose shapes what goes up.

rows.subtype: Approach: audit of privacy settings and old posts [Action]
rows.description: A teen reviews tags, location sharing and public photos, removes an old post showing the school gate and uniform, and switches off location so strangers cannot find her routine.
A teen posts more daring pictures to gain followers, feels anxious when likes drop, and finds his mood tied to numbers he does not control.

rows.subtype: Approach: handling a negative comment by pausing [Revision]
rows.description: After a mean comment, a teen waits an hour before replying, decides to ignore it, deletes and blocks, and later checks in with a friend, rather than starting an argument.

rows.subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of late nights [Thinking]
rows.description: A student sleeping at 3 am asks why, and finds it comes from late-night scrolling after a stressful day and studying during the evening's wasted hours, not from any lack of hours in the day.

rows.subtype: Approach: wind-down routine with if-then rules [Thinking]
rows.description: The student decides that if it is 10 pm then the phone charges outside the room, and a short routine of washing up and reading follows, giving the brain a repeated signal for sleep.

rows.subtype: Approach: overnight resolution to change everything [Pitfall]
rows.description: After a bad exam, the student resolves to sleep at 9 pm and wake at 4 am starting tomorrow. The unrealistic jump fails in two days and leaves the student feeling like a failure.

rows.subtype: Approach: relapse after a festival or exam week and restarting [Revision]
rows.description: After a week of late nights around a wedding, the student does not give up but simply returns to the fixed wake time the next morning, treating the slip as normal rather than proof of failure.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from a target role and its listed skills [Thinking]
rows.description: A final-year student picks three job postings for junior backend roles, lists the skills they repeat, and works backward to see which gaps matter most before graduation.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a weekly application routine [Action]
rows.description: The student sets a weekly quota of eight tailored applications, two referral messages and one mock interview, tracked in a spreadsheet, so the search becomes small daily tasks.

rows.subtype: Approach: mass applying with one generic resume [Pitfall]
rows.description: Sending the same resume to hundreds of portals feels productive, but replies stay near zero because nothing signals fit, and the student starts blaming the market instead of the resume.

rows.subtype: Approach: experiment and measure on resume versions [Revision]
rows.description: After two silent weeks, the student tries two resume versions, tracks which gets callbacks, and finds that the one leading with projects outperforms the one leading with marks.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing warning signs and taking them seriously [Thinking]
rows.description: A team lead notices constant fatigue, irritability and dread on Sunday nights. Instead of pushing through, he concludes this is a pattern that needs a change, not just a rest weekend.

rows.subtype: Approach: root cause analysis of the work drivers [Thinking]
rows.description: Asking why he is exhausted, he finds unclear priorities, no leave in eleven months and taking on other people's tasks. Naming causes allows changes beyond simply resting.

rows.subtype: Approach: pushing through with more effort [Pitfall]
rows.description: Believing he just needs discipline, he adds early morning work and cuts rest. His performance drops further, errors increase and the exhaustion deepens.

rows.subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan when relapse signs appear [Revision]
rows.description: Three weeks after returning, sleep worsens as deadlines return. She tells her manager, drops a commitment and adds a weekly counselling session, treating the relapse as information.

rows.subtype: Approach: maximising with a decision matrix [Thinking]
rows.description: After Class 10, a student scores Science, Commerce and Humanities on interest, marks trend, career options, cost and family support. Weighting each makes trade-offs visible rather than felt vaguely.

The student asks which tasks make hours vanish rather than which stream sounds prestigious, and notices she loves data puzzles and debate, pointing towards Economics more than the expected Science route.

rows.subtype: Approach: following friends into the same stream [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student picks Science only because his whole friend group has. Friendship is a real comfort, but it says nothing about his aptitude, and Physics becomes a struggle after the first term.

Told that a change of stream after Class 11 is possible at some schools and that many careers accept multiple routes, the student relaxes, chooses the best current fit and sets a review point after the first term.

rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising urgent versus important tasks [Thinking]
rows.description: Right after a layoff, a developer sorts tasks: securing health cover and understanding severance are urgent, while polishing the portfolio and networking are important but can be staged.
The person totals rent, EMI and family costs, computes how many months savings plus severance will last, and trims subscriptions so the job search has a clear time limit.
The developer sends three hundred identical applications on job portals in a week. Few replies arrive, and the person feels worse, mistaking activity for progress.

rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing interview feedback and adjusting [Revision]
rows.description: After several rejections at the final round, the person asks for feedback, learns that system design answers were vague, and practises with a friend before applying again.

rows.subtype: Approach: gathering documents and understanding the facts [Thinking]
rows.description: Before discussing a dispute over the ancestral house, a sibling collects the papers, checks who is named on them and what each relative is assuming. Facts reduce guesswork.

rows.subtype: Approach: consulting a lawyer for general guidance [Action]
rows.description: Unsure of the rules, the siblings ask a lawyer to explain the general legal position and the options for settlement. They use the advice to frame discussion, not as a weapon.
A relative threatens to go to court and stops speaking to others. Positions harden, the elders are distressed, and the possibility of a settlement moves further away.

rows.subtype: Approach: reopening talks after a stalemate with a cooling period [Revision]
rows.description: When talks break down, they agree to pause for a month with no messages on the subject. On resuming, tempers are lower and one proposal, the rental option, is accepted.

rows.subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
rows.description: A student who failed two courses asks why repeatedly and traces the failure to missed early classes after a family illness and to hesitation in asking for help, not to lack of ability.

rows.subtype: Approach: talking honestly with an academic advisor [Action]
rows.description: The student meets the advisor, brings the marksheet, explains what happened, and learns about backlog exam dates, credit rules and a lighter course load for the next term.

rows.subtype: Approach: avoidance and hiding the result [Pitfall]
rows.description: Afraid of family reaction, the student says nothing and skips backlog forms, and the lapsing deadlines make the situation worse than the original failure.

rows.subtype: Approach: tracking weekly progress and adjusting [Revision]
rows.description: Each Sunday the student checks attendance and test scores against targets, and after three weeks of weak scores in one subject swaps solo study for a peer group.
A graduate scores two offers on learning, pay, commute, team and stability, gives each a weight from personal priorities, and sees a smaller company edging ahead.
The graduate lists advantages and drawbacks of each offer on paper and finds that the list mostly shows what is already felt, but it also exposes an overlooked relocation cost.

rows.subtype: Approach: choosing by brand name alone [Pitfall]
rows.description: A candidate takes the famous company because relatives will be impressed, without checking the role, and later finds the work is repetitive support with little growth.
A week after accepting, the candidate learns that the joining location was moved. Rather than ignoring it, they ask HR to clarify in writing and reconsider only if the answer differs.
The person lists what matters most: career growth, closeness to ageing parents, savings and lifestyle, then checks how each country and staying home would serve those values.

The person scores three countries on salary, visa route, living cost, family distance and work culture, with weights based on personal priorities, and compares totals while noting the scores are approximate.
Seeing classmates post photos from abroad, the person applies to the same country without asking whether the life fits. Social comparison drives the choice more than personal reasons.

rows.subtype: Approach: revisiting the choice after arrival [Revision]
rows.description: Six months after moving, the person checks against the original values, finds that career goals are met but community is missing, and joins local groups and schedules regular calls home.

rows.subtype: Approach: first-principles reading of the core concept [Thinking]
rows.description: Before jumping into a framework, a student learns what problem it solves and its main building blocks, so later tutorials fit into a clear map.

rows.subtype: Approach: building a small project immediately [Action]
rows.description: The student follows a short tutorial for one day, then builds a simple expense tracker with the new tool, and learns more from errors than from videos.
The student watches course after course, nodding along, but cannot write anything from a blank file, since watching felt like learning but built no skill.
