rows.subtype: Approach: teaching back to check understanding [Revision]
rows.description: The student explains the concept to a junior and discovers gaps at the second question, then goes back to fix that piece before moving on.

rows.subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
rows.subtype: Approach: breaking work into estimated pieces to test feasibility [Thinking]
rows.description: Told to deliver a payments feature in two weeks, a developer lists every task with hours and sees it needs six weeks. The numbers give her a factual base rather than a feeling.

rows.subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
rows.subtype: Approach: offering scope options instead of a flat no [Action]
rows.description: She brings the manager three choices: full feature in six weeks, core flow in two weeks with manual reconciliation, or a two-week prototype. The manager picks the core flow.

rows.subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
rows.subtype: Approach: accepting silently and working nights [Pitfall]
rows.description: A junior lead says yes without checking the estimate and starts working until midnight. Quality falls, bugs reach production, and the manager assumes the deadline was reasonable next time.

rows.subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
rows.subtype: Approach: early risk flag with updated forecast [Revision]
rows.description: Midway, a vendor delay appears. She tells the manager the same day, shares a revised date, and suggests one task be moved to another team, avoiding a last-minute surprise.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from exam dates and syllabus weight [Thinking]
rows.description: A Class 10 student counts backward from the March exam date, lists chapters by marks weightage, and sees that Science and Maths need the most hours, so those get the early mornings.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition into chapter-level checklists [Action]
rows.description: The student turns each subject into a tick-box list of chapters, past-paper sets and formula sheets, and ticks items off nightly, which makes progress visible instead of a vague feeling of being behind.

rows.subtype: Approach: copying a topper's timetable without fit [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student adopts a classmate's 5 am to midnight routine from social media. It ignores her own energy pattern and school hours, so by week two she is exhausted and abandons the whole schedule.
After missing two days to fever, the student sees the plan had no gaps. She rebuilds it with one free half-day per week and moves the missed chapters there instead of piling them on top.

rows.subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
rows.subtype: Approach: establishing the facts before acting [Thinking]
rows.description: On noticing inflated numbers in a client report, an analyst re-checks the calculations and sources and separates what is known from what is suspected before accusing anyone.

rows.subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
rows.subtype: Approach: consulting a mentor outside the company [Action]
rows.description: The employee talks in general terms to a trusted mentor in another firm to test judgement and understand how others handled similar situations, without leaking confidential details.

rows.subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
rows.subtype: Approach: staying silent to protect the job [Pitfall]
rows.description: Fearing for a loan-backed salary, the employee says nothing and tells themselves it is not their business. Later the problem grows and the employee's silence weighs on their conscience.

rows.subtopic: Facing an ethical breach at work
rows.subtype: Approach: escalating to compliance if unresolved [Revision]
rows.description: When the manager dismisses the issue, the employee sends a written note to the compliance team or ethics helpline, following official process and avoiding gossip or social media.

rows.subtype: Approach: making a guest list with a limit on numbers [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy wants to invite his whole class but his parents can host fifteen. He lists close friends and cousins first, counts, and cuts a few, choosing who matters most.

rows.subtype: Approach: dreaming up ideas and then choosing one [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl brainstorms a treasure hunt, a movie and a pizza party, then compares them for cost, space and fun. She picks the treasure hunt because it works in their small flat.

rows.subtype: Approach: planning only the fun parts and ignoring food and time [Pitfall]
rows.description: A girl plans five games but forgets snacks and how long each takes. On the day, kids get hungry at 5 pm and the games run beyond the time when parents come to pick them up.

rows.subtype: Approach: checking the budget with a parent and trimming [Revision]
rows.description: The costs of balloons, return gifts and cake exceed what a parent set aside. The child cuts return gifts to small pencil sets and makes decorations from coloured paper at home.
A child follows a picture list taped inside the cupboard: water bottle, lunch box, notebook, pencil box. Each item is put in and ticked.
A child asks mother, "What do I need for tomorrow?" and she reads the timetable aloud. The child then puts in the books she names.
A child throws items in quickly and later finds the lunch box left on the table. Packing felt finished without any check against the list.
After forgetting the water bottle, a child pretends to walk through the school day, saying "Now I am thirsty, I need my bottle." The rehearsal shows what is missing.
A toddler twists, pulls, bangs the lid on the floor and pokes at the edge of a snack box. Each action is tried for a few seconds and dropped if nothing gives.
Having watched father twist the lid off a tiffin box, a toddler copies the twisting wrist motion on a box of raisins, though the twist goes the wrong way and the lid does not open.
The lid stays stuck and a toddler grows red in the face, throws the box across the room and screams. Strong feeling ends the experimenting that might have opened it.
Once, pressing the lid corner popped a box open. The toddler now presses the corner of every lid and box, and is puzzled when a screw-top bottle does not respond.

rows.subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
rows.subtype: Approach: fixing a total budget and working backward [Thinking]
rows.description: A group of teens with a school trip fund of 3,000 rupees each subtracts fixed costs for transport and stay, and sees only about 800 remains for food and entry tickets.

rows.subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
rows.subtype: Approach: comparing transport and stay options [Thinking]
rows.description: Students compare a sleeper train, a bus and a shared taxi for price, time and safety, and choose the train for the overnight leg while accepting slower travel to save money.

rows.subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
rows.description: The group plans eight places in two days, then exhausted by travel time, skips half of them and pays for tickets they never use, having ignored how slow moving actually is.

rows.subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
rows.subtype: Approach: replanning when a booking fails [Revision]
rows.description: When the planned hostel is full, the group calls two alternatives, chooses one with a parent's approval, adjusts the food budget to cover it, and updates the shared plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: contain by changing passwords and turning on two-factor login [Action]
rows.description: After a company email says an app was breached, the person changes the password on that site and on any other site where it was reused, and enables two-factor authentication. Acting at once limits further damage.

rows.subtype: Approach: contact the bank and freeze cards if financial data is affected [Action]
rows.description: Since a card number was in the leak, the person calls the bank using the number printed on the card, blocks it and asks about alerts on transactions. Using an official channel avoids a fake helpline.

rows.subtype: Approach: ignore the notice as spam [Pitfall]
rows.description: The user assumes the email is junk and deletes it. Weeks later, someone uses the leaked details for phishing calls, and the delay makes it harder to trace.

rows.subtype: Approach: report to the company and cybercrime portal when misuse appears [Revision]
rows.description: When a suspicious transaction appears, the person moves from prevention to reporting: complaint to the bank, the cybercrime portal, and the service that leaked the data, keeping screenshots. Steps shift with new evidence.
When a friend asks to copy the maths answers, a girl says no and offers to explain the method after class instead, holding firm without ending the friendship.

rows.subtype: Approach: thinking of what the test is for [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy reasons that copying gives marks but no learning, and that he would be lost in the next chapter, so helping someone cheat does not truly help them.

rows.subtype: Approach: giving in to keep the friendship [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child shows his answers because he fears the friend will stop talking to him, and worries afterwards, since the teacher may blame both and the fear kept growing.

rows.subtype: Approach: telling the teacher when the friend will not stop [Revision]
rows.description: After saying no twice, a boy learns that the friend plans to bring a chit into the exam, so he speaks privately with the teacher, thinking that stopping a bigger problem is worth it.

rows.subtype: Approach: following a routine of daily watering [Action]
rows.description: A girl plants tulsi and marigold in old tins, and waters them each morning before school, checking the soil with a finger to see whether it is still damp.

rows.subtype: Approach: finding out what each plant needs [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy asks the nursery man and learns that chilli needs sun while mint likes shade, and decides to place pots by the window and beside the wall accordingly.
A child pours water on the seedlings several times a day thinking more means faster growth, and the roots rot until the leaves yellow and the plants droop.

rows.subtype: Approach: moving the pots after the leaves burn [Revision]
rows.description: When the leaves of the rose plant turn crisp in the afternoon heat, the girl shifts it to partial shade and covers the soil with dry leaves to hold moisture.

rows.subtype: Approach: breaking the project into tasks and owners [Action]
rows.description: A team building a science model lists research, materials, construction and presentation, gives each member a task that matches their strengths and sets a date for each stage.
The leader sees that painting cannot start until the frame dries, and that testing needs a working circuit, so she starts those dependent tasks first and lets independent ones run in parallel.
Not trusting others, the leader does most work at night and gets exhausted. The team feels sidelined, the quality drops, and members learn nothing from the project.

rows.subtype: Approach: inviting dissent and choosing by criteria [Revision]
rows.description: After the failure, the leader asks each member to state one concern and scores ideas on cost, time and feasibility, so the next decision uses evidence rather than confidence.

rows.subtype: Approach: weighing danger against being laughed at [Thinking]
rows.description: Dared to jump from a high wall, a boy imagines a broken leg against a moment of teasing, and decides that a few jokes will be forgotten sooner than an injury.

rows.subtype: Approach: predicting what could go wrong [Thinking]
rows.description: Before agreeing to walk on the railway track, a child asks what happens if a train comes or his foot slips, and the answers make the choice clear.

rows.subtype: Approach: accepting the dare to prove courage [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy climbs the tree over the pond because friends call him scared, and ends up stuck and scraped, showing how a wish for approval can outweigh good sense.
After a friend gets hurt on a risky bicycle stunt, the boy admits he should have refused, tells his parents the truth and helps the friend, deciding to speak up early next time.

rows.subtype: Approach: gathering information from doctors first [Thinking]
rows.description: When a parent receives a serious diagnosis, the son asks the treating specialist to explain the stages, choices and unknowns, taking notes and avoiding decisions based on social media claims.
The siblings divide roles: one handles hospital visits, one manages paperwork and insurance, one keeps relatives informed. A shared chat and weekly call keep everyone aligned.

rows.subtype: Approach: panic buying every suggested remedy [Pitfall]
rows.description: Anxious relatives push expensive unproven cures and the young adult, wanting to do something, spends savings on them. The family's money and energy drain without medical guidance.

rows.subtype: Approach: revising the plan after treatment response [Revision]
rows.description: When the first treatment plan brings side effects, the family talks with the doctor about changes, updates schedules at work and home, and adapts finances rather than sticking to the first plan.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition with a shared board [Action]
rows.description: A team of four splits the project into modules, puts tasks on a shared board with owners and dates, and reviews it briefly twice a week.
The team notices that the data pipeline must exist before model training and the interface can be built in parallel, so the pipeline owner gets support first.

rows.subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
rows.description: Confident that the project is easy, the team postpones coding until the final month, then finds integration bugs and rushes through a barely working submission.

rows.subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
rows.description: When a milestone slips twice, the team asks why repeatedly and finds that unclear requirements, not laziness, caused it. They write a one-page spec and agree on a definition of done.

rows.subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis with five whys [Thinking]
rows.description: A student failing Maths asks why repeatedly and finds the trail leads back to weak fractions and algebra basics from Class 8, so the problem is foundations rather than the current chapter.

rows.subtype: Approach: seeking help from teacher or tutor [Action]
rows.description: The student stays back after class, shows the last three test papers to the teacher, and agrees on a twice-weekly doubt session, which is cheaper and more targeted than a full extra coaching batch.

rows.subtype: Approach: avoidance by studying favourite subjects [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student keeps revising English and Biology because they feel good, while Maths gets skipped. Marks in strong subjects rise slightly, but the failing subject continues to drag the overall result.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing no improvement and switching method [Revision]
rows.description: After a month of re-reading notes with little score change, the student admits passive reading is not working and shifts to closed-book practice questions, which quickly shows real weak spots.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.subtype: Approach: defining what AI may and may not do [Thinking]
rows.description: The team lead lists uses that are allowed, such as drafting tests and summarising public documents, and those that are not, such as pasting customer data or secrets into public tools.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.subtype: Approach: piloting on low-risk tasks first [Action]
rows.description: The team tries AI tools on documentation and unit test drafts for a month, measures time saved and error rates, and only then considers wider use in critical code.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.description: A junior developer merges AI-written code without reading it. The code contains an insecure query, which passes basic tests and reaches production before a reviewer notices.

rows.subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
rows.subtype: Approach: incident review after an AI-related error [Revision]
rows.description: When an AI-generated report included a wrong number, the team traced how it passed review, added a verification step and updated the policy, treating the tool as a fallible colleague.
After a harsh post about a product, the founder waits a day, aware that an angry reply written in the moment usually makes things worse and spreads the post further.

rows.subtype: Approach: taking the conversation to private channels [Action]
rows.description: For a customer-specific complaint, the company offers a direct call or email for details and returns later to say the matter was resolved, protecting privacy and avoiding a public fight.
The founder argues point by point with critics and attacks their motives. Screenshots circulate, and the argument draws far more attention than the original complaint.

rows.subtype: Approach: using legal remedies only for real harm [Revision]
rows.description: When some posts contain false and harmful claims, the person collects screenshots and consults a lawyer about lawful options, but does not threaten critics over honest disagreement.

rows.subtype: Approach: divergent brainstorming of problems seen daily [Thinking]
rows.description: A student lists irritations from hostel life, such as laundry delays and mess complaints, and picks the one that classmates mention most often as a candidate problem.

rows.subtype: Approach: talking to twenty potential users first [Action]
rows.description: Before building anything, the student interviews twenty hostel residents about how they handle laundry and what they pay, and learns that pricing matters more than an app.

rows.subtype: Approach: falling in love with the idea [Pitfall]
rows.description: The founder hears only encouraging feedback from friends, ignores polite doubts, and spends savings on a logo and website before checking whether strangers want the product.
Noticing that customers use the service mainly for exam-week printouts, the founders narrow the idea to a notes-and-printing service and see orders grow.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the funding target [Thinking]
rows.description: A founder needs eighteen months of runway, calculates the amount, then works back to the number of investor meetings, the pitch deadline and the metrics needed by that date.

rows.subtype: Approach: building a target investor list [Action]
rows.description: The founder lists sixty angels and seed funds that have backed health-tech in India, ranks them by fit and warm introductions, and tracks each contact in a shared sheet.
A founder sends the same deck to two hundred investors. Most reject quickly because the startup does not match their focus, and the team's time is wasted on mass emailing.

rows.subtype: Approach: revising the story after repeated no's [Revision]
rows.description: After fifteen rejections citing the same concern, the founder stops pitching, fixes the traction gap by signing three pilot customers, and returns to investors with better evidence.

rows.subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of a low-pressure invitation [Thinking]
rows.description: The student imagines asking a classmate to join a group study session or a school event, picks words that are easy to decline, and prepares a calm reply for either answer.

rows.subtype: Approach: building a friendly connection first [Action]
rows.description: Over a few weeks the student chats about shared interests in class projects and clubs, watching whether the other person seems comfortable, before suggesting a casual activity in a group.
Inspired by films, a student plans to ask in front of the whole class with flowers. The audience pressure makes a comfortable answer difficult and can embarrass the other person, whatever the reply.

rows.subtype: Approach: handling a rejection and recovering [Revision]
rows.description: After a polite no, the student thanks her, gives space, spends time with friends and sport, and notes that disappointment fades. Continuing normal friendly behaviour keeps the classroom comfortable.

rows.subtype: Approach: inversion asking how the offer could be a trap [Thinking]
rows.description: A student offered a promised monthly return of 10 percent by a college senior asks what would have to be true for that to be real, and sees that no lawful investment guarantees it. Imagining the trap first reveals warning signs.

rows.subtype: Approach: check registration with the regulator before paying [Action]
rows.description: Before sending money, the person looks up whether the platform and the adviser are registered with SEBI or the relevant regulator, and reads reviews and complaints. A few minutes of checking replaces trust in a persuasive pitch.

rows.subtype: Approach: fear of missing out drives a quick decision [Pitfall]
rows.description: Seeing friends post screenshots of gains, a young worker rushes into a Telegram tip group and transfers savings within an hour. Social proof and urgency shut down checking, and the money cannot be recovered.

rows.subtype: Approach: report and stop after noticing withdrawal blocks [Revision]
rows.description: When the app asks for a further fee to release money, the person sees the pattern, stops paying, saves the chats and screenshots, and files a complaint on the cybercrime portal and with the bank. Cutting losses early limits harm.

rows.subtype: Approach: breaking the song or play into small parts [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl in a school play divides her part into four scenes and learns one scene each day. This makes the long script less scary and she can check her progress.

rows.subtype: Approach: rehearsing in front of a mirror or family [Action]
rows.description: A boy practises his poem recitation in front of his family after dinner. They tell him to slow down and look up, and he improves before the day comes.

rows.subtype: Approach: practising only the parts she already knows well [Pitfall]
rows.description: A girl keeps repeating the first verse of the song because she enjoys it. On stage she is confident at first, then forgets the second verse she has barely practised.

rows.subtype: Approach: recording a practice and noticing mistakes [Revision]
rows.description: A boy records his speech on his mother's phone and finds he speaks too fast and mumbles the end. He adjusts by pausing after each sentence and re-records to compare.

rows.subtype: Approach: short daily practice at a fixed time [Action]
rows.description: A girl learning harmonium practises fifteen minutes right after evening snack, and this routine makes it easier than trying to choose a time every day.

rows.subtype: Approach: breaking a song into small parts [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy stuck on a tabla piece practises the first two beats slowly, then adds the next, thinking that a hard piece is only many small easy pieces joined together.

rows.subtype: Approach: playing only the parts already known [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child keeps repeating the easy opening of a song because it sounds good, and so the difficult middle never improves, and the lesson feels the same each week.

rows.subtype: Approach: using a teacher's feedback to correct errors [Revision]
rows.description: After the guitar teacher points out wrong finger placement, the girl slows down, watches her hand in a mirror, and fixes the chord that kept sounding muffled.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.subtype: Approach: gathering facts from several sources [Thinking]
rows.description: Before joining a student march about fee hikes, the teen reads the notice, the college statement and reports from different outlets, checking who organises it and what exactly is being demanded.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.description: The teen asks which principle matters most, such as fairness or safety, and whether joining serves that cause, or whether a letter, petition or school council meeting might achieve it better.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.subtype: Approach: joining because friends are going [Pitfall]
rows.description: The teen goes along because of excitement and fear of missing out, without knowing the demands. When tensions rise, there is no clarity about what is being supported or how to leave.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.subtype: Approach: changing plan when the situation shifts [Revision]
rows.description: When news reports say the gathering has turned tense, the teen decides not to go and instead helps with a peaceful awareness activity, showing that plans should change with new information.

rows.subtype: Approach: pause and avoid replying in the heat of the moment [Thinking]
rows.description: After a badly received post, the student sees hundreds of hostile comments and decides to wait a day before responding. A delay lets emotion drop and stops a reply that fuels the storm.

rows.subtype: Approach: lock accounts, mute and save evidence of threats [Action]
rows.description: The person sets accounts private, mutes keywords, saves screenshots of abusive messages and reports them to the platform. Protection and records come before any public statement.

rows.subtype: Approach: reply to every critic to set things straight [Pitfall]
rows.description: The person answers one comment after another through the night, and each reply attracts new attacks and screenshots. Engagement feeds the pile-on and exhausts the person.

rows.subtype: Approach: return with limits on screen time and a support routine [Revision]
rows.description: Weeks later, the student rejoins with a smaller circle, checks messages only at set times and speaks to a counsellor about the stress. Recovery involves rebuilding a healthier relationship with the platform.

rows.subtype: Approach: values-first reflection before naming jobs [Thinking]
rows.description: A student asks what a good working life should feel like before listing careers, noting she wants independence, steady income and work that helps people, then checks which fields match.

rows.subtype: Approach: weighted decision matrix across careers [Thinking]
rows.description: A student scores medicine, engineering and design on interest, effort needed, cost and job security, weights each criterion, and sees that his top choice depends heavily on how he weighted salary.

rows.subtype: Approach: following family expectation without examining it [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student picks the science stream because the father and elder brother are engineers, never asks whether he likes it, and by class eleven is bored and hiding poor marks.

rows.subtype: Approach: revisiting the choice after weak feedback [Revision]
rows.description: After scoring poorly in chemistry despite steady effort, a student meets a school counsellor, admits medicine may not suit her, and shifts to a data and statistics path she had been avoiding.
A project lead draws who is affected, sales wants speed, engineers want quality, finance wants low cost, and writes each group's actual concern, not just their stated demand.
Instead of choosing a side, the lead asks what would satisfy all key needs, and proposes launching a limited feature set now with quality work following in the next release.
The manager gives in to the most forceful executive each time. Quieter teams feel ignored, and the product drifts as decisions follow pressure rather than the overall goal.

rows.subtype: Approach: explaining the decision to those who lost [Revision]
rows.description: After the choice, the lead meets the disappointed team, explains the reasons, and agrees on a follow-up for their concerns, keeping the relationship intact for later decisions.

rows.subtype: Approach: getting used to water in the shallow end first [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy afraid of water begins by standing in the shallow part and splashing. He reasons that if he can feel safe there, he can take the next step to floating.

rows.subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
rows.description: A boy watches an older swimmer's arm movement and copies it on the poolside. He tries it in the water with the coach watching, who fixes his elbow position.

rows.subtype: Approach: jumping into the deep end to prove he is brave [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy tries to impress friends by jumping into the deep pool without the coach. He panics and needs to be pulled out, and learns that courage without skill is dangerous.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing she is tense and relaxing her body [Revision]
rows.description: A child sinks each time she tries to float. The coach points out she is stiff, so she takes a slow breath, relaxes her arms and lets the water hold her.

rows.subtype: Approach: five whys on the churn numbers [Thinking]
rows.description: A team sees users leaving within a week. Asking why five times leads from a poor onboarding flow to the discovery that the users were never the ones who paid or decided.
The founder calls fifteen users who stopped using the fitness app and asks what they do now instead. Most say they use a WhatsApp group with a trainer, which suggests a different product.
After two years of work, the team keeps adding features to the same product because stopping feels like admitting waste. Each new release adds cost but no growth.

rows.subtype: Approach: cutting losses and shutting down cleanly [Revision]
rows.description: When six weeks of tests show no demand, the founders decide to wind down, refund advance payments, thank users and share the codebase notes, keeping their reputation for the next venture.

rows.subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
rows.subtype: Approach: splitting money into spend, save and give [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl with two hundred rupees a month divides it into three jars, so some goes to a treat, some toward a book she wants, and a small amount for the temple or a needy friend.

rows.subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
rows.subtype: Approach: comparing prices at different shops [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl notices the same notebook costs ten rupees less in the lane shop than in the school store, and decides that a little walking saves money for something else.

rows.subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
rows.subtype: Approach: spending it all at once on impulse [Pitfall]
rows.description: The child buys stickers and sweets the day the pocket money arrives, and by the second week has nothing left when a friend's birthday needs a small gift.

rows.subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
rows.subtype: Approach: goal too big for the time available [Revision]
rows.description: The boy realises that a two thousand rupee cycle will take years at his rate, so he switches to a cheaper target and asks his uncle if he can earn extra by helping with chores.
After a low result, the student allows a day of disappointment, talks to a friend and avoids big decisions, knowing that plans made in shock, such as quitting school, are often regretted.

rows.subtype: Approach: analysing what happened with the answer sheet [Action]
rows.description: The student requests the paper review, sorts lost marks into knowledge gaps, time management and carelessness, and finds that poor time management in the last section caused most of the loss.
The student concludes that one failure means a ruined future and stops studying. The thought feels certain but skips the evidence, and it makes real recovery less likely.

rows.subtype: Approach: asking for professional help when hopeless [Revision]
rows.description: If sadness and hopelessness persist, the student and parents approach the school counsellor or a helpline, since heavy despair after failure needs care from trained people and not only willpower.

rows.subtype: Approach: listing skills and free hours first [Thinking]
rows.description: A student lists what they can do, such as tutoring, design or typing, and counts how many hours remain after classes, so the idea fits real time.

rows.subtype: Approach: budget and pricing with cost tracking [Thinking]
rows.description: The student works out costs, time per job and a fair rate per hour, and notices that the first price barely covers data and travel.
Attracted by videos claiming easy earnings from trading or paid schemes, a student joins without checking, risking savings and time and learning nothing about real skills.

rows.subtype: Approach: measuring results and dropping weak options [Revision]
rows.description: After a month the student compares hourly earnings for tutoring, freelance work and data entry, and drops data entry because it pays least for the effort.
A toddler tries lying belly-first on the cushion, then hooking a knee up, then rolling sideways, and stays with the version that gets the knee over the edge.
A toddler watches an older brother turn around, sit and swing legs up. The toddler copies the sequence loosely and lands halfway across the cushion, closer than before.
A toddler scrambles at the tall armrest instead of the seat, slips and is caught by a grandparent. Eagerness outruns any check of whether the spot is safe.
A knee on the cushion edge helped last time, so a toddler starts every climb that way and steadily gets faster.

rows.subtype: Approach: brainstorming many questions and picking one [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl writes ten questions she wonders about, such as whether plants grow towards light. She picks the one she can test with materials at home, in the time she has.

rows.subtype: Approach: planning a simple experiment with a fair test [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy plans to grow beans in two cups, one on the windowsill and one in a dark cupboard. He decides that the soil, water and cup size must be the same so the test is fair.

rows.subtype: Approach: choosing a fancy project he cannot finish [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child chooses to build a working volcano with lights and sound that looks like a friend's. He runs out of time and materials, and his project stays half done.

rows.subtype: Approach: repeating the experiment when the result looks odd [Revision]
rows.description: One bean plant in the dark grows taller than expected. The girl realises she left the cupboard open, so she repeats the test with the door shut, and the result is clearer.

rows.subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
rows.subtype: Approach: deciding values and limits in advance [Thinking]
rows.description: Before a party, the student decides what he will not do, such as riding with an unsafe driver or trying substances, so that decisions in the moment follow a rule already thought through.

rows.subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
rows.subtype: Approach: prepared refusal lines and exit plan [Action]
rows.description: The student prepares a short refusal, such as no thanks, I am good, and agrees with a parent on a code word to be picked up, so leaving does not require an argument or explanation.

rows.subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
rows.subtype: Approach: going along to avoid being excluded [Pitfall]
rows.description: Worried about being called boring, the student joins a risky dare. The fear of social loss feels larger than the real danger in that moment, and the consequences fall on him alone.

rows.subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
rows.description: After a risky evening the student admits it was a mistake, tells his parents what happened, and plans different company, earlier exit times and a firm rule for next time rather than hiding it.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition into milestones and owners [Thinking]
rows.description: A 24-year-old engineer made lead of a billing module splits it into five deliverables, estimates each with the team, and notes which risky piece needs the earliest start.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the client demo date [Action]
rows.description: The new lead fixes the demo date, marks integration testing two weeks before it, then places design and coding deadlines behind that. The team sees a shared calendar on day one.

rows.subtype: Approach: doing the hardest tasks personally to be safe [Pitfall]
rows.description: Fearing mistakes, the new lead keeps every difficult module for himself. He works late, teammates sit underused, and the deadline slips because he becomes the single bottleneck.

rows.subtype: Approach: admitting overload and re-scoping with the manager [Revision]
rows.description: Noticing two sprints behind, the lead brings a clear list to her manager: what is done, what is at risk, and what can be cut. Two features move to phase two and morale recovers.

rows.subtype: Approach: budget and affordability working backward from the EMI [Thinking]
rows.description: A couple decides the loan payment should stay under a third of their monthly income. From that they work out the loan amount and the price range they can afford.
They agree on must-haves such as a metro-friendly location and a school nearby, and treat a balcony as optional. The list keeps viewings focused and disagreements short.

rows.subtype: Approach: buying in a rush from fear of rising prices [Pitfall]
rows.description: Hearing that prices will go up, the couple pays a booking amount on the first flat that seems fine. Later they find hidden maintenance costs and a longer commute than they expected.

rows.subtype: Approach: satisficing with a clear stopping rule [Revision]
rows.description: After the long search, they set a rule: choose the first property that meets all must-haves within the budget. They decide within a month and feel relieved.
A teenager feels a pounding heart, dizziness and a sense that something terrible is happening, with no clear reason. It is frightening but passes, and fearing the next one can make life smaller.

rows.subtype: Living in fear of the next attack [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult avoids crowds, trains or exams in case panic strikes again. Understanding what happens in the body and getting professional guidance reduce fear.

A teenager under exam or assignment pressure copies work and tells themselves it is just this once. Fear of failure and a common culture of copying make it feel normal, while the habit erodes their own ability.

rows.subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]
rows.description: A student fabricates a data point or lets a team member's uncredited work pass as theirs to meet a deadline. Rationalisations such as everyone does it soften the guilt without removing the harm.
A child cheers for a cricket team or film hero and wears the colours proudly. Loving the same thing as others gives instant belonging and a story to be part of.
A teenager's music, series or team becomes part of who they are. They feel understood by other fans and defensive when their idol is criticised, as though the criticism were personal.
A young adult defends a star or leader whatever they do, since criticising them feels like criticising oneself. Parasocial closeness feels real while the figure does not know they exist.
A child feels happy when told he got 8 of 10 right and sad when told he got 2 wrong. Identical facts feel different depending on how they are put.
A teenager reacts strongly to being called a 40 percent failure rather than 60 percent successful. The wording swings his mood and his choices.
A child who has moved schools remembers the old class as perfect and forgets the quarrels. Distance smooths rough edges of the past.
A teenager feeling pressure remembers early childhood as carefree and longs for it, forgetting its fears and limits. Comfort and loss colour the picture.
A student in a hostel far from home idealises home life and old friends, and may feel homesick with love mixed with a bit of avoidance of present challenges.
A toddler opens every drawer, tastes leaves and pulls things apart. Curiosity is the engine of early learning, and safety-proofing works better than constant saying no.
A child asks why the sky is blue, why grandma is old, why the moon follows the car. Answers matter less than an adult who treats the questions as worth answering.
A teenager explores sex, religion, risky videos or rebellious ideas partly from real interest. Curiosity that is met with panic goes underground, while calm answers keep the door open.

A hearing or deaf toddler may use signs or gestures for "more", "milk" or "all done" before speech. Deaf children exposed to a signed language from birth learn it on the same timetable as spoken languages.
A school-age signer fingerspells names or unfamiliar words and uses name signs given by the community. Fingerspelling is a tool within a full language, not the language itself.

rows.subtype: Sign language in workplaces and public life [Expressing]
rows.description: A young signer works through interpreters or video relay and expects equal access. Colleagues can learn a few signs, face the person and avoid assumptions about ability.

rows.subtype: Hitting a sibling after being scolded [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler told off by a parent turns and pushes a younger sibling or throws a toy; the anger has no safe target so it lands on someone smaller and less threatening.

rows.subtype: Kicking the bag after a teacher's rebuke [Actor]
rows.description: A child humiliated in class comes home and slams doors or snaps at the family dog; the feeling belongs to school but is spent where it feels safe.
A child is told by an older student or adult to hide something, pick on someone or keep a secret. They feel a pull between obedience and a stomach-sinking sense of wrongness.

rows.subtype: Teacher or coach crossing a line [Receiver]
rows.description: A student is pressured by a coach, tutor or senior to do something that feels wrong, with respect and fear mixed. They may freeze or comply because refusing an authority feels unthinkable.
A toddler believes that his wish or a gesture can make things happen, such as a wave making a toy move. He cannot yet separate thought from the physical world.
A preschooler believes in monsters under the bed, the tooth fairy and special words that protect him. Imagination is vivid and the line with reality is soft.
An older child avoids stepping on cracks, taps things or wears a lucky shirt for exams. He half knows it is not logical and still feels safer with it.
A toddler's emotion flashes on quickly and off just as fast, from tantrum to giggle within minutes. Short displays move on with distraction, while lasting ones suggest a need or a health issue.

A preschooler wails theatrically over a small bump or squeals with over-large delight. Exaggeration often seeks attention or shows big feelings without control, and a calm response teaches proportion.

rows.subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
rows.subtype: Staying calm and finding an exit [Response]
rows.description: A person in a crowd notes exits, keeps their arms up and moves with the flow, not against it. Planning ahead and staying calm protects them and others around them.

rows.subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
rows.description: A friend messages the target privately, helps them stop reading comments and, if needed, reports abuse. Steady human contact matters more than public defence.

rows.subtype: Likes and dislikes as strong assertions [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler shows likes and dislikes by grabbing, refusing food or saying "mine" and "no". Firm refusal expresses growing independence and preference rather than defiance alone.

A teenager states likes and dislikes about touch, photos, sharing and closeness, and expects a "no" to be respected. Everyone has the right to refuse; adults and peers should stop and a trusted adult should be told if a refusal is ignored.

A young professional asks for deadline clarity, breaks, accommodations or leave and states preferences on how to be contacted. Framing a need with a reason and an alternative usually gets a better hearing.

A toddler bounces with delight, stamps feet in frustration or runs in circles from excitement. Whole-body motion often shows feeling before language does; naming it, for instance you are so happy, builds emotional words.

rows.subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
rows.description: A schoolchild paces before a test or bounces a leg while waiting. It can signal nerves, excitement or need for movement, and a child with a lot of energy is not necessarily defiant; movement breaks often help focus.

A teenager dances in a group, at a wedding baraat, on a practice reel or at a school event to show joy and belonging. Styles vary by culture and gender norms; pressure to perform or teasing can turn joy into shame, so choice matters.
A toddler waves, says bye-bye or babbles hello to show recognition and social interest. Shyness may lead to hiding instead, so adults do not force a greeting.

rows.subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
rows.description: A child says hello, offers a seat, shares a snack or shows the new student around. Warm welcoming teaches inclusion, and shy children can still welcome with a smile or wave.

A young adult in an interview or new college introduces self with name, role and a short line about interests. Confident, clear greetings build trust, and norms differ across cultures for title use and eye contact.

Playful teasing among friends can shift into mocking or ridicule when one person is hurt or cannot laugh along. Watching the target's face, the power balance and repetition helps children tell fun from unkind, and they should tell an adult about ongoing harm.

A young adult may face "Do this or I leave" from a friend, partner or family member. Some ultimatums state a real boundary, others are pressure or control; consider whether choices are respected and seek support if fear or coercion is present.

A child in some settings learns to kneel, bow or stand when elders or teachers enter, for example touching feet or standing to greet. Meaning is respect in that culture, not weakness, and rules differ across families, faiths and schools.

A young professional meets bosses who lean back, sit tall or stand close, and finds that posture signals status differently across offices and cultures. Guessing attitude from body position alone is risky; behaviour over time tells more.

A young child reads a scolding mostly through the adult's face, volume and tone and may feel unlovable rather than corrected. Short, calm correction of the act, not the child, helps the message be understood.
A child receiving a reprimand may look down, argue, cry or go silent, and the reaction does not prove guilt or indifference. Adults do better focusing on the behaviour and the fix rather than shame.
A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.
A teenager mocks their own braces or marks before anyone else can; it wins acceptance but repeated self-mockery can teach others to see them as a target.
A child lying in bed wonders what if they fail or something happens to their mother; worry tries to prepare for danger but mostly manufactures alarms, and a calm routine and reassurance help.
A teenager thinks of every possible way an exam could go wrong and can barely start studying; worry feels like responsibility, though it often replaces action.
A child who received festival gift money feels free to spend it all on sweets, but would never spend the same amount from his pocket money. The source changes how the money feels.
A teenager treats a prize or a gift as fun money and spends it quickly, while guarding money he earned. Every rupee is the same but the mind sorts them differently.
A student spends a tax refund or a bonus carelessly while pinching on small daily costs. Separate mental accounts stop him seeing his whole financial picture.
A child hears why can't you be like your cousin and is left feeling inadequate. Children often take sarcasm literally and carry comparison into their self-image for years.
A teenager addressed like a small child by a teacher or a relative feels disrespected and turns defiant. Treating them as a developing adult with real opinions draws cooperation.

A teenager recognises thumbs-down and rude gestures, including the raised middle finger, as insults or strong disapproval, and learns to step back, stay calm and tell an adult if it comes from bullying. Using them hurts others and can bring consequences.
A young adult reads the thumbs-up, folded-hands and wave emoji as modern equivalents of gestures, but the thumbs-up may seem curt or passive-aggressive to some. Norms differ by age and workplace.

rows.subtype: My view is the only view [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler hides his face and believes no one can see him, or shows a picture facing himself. He cannot yet imagine that others see differently.
An older child begins to understand that friends may believe or want different things, but still struggles when his own strong feelings are involved.
A teenager feels that his experiences are unique, that nobody has felt this before, and that everyone is watching him. It gradually softens as he meets more people.
Adults worry when a quiet child prefers being alone and push them into groups. Checking for real distress is wise, but preference for solitude is often just temperament.
A friend notices someone slowly declining every invitation and replying less. Gentle, low-pressure reaching out matters, since withdrawal often grows quietly when nobody checks.
A young man tells his family clearly that he will not take dowry and that the marriage will not depend on it. Speaking early, with firm respect, protects both the bride and his own integrity.
A relative who objects to dowry or gender pressure says so calmly at the planning stage and finds allies among elders. Change is often slower than anger, but one clear voice makes others braver.
A teenager checks hair, fixes clothes or hides behind a phone when feeling watched. It can signal self-consciousness, ordinary grooming or a wish to look good; teasing about it deepens insecurity.

rows.subtype: Covering the mouth and cultural norms [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult covers the mouth when laughing, yawning or coughing, which shows manners in many places but shyness in others. It can also signal surprise or embarrassment, so meaning depends on the cultural setting.

A young adult picks up a phone, taps or scrolls in awkward moments as a comfort or an escape. It may show boredom, anxiety or urgent work, and others often read it as disrespect; a short explanation prevents hurt.
A child hears repeatedly the story of how they were born, how the family struggled or what a grandfather did. Family narratives give a child a place and a sense of belonging.
A young adult labelled as the difficult one or the lazy one in the family lives inside that story. Stepping out of an assigned role takes many small acts of behaving differently.
A teenager who said something awkward at a party replays it for days and imagines everyone still thinking of it; repetition feels like problem solving but deepens the sting.
A student who failed a paper asks over and over why it happened and what it says about them without arriving at any plan; thinking about causes without action keeps the mood low.

A school-age child sees a classmate narrow the eyes and reads suspicion or anger, though the person may be squinting at a bright board. Checking the context, such as light and vision, avoids unfair conclusions.
A teenager with heavy, half-closed eyes after late screen time may look bored or rude in class, but is often simply tired. Adults can ask about sleep before assuming disrespect.

A parent sees a teenager absorbed for hours and cannot tell whether it is flow or compulsion. The difference shows afterward: flow leaves a person energised and having grown, while capture leaves them drained and restless.
A coworker sees a teammate gone silent and intense at their desk and waits before interrupting. Recognising flow in others and holding non-urgent questions is a quiet form of respect.

A child with a fracture or bad fall may be scared, angry at being stopped from playing and worried about the future. Comfort, honest information and small achievable goals help the mind heal along with the body.
A young adult in recovery feels impatient, dependent on others and annoyed at the slow pace, and may swing between overdoing and giving up. Steady, measured progress is better than either extreme.

A person after a road accident or serious injury may feel jumpy, avoid the place or vehicle and replay the event. Time, support and, if fear lingers, professional help allow trust in the world to return.
A toddler squeezes the eyes shut when scared, tired or refusing to look, and blinks slowly when sleepy. These are protective or tired signals, not defiance.
A preschooler finds winking hard and may blink both eyes, while a wink tells a friend about a joke or secret. Winking is playful, and its meaning depends on the shared understanding.

rows.subtype: Widening the eyes as a listening cue [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional widens the eyes slightly to show interest and encourage a speaker. It works when natural, and a fixed wide-eyed look may seem strained.
A child with a homemade tiffin, a regional accent or older clothes is laughed at. They may shrink, copy the group or quietly resent it, learning early that difference carries a price.
A teenager is told that skipping class, vaping or a prank is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion if they refuse. The threat is social, so it feels bigger than the act itself.
A child realises that a sibling who broke a toy was scared and not mean. Perspective-taking at this age is real but effortful and often fades under anger.
A teenager quarrelling with a parent can only see their side, though calm afterwards they understand the parent's fear. Emotion narrows the view, and wisdom includes waiting until it widens.
A toddler shakes the head to say no, often before speaking clearly, showing refusal or a wish for control. It is meaningful communication that adults can respond to with respect.
A child lowers the head after doing something wrong or when embarrassed, showing shame or fear. Kind correction helps the child learn without feeling worthless.

rows.subtype: Bowing the head in respect and mourning [Expressing]
rows.description: An adult bows the head at a funeral, prayer or a formal greeting to show respect or grief. The meaning shifts with setting and tradition, and observers follow local custom.

A child hears a tut or a click of the tongue meaning disapproval in some places, or a sound of sympathy or a yes in others. Culture and tone change the meaning, so a listener should not jump to conclusions.

A teenager snorts or clears the throat, and peers may read it as mockery, warning or a real need. The sound is ambiguous; a child with a cold or a tic should not be blamed, and asking calmly avoids unfair conclusions.

A young adult whistles or hums for calm or joy, but whistling at a person in public can be unwelcome harassment. Recognising when a sound crosses into disrespect helps, and anyone targeted may leave and report it.
A child shares a toy with the friend who shared last time, and refuses the one who never does. Early fairness is expressed as "you did for me, I do for you".
A child notes who helped whom, and objects loudly to unequal splits, even when they would receive the extra. A sense that fairness matters is emerging, sometimes rigidly.
A child holds the shoulders tight before saying something in class, showing nervousness. Slow breaths and a friendly nod from the teacher help.
A teenager rolls the shoulders to release tension before a match or exam, or holds them tense when anxious. Noticing and releasing them is a useful calming tool.
A young professional holds tension in the shoulders during deadlines, and stretching or brief breaks help. Colleagues may read tight shoulders as irritation when it is strain.
A school-age child suggests how to play a game or advises a friend on a problem. Advice that is not asked for can feel bossy, so asking would you like ideas is kinder.
A young adult leading a team or lab gives clear directions with the reason and expected result. Commanding without explanation may achieve compliance but weaken trust.
A child is challenged with chicken, or told everyone does it, to make them join something unsafe or unkind. Fear of exclusion is strong, and the need to belong can outweigh judgement.

rows.subtype: Pressure from friends to prove loyalty [Receiver]
rows.description: A teenager is told that a real friend would skip class, drink or share a picture. The friendship is used as leverage, and refusing feels like risking the whole group.
A parent thanks the bus conductor, waits patiently in line and apologises for a bump. Children learn public manners far more from watching than from being told.
A person says excuse me, the line starts there, without heat. Calm, friendly firmness usually works, and if it turns hostile they let it go.

A teenager uses ugh for irritation, fatigue or dramatic humour. Others may take it as rudeness, but often it is harmless venting; a teen can learn to add a few words such as that was a long day to avoid confusion.

rows.subtype: Um, uh and filler in public speaking [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional replaces um and uh with a pause while presenting, which reads as more confident. Fillers are normal and do not mean ignorance, and a short silence can help both speaker and audience.
A young child believes that hoping hard or a special ritual can change the roll of a dice or a match result. Feeling in charge is comforting.
A teenager thinks that choosing his own lottery number or lucky scratch card gives him better odds. Effort and choice feel like they influence pure chance.
A young adult believes skill or a system will beat random outcomes, doubling down after losses. Feeling of control keeps him playing when odds are against him.
A child who spilled milk hides and says I am bad. Young children treat errors as identity, and an adult saying you made a mistake, you are not a mistake gives a first template of self-forgiveness.
A teenager replays an embarrassing moment or a harsh remark for days. Harsh self-review feels like accountability but mostly produces shame and avoidance.
A young adult who wasted a year or hurt a partner keeps punishing themselves through lost opportunities. Learning that the past self did the best it knew at the time allows moving forward.
A wise worker sets personal milestones ahead of the real date and finishes a rough draft early. This leaves room for surprises and makes the final days about improving, not scrambling.

rows.subtype: Warning early when a deadline will slip [Response]
rows.description: A responsible worker tells others as soon as a date looks unsafe, with a new realistic date and options. Early bad news can be planned around; late bad news is felt as a betrayal.
A child in a railway station or fair holds an adult's hand and is anxious about getting lost. Knowing a parent's phone number and where to wait if separated gives safety that fear alone does not.

A teenager taking a bus or train alone feels excited and a little afraid, checking the ticket and stops repeatedly. Small independent trips build competence when the route and a contact person are agreed in advance.
A young traveller follows navigation blindly onto a wrong or unsafe road and only then looks up. Apps assist judgment but do not replace noticing what is actually around.
A child declares that there is nothing to do and clings to a parent. Boredom is a signal that the mind wants to generate its own activity, but the child does not yet know how.
Left without screens on a long summer afternoon, a child builds a fort, invents a game or draws for hours. Tolerated boredom is where self-directed interest first grows.
A teenager scrolls compulsively, switching apps to escape a flat feeling. The boredom is less about lack of options and more about intolerance for an empty moment.
A young resident notices that a few people dominate a housing society meeting and others stay silent. Showing up, asking for written rules and speaking fairly help such groups work for all.
An observer sees a small quarrel take on religious or caste colour as people take sides. Refusing to join the labelling, cooling talk and involving neutral elders help stop it spreading.

A child beginning puberty may feel embarrassed, moody and suddenly self-conscious about their body. Without warning, a growing body can feel like a stranger, and honest simple explanations reduce shame.
A teenager's feelings can swing from delight to despair within hours as hormones and a still-maturing brain interact. The intensity is real, even when the trigger looks small to adults.
Resisting immediate impulses or temptations to secure a larger, delayed reward.
Learning to regulate choices made under intense emotional arousal or peer pressure.
Integrating systemic impacts, ethical principles, and risk management into high-stakes decisions.

rows.subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
rows.subtype: Stepping out of a fixed family role [Response]
rows.description: A young adult quietly stops playing the peacemaker or the rebel and responds as themselves. The family may resist at first, and steady, kind consistency usually allows the system to adjust.

rows.subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
rows.description: A young couple agrees together on what they will share and what they will keep private, then communicates it kindly. Boundaries offered with warmth are usually accepted sooner than boundaries offered in anger.
A young child can learn to breathe slowly by blowing bubbles, smelling a flower and blowing out a candle. Practised when calm, this gives the child a tool that is easier to reach when upset.
A student about to present slows the exhale, drops the shoulders and pauses before the first sentence. The steadier breath calms the voice and thinking, and does not need anyone to notice it.
A student sees a rumour about a teacher spread through school until everyone treats it as fact; every repetition makes it feel more believable and harder to question.
An adult sees one dramatic news story about a rare event push the whole locality into over-caution while common everyday risks are ignored.
A teenager learns to criticise the act or plan rather than the person, and to accept feedback without collapsing or attacking. "That part is unclear" is more usable than "You are useless".

rows.subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
rows.description: A young adult listens to feedback, asks clarifying questions and separates useful points from unfair ones. Immediate defence or total self-blame both make learning harder.

rows.subtype: Scolding and reprimanding as a supervisor [Regulating]
rows.description: A young supervisor reprimands by describing the behaviour and its impact, keeping voice calm and giving a path to improve. Sarcasm, humiliation or repeated scolding harms the relationship and can amount to bullying.
A child who commands peers may be leading, anxious, or copying adult tone. Adults can coach the child to swap commands for invitations, such as how about we.
A teenager weighs recommendations from friends and influencers about trends, products and risks. Advice that carries pressure to do something unsafe or secret is a reason to consult a trusted adult.

rows.subtype: Rituals to keep bad things away [Actor]
rows.description: A child repeats handwashing, touching or checking, or must say certain words to prevent harm. It feels unavoidable, and scolding makes it worse; a doctor or child psychologist can guide the family.
A teenager may have upsetting thoughts they hate and fear meaning something about them. Such thoughts are common and do not show who a person is; shame keeps them secret, and professional help works.
A young adult spends hours checking or arranging things, arrives late and hides it from friends. Compulsions relieve fear briefly and then demand more, and seeking a qualified clinician is wise.
A city child on a holiday sees animals, fields and a slower rhythm and is thrilled by mud and mangoes. It is easy to romanticise; the child may learn later of hard work behind such simplicity.
A villager sees urban youth as selfish, disconnected from family and soil. This is partly true of some and unfair to many; both sides carry stereotypes worth unlearning.

A child bites a lip, covers the mouth or looks down to hold back a giggle in a quiet moment. It shows awareness of rules and effort at self-control; a brief movement break or a whisper later helps release it.

rows.subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager laughs along with a group joke that feels unkind or hides hurt behind a laugh. Fake laughter can protect belonging but leave the person uneasy; choosing safe friends and a calm boundary such as that is not funny is healthier.

rows.subtype: Laughing in meetings and difficult talks [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional uses a light laugh to ease tension, or holds one back in a solemn moment. A chuckle can build rapport, but laughing at a colleague's concern or a serious issue can seem dismissive.
A toddler who lacks words may grab, hit or bite when frustrated, tired or overwhelmed. It signals a strong feeling, not malice; adults can step in, name the feeling and show a safer action.
A preschooler says "You're mean!" or "It's your fault!" in a squabble. Blame is a simple way to explain distress; adults can help the child state what happened and what they wanted.

rows.subtype: Meeting the individual behind the label [Response]
rows.description: A teenager gets to know a person from a disliked group through shared work or sport. Cooperation toward a common goal is the strongest known way to soften group bias.
A mature adult checks their own assumptions, seeks out different views and speaks up when a group is mocked. They stay loyal to their own people without needing others to be lesser.

A parent who talks about periods, voice changes or body hair before they happen, in plain and unhurried words, gives a child confidence. Silence and giggling leave children to learn from rumour and fear.

A teenager learns that big feelings pass, and finds outlets such as sport, music, writing or talking to a trusted person. Waiting an hour before sending a message or slamming a door prevents many regrets.

rows.subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
rows.description: A child learns that getting help from a teacher or parent is not tattling but caring. They practise saying I need help and pointing at one specific adult.

rows.subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
rows.description: A teenager chooses a low-risk action such as checking on the victim, distracting the aggressor or calling an adult. Safe helping is a range of options, not a heroic all-or-nothing.

rows.subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
rows.description: An adult in an emergency points at one person and says you, call an ambulance, you, bring water. Naming someone breaks the diffusion of responsibility and gets action moving.

rows.subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
rows.description: A child who has enough at home feels sad on seeing a classmate's new bicycle and phone. The hurt comes from comparison, not from actual lack.

A teenager compares their marks, clothes or family situation with peers who are a step ahead, and feels cheated even though their own situation is decent. Feeling deprived depends on who one looks at.

A graduate who expected a job like their seniors got, and did not, feels bitter and entitled to something being withheld. Frustration is sharper when a group seems to be getting what they believed they deserved.
A toddler claps when others clap and waves along with a group song. Joining in shows delight and belonging, and imitation is how children learn shared signals.
A teenager joins a school vigil or memorial, showing grief and solidarity with silence, flowers or lamps. Each participant may feel different things, and some may cry while others feel numb.

A young adult joins hashtags, petitions, group chats or shared black-profile-picture moments to show solidarity. Digital unity is easy to join and quick to fade, and it works best paired with real support.
After the match ends a child says he knew that team would lose. The mind quietly rewrites earlier uncertainty into a neat, predictable story.
A teenager whose friend failed an exam says it was obvious, ignoring that the outcome looked open beforehand. Judging past choices by known results is unfair to the decider.

rows.subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
rows.description: A child begs to try the tallest slide and every new game; excitement and challenge feel like life itself, and boredom feels worse than a little risk.

rows.subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
rows.description: A young adult stands for student leadership to shape decisions and be respected; the wish for influence can serve a group well or slide into wanting control over others.

rows.subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
rows.description: A young professional chooses a steady job and saves carefully, valuing certainty and safety for family over chances; calm and worry can both come with the choice.

A teenager who falls silent or stops abruptly mid-sentence may be hurt, embarrassed, angry or simply thinking. Silence is ambiguous, so a caring reply gives space and leaves the door open to talk later.

In some Indian and other group settings overlapping speech signals engagement, while in others it signals disrespect. A young professional watches the local norm before judging someone as rude or passive.
A child cries harder over losing a marble than he celebrates winning one. Giving up something owned feels heavier than getting an equal thing.

rows.subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager avoids trying a new sport or friend group because losing his current standing feels worse than any possible gain. Safe choices shrink his world.
A young adult holds a losing stock or a failing project too long to avoid the pain of realising the loss, while selling winners too soon.
A toddler explores, checks back with a caregiver, protests at parting and is soothed on return. Trust that comfort will come lets the child venture out, and feelings can be shown openly.
A child makes friends, handles quarrels and asks for help without shame. Assumes people generally mean well, and can recover after a disagreement.
A young adult can say what they need, tolerate a partner's need for space and repair after fights. Closeness and independence coexist without constant fear of loss.

rows.subtopic: Money attitudes, family finances, gifting, borrowing between relatives
rows.description: A toddler sees notes handed over as blessings or coins as sweets and understands only that giving pleases people. Money at this age is a shiny object and a source of adult smiles.

rows.subtopic: Money attitudes, family finances, gifting, borrowing between relatives
rows.description: A child hears parents argue about bills or school fees and quietly asks for less. Children sense strain even when hidden; simple honest explanations calm them more than silence.

rows.subtopic: Money attitudes, family finances, gifting, borrowing between relatives
rows.description: A young adult sees parents keep income, debts or property secret and feels shut out. Money silence can protect pride but also hides risks; gentle open talk is often a sign of trust.

rows.subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler tracks a caregiver with the eyes and looks where a parent points, sharing attention on an object. Steady following shows interest and trust, and early lack of it may be worth discussing with a paediatrician.
A preschooler looks down when told off, showing shame, fear or attempts to avoid more upset. Demanding eye contact adds pressure, so a calm tone and gentle words work better.

rows.subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
rows.description: A child looks away when scolded, praised in public or caught out; it usually signals shame, shyness or discomfort, not defiance. In some families lowered eyes toward elders also show respect.
A teacher who points out that the child kept trying different methods and it paid off teaches that ability grows with effort; specific process praise supports challenge seeking.

An adult replaces the thought that they cannot do this with the thought that they cannot do it yet and asks what to try next; the word acknowledges the present without closing the future, though effort needs good strategy.
A toddler screams for the biscuit at this moment and cannot be comforted by a promise for later. The present is the only time that feels real.
A preschooler can wait a little for a treat when distracted by a game or a song, though he struggles when staring at it. Waiting skills grow with practice and support.
A teenager promises to study tomorrow and scrolls tonight, sure his future self will feel more like working. Tomorrow is always the better time to be disciplined.

rows.subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
rows.description: A teenager tries to tell whether a classmate is interested, puzzled or bored from face and voice. These cues are hints only, and asking is better than assuming.

rows.subtype: Thoughtful, interested and doubtful in meetings [Interpreting]
rows.description: A young professional reads pauses, notes, raised brows and short replies from colleagues. These signals suggest interest or doubt but never prove it, so asking for views is more reliable.

rows.subtype: Talks to teddy and feeds the doll [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler pats a teddy, says it is hungry and puts it to bed; treating objects as feeling beings is natural play that practises care.

rows.subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager describes an AI chatbot as understanding and caring, and feels hurt when it changes; the mind is quick to see a person behind fluent words.

rows.subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult says "my laptop hates me" or names the car and coaxes it; attributing motive to things makes their behaviour feel explainable and less random.
A child who takes a classmate's pencil case says they are just borrowing it, or calls cruel teasing a joke; softer words make the act feel less harmful and less of a personal choice.
A teenager labels repeated nasty comments about a peer as banter and says everyone jokes like that; the label hides how the target feels.

rows.subtype: Wants warm, sweet, soft things now [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler seeks sweets, cuddles and bubbles and cries when they stop; seeking pleasure and comfort is a simple, natural drive at this age.

rows.subtype: Lives for fun and good times [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager plans around films, outings and food, and finds long-term duty dull; the love of enjoyment brings vitality and friends, and can crowd out work if it rules everything.

rows.subtype: Pleasure versus duty in the hostel [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult skips a study session for a late-night outing and enjoys it fully while feeling a pinch of guilt; enjoyment and responsibility pull in different directions.
A toddler is guided by a parent to fold hands or bend toward a grandparent's feet and does it as a game. The child feels the smiles and blessing in return and links the gesture to warmth.
A teenager asks whether touching feet is real respect or habit and sometimes does it hurriedly. Doing it with attention to the person makes it real; doing it for show empties it.
A young adult chooses between touching feet, a handshake or a namaste depending on age, gender, faith and comfort of the person. Reading the other person's cue is more polite than one fixed rule.

Adults teach young children that bodies are private, that no adult should ask for secrets from parents, and that they can always tell a trusted grown-up. Simple repeated rules protect better than fear.

A parent or teacher who hears a child mention a secret, gifts or pressure stays calm, thanks the child for telling, believes them and acts to protect. Reactions of anger at the child can stop future telling.
A student makes a joke or a compliment based on a group stereotype, sincerely thinking it is friendly. They are shocked to learn it hurt, because the intent was kind but the effect was not.

rows.subtype: Being told about an unintended slight [Actor]
rows.description: A person is quietly told that their comment came across badly. They feel defensive, embarrassed and misjudged, and do better by listening, apologising for the effect and adjusting without demanding comfort.
A teenager whose speech races when anxious can practise measured pace by pausing at full stops and breathing out first. A steadier pace often helps the speaker feel calmer as well as sound calmer.

rows.subtype: Measured pace in interviews and presentations [Regulating]
rows.description: A young adult in an interview or seminar who keeps a measured pace with deliberate pauses appears organized. Slowing too much may read as disinterest, so pace should fit the room and topic.

rows.subtype: Measured voice in delivering hard news [Regulating]
rows.description: A young manager or clinician delivering bad news uses a slow, measured pace and clear sentences so the listener can take it in. Rushing through it to end the discomfort tends to sound cold.
One toddler cries in a nursery and others begin to cry or look worried without knowing why. Emotions pass quickly between very young children.

rows.subtype: Laughter and panic in a class [Actor]
rows.description: A giggle spreads through a classroom until nobody can stop, or a rumour of an exam change spreads worry through everyone. Feelings move through groups faster than facts.

rows.subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager at a match, concert or rally is swept up in the crowd's energy, feeling joy or anger that is not entirely their own. Shared feeling can be warm and can make them act unusually.

A toddler climbs into a lap, cuddles or holds a hand to seek comfort and closeness. This is a core way of feeling safe; warm, responsive touch supports secure attachment, and a child who pulls away should be respected.

A gentle stroke of the hand or hair between partners or close family conveys tenderness. It is welcome only with clear consent and context; if the other person stiffens or pulls away, stop and check in.

rows.subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
